_schema: life_bank — REAL encyclopedia concepts. Every entry traces to a real searched source (Wikipedia/web) with a verbatim quote (R5). NO invention (R12).
_provenance: Freshly harvested from real Wikipedia by 13 parallel branch-agents (Run 31 Phase 0) + merged-in REAL Run 29 life_bank (craft/sensory-skill, carries its own source+verbatim).

concepts.name: Counterpoint
concepts.summary_verbatim: Counterpoint is the relationship of two or more musical lines (also called voices or parts) that are harmonically interdependent yet independent in rhythm and contour.
mechanism_atoms: Multiple melodic voices move simultaneously, each preserving rhythmic and contour independence from the others
Voices are harmonically dependent — their combination must satisfy rules of consonance and dissonance resolution
The term derives from Latin punctus contra punctum ('point against point'), capturing the note-against-note logic
Species counterpoint codifies the technique in graded constraint levels, from note-against-note (first species) to florid (fifth species)
Imitation — one voice echoing another's melody at a time delay — is a primary structural tool, as in fugues and canons

concepts.name: Harmony
concepts.summary_verbatim: In music, harmony is the concept of combining different sounds in order to create new, distinct musical ideas.
mechanism_atoms: Harmony organizes simultaneous pitches into chords, which are categorized by consonance or dissonance
Tonal harmony operates through chord progressions that create tension (dominant) and resolution (tonic)
Voice leading rules govern how individual voices move between chords to minimize awkward leaps
Theories of harmony seek to describe or explain the effects created by distinct pitches or tones coinciding
Harmonic rhythm — the rate at which chords change — shapes the energy and momentum of a piece

concepts.name: Polyrhythm
concepts.summary_verbatim: Polyrhythm is the simultaneous use of two or more rhythms that are not readily perceived as deriving from one another, or as simple manifestations of the same meter.
mechanism_atoms: Two or more independent metric streams coexist simultaneously, creating cross-rhythmic tension
Common patterns include 3-against-2 (hemiola) and 4-against-3, where pulses align only at the lowest common multiple
The listener perceives both streams simultaneously rather than reducing one to an ornament of the other
Polyrhythm is structurally central to Sub-Saharan African music, where interlocking rhythmic layers form composite patterns
Displacement between onset points of the two rhythms creates syncopation and drives forward momentum

concepts.name: Equal Temperament
concepts.summary_verbatim: An equal temperament is a musical temperament or tuning system that approximates just intervals by dividing an octave (or other interval) into steps such that the ratio of the frequencies of any adjacent pair of notes is the same.
mechanism_atoms: The octave is divided into 12 equal logarithmic steps, each with frequency ratio equal to the 12th root of 2 (~1.0595)
All intervals except the octave are slightly detuned from pure just-intonation ratios, distributing tuning error evenly
Enharmonic equivalents (e.g., C# and Db) become identical pitches, enabling free modulation to all keys
The system trades perfect consonance in any one key for consistent (impure) consonance across all keys
Equal temperament became standard for keyboard instruments in the 18th–19th centuries, enabling composers like Bach to exploit distant key relationships

concepts.name: Syncopation
concepts.summary_verbatim: In music, syncopation is a variety of rhythms played together to make a piece of music, making part or all of a tune or piece of music off-beat.
mechanism_atoms: Accents are placed on normally weak beats or between beats, contradicting the established metric pulse
The tension between the expected downbeat and the displaced accent creates forward rhythmic drive
Syncopation is a defining feature of jazz, reggae, and funk, where the backbeat or offbeat carries the primary accent
Tied notes across barlines and rests on strong beats are common notational mechanisms for producing syncopation
Anticipation — sounding a note slightly before the beat it harmonically belongs to — is a common syncopation technique

concepts.name: Sonata Form
concepts.summary_verbatim: Sonata form (also sonata-allegro form or first movement form) is a musical structure generally consisting of three main sections: an exposition, a development, and a recapitulation.
mechanism_atoms: The exposition introduces two contrasting themes (or theme groups) in different keys, establishing tonal conflict
The development section transforms and fragments the thematic material through distant keys, heightening harmonic tension
The recapitulation restates both themes in the home (tonic) key, resolving the tonal conflict established in the exposition
A coda may follow, confirming the tonic and providing closure beyond the recapitulation
The structure enacts a narrative of departure, intensification, and return that organizes large-scale listener expectation

concepts.name: Fugue
concepts.summary_verbatim: In classical music, a fugue is a contrapuntal, polyphonic compositional technique in two or more voices, built on a subject (a musical theme) that is introduced at the beginning in imitation (repetition at different pitches), which recurs frequently throughout the course of the composition.
mechanism_atoms: A short subject is announced by one voice alone, then imitated successively by each remaining voice in the exposition
After each voice enters with the subject, it continues with a countersubject while the next voice takes the subject
Episodes between subject entries develop motifs from the subject through sequence and modulation, creating contrast
Stretto — overlapping entries of the subject before the previous entry completes — heightens contrapuntal density near climaxes
The fugue is regarded as the most fully developed procedure of imitative counterpoint since the 17th century

concepts.name: Leitmotif
concepts.summary_verbatim: A leitmotif or leitmotiv is a short, recurring musical phrase associated with a particular person, place, or idea.
mechanism_atoms: A brief melodic, harmonic, or rhythmic cell is assigned to a character, object, or concept, becoming its musical identifier
Recurrence of the motif signals the associated referent's presence or relevance, even when not visible on stage
The motif may be varied — in rhythm, harmony, orchestration — to reflect changes in the associated character or situation
Multiple leitmotifs can be combined contrapuntally to represent simultaneous dramatic conditions or relationships
Wagner's Der Ring des Nibelungen employs hundreds of leitmotifs, creating a continuous web of musical-dramatic cross-reference

concepts.name: Pentatonic Scale
concepts.summary_verbatim: A pentatonic scale is a musical scale with five notes per octave, in contrast to heptatonic scales, which have seven notes per octave (such as the major scale and minor scale).
mechanism_atoms: Five pitches span the octave, leaving gaps of a minor third (or larger) between some adjacent scale degrees
The absence of semitone adjacencies in the major pentatonic creates a tonally stable, open sound with few dissonant intervals
Pentatonic scales were developed independently by many ancient civilizations and remain prevalent worldwide
The minor pentatonic (root, minor 3rd, 4th, 5th, minor 7th) is foundational to blues and rock improvisation
Because any rotation of the pentatonic pattern avoids tritones and leading tones, melodies based on it are culturally versatile

concepts.name: Unreliable Narrator
concepts.summary_verbatim: An unreliable narrator is a narrator whose credibility is compromised.
mechanism_atoms: The narrator's account diverges from an implied 'true' version of events due to ignorance, mental illness, personal bias, or deliberate deception
The gap between what the narrator reports and what actually occurred becomes the site of dramatic irony and reader interpretation
Unreliability may be signaled immediately (an opening false claim) or revealed gradually through internal contradictions
Wayne C. Booth coined the term in The Rhetoric of Fiction (1961), distinguishing it from the implied author's perspective
The technique forces readers to actively construct meaning rather than passively accept narrated 'facts'

concepts.name: Foreshadowing
concepts.summary_verbatim: Foreshadowing is a narrative device in which suggestions or warnings about events to come are dropped or planted.
mechanism_atoms: Early textual signals — in dialogue, setting, or plot events — prime the reader to expect (or dread) future outcomes
Foreshadowing creates dramatic irony when the audience recognizes the signal before the character does
It operates across timescales: Chekhov's Gun prescribes that a detail introduced early must pay off later in the story
The device builds suspense by activating reader prediction, making the eventual event feel both surprising and inevitable
False foreshadowing (red herring) can be used to subvert expectations, deliberately misdirecting reader anticipation

concepts.name: Dramatic Structure (Freytag's Pyramid)
concepts.summary_verbatim: Dramatic structure is the structure of a dramatic work such as a play or film.
mechanism_atoms: Freytag's pyramid divides drama into five acts: exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, and catastrophe (dénouement)
Three crisis moments punctuate the arc: the exciting force (initiating conflict), the tragic force (complicating reversal), and the force of final suspense
Rising action accumulates complications and raises stakes; falling action disperses energy after the climactic peak
The structure maps tension as an arch — energy builds toward the midpoint climax, then declines through consequence
Gustav Freytag codified this model in Die Technik des Dramas (1863), analyzing Shakespearean five-act plays

concepts.name: In Medias Res
concepts.summary_verbatim: In medias res is a narrative technique in which a story opens in the middle or end rather than the beginning.
mechanism_atoms: The story begins at a point of high action or conflict, with backstory revealed later through analepsis (flashback)
The technique suppresses causal information initially, creating mystery and compelling forward engagement
It originates in ancient epic poetry — Homer's Iliad begins with the ninth year of the Trojan War
Horace described the device in Ars Poetica as beginning 'into the middle of things' (in mediās rēs)
Narrative momentum is maintained by granting the audience immediate immersion in consequence rather than setup

concepts.name: Iambic Pentameter
concepts.summary_verbatim: Iambic pentameter is the most common meter in English poetry.
mechanism_atoms: A line consists of five consecutive iambs — each an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed syllable — totaling ten syllables
The alternating weak-strong stress pattern creates a forward-pressing, speech-like rhythm
Variations (substitutions of trochees, spondees, or pyrrhics) at specific positions add expressive inflection without breaking the metrical contract
The caesura — a mid-line pause — divides the ten-syllable line and modulates pacing within the pattern
Blank verse uses iambic pentameter without end rhyme, while the sonnet enforces it with rhyme schemes

concepts.name: Rhyme Scheme
concepts.summary_verbatim: A rhyme scheme is the pattern of rhymes at the end of each line of a poem or song.
mechanism_atoms: Lines sharing end rhymes are labeled with the same letter (ABAB, ABBA, AABB, etc.) to map the sonic architecture
End rhyme creates aural expectation and satisfaction — the matching sound signals closure or continuation
Internal rhyme, assonance, and consonance extend sound-pattern organization within and across lines
Stanzaic forms (sonnet, villanelle, terza rima) prescribe fixed rhyme schemes that constrain and shape thought
The choice of rhyme scheme controls pacing: couplets (AA) accelerate closure; cross-rhyme (ABAB) sustains suspension across four lines

concepts.name: Color Theory
concepts.summary_verbatim: Color theory or colour theory is a body of practical guidance to color mixing and the visual effects of a specific color combination.
mechanism_atoms: Colors are organized on a color wheel based on hue relationships: primary, secondary, and tertiary
Complementary colors (opposite on the wheel) produce maximum contrast and mutual enhancement when juxtaposed
The attributes hue, saturation, and value independently control the character of a color
Advancing and receding colors (warm/cool) create spatial depth illusions on a flat surface
Major advances in color theory came from Bauhaus teachers including Itten, Albers, and Kandinsky in the early 20th century

concepts.name: Linear Perspective
concepts.summary_verbatim: Perspective (from Latin: perspicere 'to see through') in the graphic arts is an approximate representation, generally on a flat surface, of an image as it is seen by the eye.
mechanism_atoms: Parallel lines receding into the distance converge at a vanishing point on the horizon line, simulating depth
Objects appear smaller as distance from the viewer increases, following consistent foreshortening ratios
Brunelleschi demonstrated the technique around 1415, and Alberti codified it in De pictura (1435)
Multiple vanishing points (two-point, three-point perspective) capture objects seen from off-axis angles
Atmospheric perspective supplements linear perspective by rendering distant objects with reduced contrast and cooler hues

concepts.name: Chiaroscuro
concepts.summary_verbatim: Chiaroscuro is a technical term used by artists and art historians for the use of contrasts of light to achieve a sense of volume in modelling three-dimensional objects and figures.
mechanism_atoms: A single directional light source creates a gradient from highlight to shadow, implying three-dimensional roundness
Deep shadows (tenebrism) suppress background detail, isolating the lit subject against darkness
The technique was most fully developed in Baroque painting, associated with Caravaggio
Transitional mid-tones (sfumato) blend highlight and shadow without a sharp edge, as in Leonardo's technique
Chiaroscuro woodcut extended the technique to printmaking using multiple blocks with different colored inks

concepts.name: Impasto
concepts.summary_verbatim: Impasto is a technique used in painting where paint is laid on an area of the surface thickly, usually thick enough that the brush or painting-knife strokes are visible.
mechanism_atoms: Raised paint surfaces cast micro-shadows, adding literal texture that interacts with raking light in real space
The visible brushstroke becomes an expressive record of the artist's gesture and the speed of application
Palette-knife application creates flat, sharp-edged planes of color distinct from the modulated marks of brushwork
Van Gogh and Rembrandt used impasto to concentrate visual weight and energy at points of pictorial emphasis
In oil painting, body can be added with mediums like stand oil; in acrylic, gel mediums extend working time and thickness

concepts.name: Rib Vault
concepts.summary_verbatim: A rib vault or ribbed vault is an architectural feature for covering a wide space, such as a church nave, composed of a framework of crossed or diagonal arched ribs.
mechanism_atoms: Diagonal stone ribs form a skeletal arch-framework that carries the vault's weight to discrete piers rather than along the full wall
The ribs subdivide the vaulted surface into webs (severies) filled with lighter infill masonry, reducing overall mass
By concentrating loads at piers, rib vaulting enables large windows between piers — central to Gothic luminosity
Ribs are constructed first as falsework guides; the lighter web panels are then built between them
Elaborations such as lierne and fan vaults multiply rib networks for decorative effect while retaining the structural principle

concepts.name: Flying Buttress
concepts.summary_verbatim: A flying buttress (arc-boutant, arch buttress) is a specific form of buttress composed of an arched structure that extends from the upper portion of a wall to a pier of great mass, in order to convey to the ground the lateral forces that push a wall outward.
mechanism_atoms: The barrel-vault ceiling of a Gothic nave exerts outward lateral thrust on the upper walls; the flying buttress intercepts this thrust
A curved half-arch (the flier) carries force outward and downward to a massive outer pier (the culée), bypassing the lower wall
Because the outer pier absorbs lateral thrust, the nave wall between ground and clearstory is freed for large stained-glass windows
Pinnacles atop the outer pier add downward compressive load, stabilizing the pier against the inclined thrust of the flier
Flying buttresses became a defining structural and visual characteristic of French Gothic cathedrals from the 12th century onward

concepts.name: Tensegrity
concepts.summary_verbatim: Tensegrity, tensional integrity or floating compression is a structural principle based on a system of isolated components under compression inside a network of continuous tension.
mechanism_atoms: Rigid compression members (struts) do not touch each other; they float within a continuous web of tension elements (cables)
Global stability arises from the geometry of the tension network rather than from rigid joints between members
The structure distributes applied loads throughout the entire tension network, avoiding local stress concentration
Buckminster Fuller coined the term as a portmanteau of 'tensional integrity' in the 1960s
Biological analogs include the musculoskeletal system, where bones (compression) are suspended in connective tissue (tension)

concepts.name: Dome
concepts.summary_verbatim: A dome is an architectural element similar to the hollow upper half of a sphere.
mechanism_atoms: The curved shell converts applied downward load into compressive hoop stresses that follow the dome's meridians
Lateral outward thrust at the dome's base must be resisted by a compression ring, drum, or buttressing walls
Oculi (central openings) reduce weight at the apex and redirect forces around the opening through ring compression
Coffered domes (e.g., the Pantheon) reduce mass while preserving structural geometry through grid-pattern recesses
Double-shell domes (e.g., St. Paul's Cathedral) separate the inner decorative surface from the outer weathering shell, with a structural cone between

concepts.name: Labanotation
concepts.summary_verbatim: Labanotation or Kinetography Laban is a notation system for recording and analyzing human movement.
mechanism_atoms: Movement is notated on a vertical staff read from bottom to top (time flows upward), paralleling music notation's left-to-right convention
Symbols encode body part, direction, level (high/middle/low), and duration simultaneously in a single cell
The staff's central column represents the body's center; left and right columns specify lateral limb actions
Duration is conveyed by symbol length, allowing rhythmic relationships between body parts to be read at a glance
The system was developed by Rudolf Laban and enables dances to be reconstructed long after their original performance

concepts.name: Montage (Filmmaking)
concepts.summary_verbatim: Montage is a film editing technique in which a series of short shots are sequenced to condense space, time, and information.
mechanism_atoms: Placing two unrelated shots in sequence causes viewers to infer a relationship or meaning not present in either shot alone (Kuleshov effect)
Eisenstein theorized that shots in collision — intellectual montage — produce a conceptual 'third meaning' beyond both images
Rhythmic montage cuts on beat, aligning shot lengths with a musical or emotional pulse
Thematic montage links shots by metaphor or symbolic association rather than spatial or temporal continuity
The technique condenses narrative time: a training sequence or journey can be compressed to seconds through selected keyframe shots

concepts.name: Continuity Editing
concepts.summary_verbatim: Continuity editing is the predominant style of film editing and video editing in the post-production process of filmmaking of narrative films and television programs.
mechanism_atoms: The 180-degree rule establishes an imaginary axis between subjects; camera stays on one side to maintain consistent screen direction
Match cuts (on action, on eyeline, on graphic form) bridge two shots so the cut is perceptually invisible
Shot/reverse-shot patterns construct conversation by alternating between speakers without disorienting the viewer
The 30-degree rule specifies a minimum camera angle change between consecutive shots of the same subject to avoid jump cuts
Consistent eyeline match — characters looking in complementary screen directions — preserves the spatial logic of the scene

concepts.name: Typography
concepts.summary_verbatim: Typography is the art and technique of arranging type to make written language legible, readable and appealing when displayed.
mechanism_atoms: Legibility refers to the distinctiveness of individual letterforms; readability refers to the ease of reading continuous text
Typeface selection (serif vs. sans-serif, weight, x-height) affects both legibility at small sizes and tone of voice
Type hierarchy — size, weight, and spacing variations — guides reader attention through layers of information
Leading (line spacing), tracking (letter spacing), and kerning (pair-specific spacing) control the density and rhythm of text blocks
Contrast between type and background is a primary legibility determinant, governed by accessible contrast ratio standards

concepts.name: Call and Response (Music)
concepts.summary_verbatim: In music, call and response is a compositional technique where there is a succession of two distinct phrases usually written in different parts of the music, where the second phrase is heard as a direct commentary on or response to the first.
mechanism_atoms: A 'call' phrase by one voice or section is followed by an 'answer' phrase from a different voice or section
The technique structures music as a dialogue, with each response completing, contrasting, or intensifying the call
In African-American musical traditions (blues, gospel, jazz), call-and-response organizes both vocal and instrumental interaction
The response may imitate, invert, or vary the call's melodic contour, creating variation-within-repetition
At the large scale, antiphonal music (two choirs in alternation) applies the same dialogic structure to entire ensembles

concepts.name: Tessellation
concepts.summary_verbatim: A tessellation or tiling is the covering of a surface, often a plane, using one or more geometric shapes, called tiles, with no overlaps and no gaps.
mechanism_atoms: Regular tessellations use a single regular polygon; only equilateral triangles, squares, and regular hexagons tile the plane without gaps
Semi-regular tessellations combine two or more regular polygons in a repeating vertex configuration
The symmetry group of a tessellation describes its invariant transformations: translation, rotation, reflection, and glide-reflection
Aperiodic tessellations (Penrose tilings) tile the plane without repeating, using matching rules that enforce long-range order
Escher's graphic art famously exploited tessellation by using figurative (animal, human) tiles that interlock seamlessly

concepts.name: Golden Ratio
concepts.summary_verbatim: In mathematics, two quantities are in the golden ratio if their ratio is the same as the ratio of their sum to the larger of the two quantities.
mechanism_atoms: The ratio φ ≈ 1.618 is the unique value where a line segment divided such that the whole is to the larger part as the larger is to the smaller
A golden rectangle can be subdivided recursively — removing a square leaves a smaller golden rectangle — producing a self-similar spiral
Consecutive Fibonacci numbers (1,1,2,3,5,8,13…) converge to φ as ratios, connecting the ratio to natural growth patterns
Architects and artists including Le Corbusier and Salvador Dalí have proportioned works to approximate φ believing it aesthetically pleasing
The golden ratio appears in the regular pentagon's diagonal-to-side ratio, linking it to pentagonal symmetry in art and design

concepts.name: Plate tectonics
concepts.summary_verbatim: Plate tectonics is the scientific theory that Earth's lithosphere comprises a number of large tectonic plates, which have been slowly moving since 3–4 billion years ago.
mechanism_atoms: The lithosphere is divided into rigid plates that move atop the ductile asthenosphere driven by slab pull, ridge push, and viscous drag from mantle convection.
Slab pull: when cold, dense oceanic lithosphere subducts it pulls the trailing plate toward the trench under its own gravitational weight.
Ridge push: hot buoyant mantle rising at mid-ocean ridges creates elevated seafloor that pushes plates laterally outward.
Plates diverge at mid-ocean ridges (creating new crust), converge at subduction zones and collision belts (destroying or deforming crust), and slide past each other at transform faults.
Seafloor spreading continuously generates new oceanic crust at divergent boundaries, while older crust is recycled into the mantle at convergent boundaries, completing the Wilson cycle.

concepts.name: Subduction
concepts.summary_verbatim: Subduction is a geological process in which the oceanic lithosphere and some continental lithosphere is recycled into the Earth's mantle at the convergent boundaries between tectonic plates.
mechanism_atoms: Cold, rigid oceanic lithosphere is slightly denser than the underlying asthenosphere, providing the negative buoyancy that allows it to sink.
Where two plates converge, the denser plate dives beneath the other and descends into the mantle along a steeply inclined slab.
The subducting slab releases water at depth, lowering the melting point of the overlying mantle wedge and generating calc-alkaline magma that rises to form volcanic arcs.
Slab pull—the gravitational weight of the cold, dense descending slab—is generally considered the dominant force driving plate motion.
Rates of convergence can reach 11 cm/year; the process has created most of Earth's continental crust over geological time.

concepts.name: Seafloor spreading
concepts.summary_verbatim: Seafloor spreading, or seafloor spread, is a process that occurs at mid-ocean ridges, where new oceanic crust is formed through volcanic activity and then gradually moves away from the ridge.
mechanism_atoms: At mid-ocean ridges, convecting mantle upwells in response to plate separation, partially melting to produce basaltic magma.
Magma rises through the linear weakness between separating plates and solidifies as new oceanic crust and lithosphere upon cooling.
Newly formed crust is symmetrically added on both sides of the ridge axis and spreads laterally, recording the history of geomagnetic reversals in magnetic stripes.
The elevated topography of ridges results from the thermal buoyancy of the hot underlying mantle; as the crust ages and cools it subsides.
Seafloor spreading was the key evidence that validated plate tectonics theory in the mid- to late 1960s.

concepts.name: Mantle convection
concepts.summary_verbatim: Mantle convection is the very slow creep of Earth's solid silicate mantle as convection currents carry heat from the interior to the planet's surface.
mechanism_atoms: Radioactive decay and residual primordial heat in Earth's deep interior create a thermal gradient; hot rock at depth is less dense than cooler rock above.
This density difference drives buoyancy-driven upwelling of hot material and downwelling of cooler, denser material over timescales of hundreds of millions of years.
The mantle behaves as a highly viscous fluid on geological timescales, allowing slow plastic deformation despite being solid at short timescales.
Upwelling limbs of convection cells supply hot material beneath mid-ocean ridges; downwelling limbs correspond to subducting slabs.
Mantle convection is the fundamental energy source that drives plate tectonics, and it also redistributes heat through the crust via mantle plumes.

concepts.name: Hotspot (geology)
concepts.summary_verbatim: In geology, hotspots (or hot spots) are volcanic locales thought to be fed by underlying mantle that is anomalously hot compared with the surrounding mantle.
mechanism_atoms: One hypothesis proposes that hotspots are fed by mantle plumes—narrow, thermally buoyant upwellings that rise as thermal diapirs from the core–mantle boundary.
As the hot plume head rises and reaches shallower depths, pressure decreases and adiabatic decompression causes partial melting of the mantle rock.
Magma produced by the plume penetrates the overlying lithosphere and erupts at the surface, building volcanic structures.
Because the tectonic plate moves over the relatively stationary hotspot, a time-progressive chain of volcanoes forms, such as the Hawaiian–Emperor seamount chain.
The products of hotspot volcanism—ocean island basalts (OIB)—have distinct isotopic compositions that distinguish them from mid-ocean ridge basalts.

concepts.name: Mantle plume
concepts.summary_verbatim: A mantle plume is a proposed mechanism of convection within the Earth's mantle, hypothesized to explain anomalous volcanism.
mechanism_atoms: A plume originates as a thermal diapir that detaches from the thermal boundary layer at the core–mantle boundary (D'' layer) and rises buoyantly through the mantle.
The plume head, which can be enormous, partially melts upon ascending to shallower depths due to adiabatic decompression.
Flood basalt provinces (large igneous provinces) are linked to the arrival of a plume head at the base of the lithosphere.
A thinner plume tail continues supplying magma after the head has dissipated, feeding long-lived hotspot volcanism.
Plumes are inferred from seismic tomography, geochemical anomalies in OIBs, and surface topographic swells surrounding hotspots.

concepts.name: Seismology
concepts.summary_verbatim: Seismology (from Ancient Greek σεισμός (seismós), meaning 'earthquake', and -λογία (-logía), meaning 'study of') is the scientific study of earthquakes (or generally, quakes) and the generation and propagation of elastic waves through planetary bodies.
mechanism_atoms: Earthquakes occur when accumulated elastic strain energy along faults is released suddenly as the rocks rupture and slip, radiating seismic waves in all directions.
P-waves (compressional) travel fastest, alternately compressing and dilating the medium along their propagation direction, and can pass through both solids and liquids.
S-waves (shear) travel at roughly 60% of P-wave speed, displacing the medium perpendicular to propagation, and can only travel through solids.
Surface waves (Love and Rayleigh) travel along the Earth's surface and have lower frequencies but often cause the greatest ground shaking.
Seismic wave velocities depend on the density and elastic moduli of the medium, allowing tomographic imaging of Earth's interior structure.

concepts.name: Isostasy
concepts.summary_verbatim: Isostasy (from Greek ísos 'equal' and stásis 'standstill') or isostatic equilibrium is the state of gravitational equilibrium between Earth's crust (or lithosphere) and mantle such that the crust 'floats' at an elevation that depends on its thickness and density.
mechanism_atoms: The crust behaves like a buoyant block floating on the denser, viscous mantle; thicker or less dense crustal columns stand higher (Airy isostasy).
Pratt isostasy explains lateral topographic variation by differences in crustal density rather than thickness alone.
When a load is added (e.g., an ice sheet or mountain range), the crust depresses; when the load is removed, the crust rebounds toward equilibrium.
The mantle's viscosity means isostatic adjustment is time-dependent—complete equilibration can take thousands to tens of thousands of years.
Post-glacial rebound following ice-sheet melting is a direct, measurable expression of isostatic adjustment, with ongoing uplift rates of ~1 cm/year in formerly glaciated regions.

concepts.name: Post-glacial rebound
concepts.summary_verbatim: Post-glacial rebound (also called isostatic rebound or crustal rebound) is the rise of land masses after the removal of the huge weight of ice sheets during the last glacial period, which had caused isostatic depression.
mechanism_atoms: Massive ice sheets (up to 3–4 km thick) loaded the crust and depressed it isostatically into the viscous asthenosphere during glacial maxima.
As ice melted at the end of the last glacial period (~20,000–10,000 years ago), the load was removed and the crust began to recover.
Rebound occurs in two phases: an initial near-instantaneous elastic rebound as the ice unloads, followed by a slow viscous flow of the asthenosphere back under the uplifting crust.
Because mantle viscosity is very high, full isostatic equilibrium has not yet been reached; uplift continues today at rates up to several mm/year in Scandinavia and Canada.
Rebound affects sea level (relative sea level may fall where uplift exceeds eustatic rise), geoid shape, and can trigger earthquakes and volcanic activity.

concepts.name: River delta
concepts.summary_verbatim: A river delta is a landform, typically triangular, created by the deposition of the sediments that are carried by the waters of a river, where the river merges with a body of slow-moving water or with a body of stagnant water.
mechanism_atoms: As a river enters a standing body of water its velocity and sediment-carrying capacity drop abruptly, causing bedload and suspended sediment to deposit.
The river distributary network builds outward into the receiving basin, with avulsion events periodically shifting the dominant lobe as sediment chokes channels.
Delta morphology is controlled by the balance of fluvial sediment supply, wave energy, tidal energy, and basin subsidence.
Compaction of fine-grained deltaic sediments causes subsidence, which, combined with eustatic sea-level change and sediment starvation, leads to delta land loss.
Sedimentary facies in a delta prograde in predictable vertical sequences (coarsening-upward cycles) that are used to reconstruct ancient depositional environments.

concepts.name: Crystallization
concepts.summary_verbatim: Crystallization occurs in two main phases: the first is nucleation, the appearance of a crystalline phase from either a supercooled liquid or a supersaturated solvent; the second step is known as crystal growth, which is the increase in size of particles and leads to a crystal state.
mechanism_atoms: Nucleation begins when random thermal fluctuations in a supersaturated or supercooled medium produce a cluster of atoms or ions large enough (critical nucleus) to be thermodynamically stable.
Homogeneous nucleation occurs in the bulk liquid; heterogeneous nucleation (far more common) occurs on surfaces, impurities, or pre-existing crystals, requiring less free energy.
Once a stable nucleus forms, crystal growth proceeds by attachment of solute atoms or molecules to the growing lattice surfaces, propagating the ordered crystal structure outward.
Growth rate is governed by diffusion of material to the crystal surface and by the rate of incorporation into the lattice; temperature and degree of supersaturation control which step is limiting.
In igneous geology, cooling rate determines crystal size: slow cooling yields large crystals (plutonic rock); rapid quenching yields microcrystalline or glassy textures.

concepts.name: Stellar nucleosynthesis
concepts.summary_verbatim: In astrophysics, stellar nucleosynthesis is the creation of chemical elements by nuclear fusion reactions within stars.
mechanism_atoms: In low- to intermediate-mass main-sequence stars (≤1.3 solar masses), hydrogen fuses to helium via the proton–proton chain, releasing energy that supports the star against gravitational collapse.
In more massive stars (>1.3 solar masses), the CNO cycle dominates hydrogen burning, using carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen as catalysts.

After hydrogen exhaustion, stars fuse helium into carbon and oxygen (triple-alpha process); successive burning stages in massive stars fuse heavier elements up to iron, releasing progressively less energy.
Elements heavier than iron are produced by neutron capture: the s-process (slow, in AGB stars) and the r-process (rapid, in neutron star mergers and core-collapse supernovae).
Supernovae and stellar winds disperse newly synthesized elements into the interstellar medium, where they become incorporated into subsequent generations of stars and planets.

concepts.name: Stellar evolution
concepts.summary_verbatim: Stellar evolution is the process by which a star changes over the course of time.
mechanism_atoms: A protostar forms when a dense region of a molecular cloud collapses under gravity, converting gravitational potential energy to thermal energy until hydrogen fusion ignites in the core.
On the main sequence, the star is in hydrostatic equilibrium: thermal pressure from core fusion balances gravitational contraction; stars remain here for most of their lives.
When core hydrogen is exhausted, the core contracts while the outer envelope expands and cools, evolving the star off the main sequence into the red giant or red supergiant branch.
Low- to intermediate-mass stars shed their outer envelopes as planetary nebulae, leaving a white dwarf; massive stars end in core-collapse supernovae, leaving neutron stars or black holes.
A star's initial mass is the primary determinant of its evolutionary track and lifetime: more massive stars burn faster and live shorter lives (Vogt–Russell theorem).

concepts.name: Main sequence
concepts.summary_verbatim: In astronomy, the main sequence is a classification of stars which appear on plots of stellar color versus brightness as a continuous and distinctive band.
mechanism_atoms: Stars on the main sequence derive their luminosity from hydrogen fusion in their cores, with the rate of fusion self-regulated by the balance between thermal pressure and gravity (hydrostatic equilibrium).
More luminous (and hotter) main-sequence stars have higher core temperatures that sustain faster fusion rates, making them more massive but shorter-lived.
The main sequence occupies a diagonal band on the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram running from hot, luminous O-type stars to cool, faint M-type red dwarfs.
A star settles onto the zero-age main sequence (ZAMS) once nuclear burning supplants gravitational contraction as the primary energy source.

Stars gradually evolve toward higher luminosity along the main sequence as hydrogen is depleted in the core and the stellar structure adjusts, eventually departing the main sequence when the core hydrogen is exhausted.

concepts.name: Orbital resonance
concepts.branch: earth & space science / astronomy / celestial mechanics
concepts.summary_verbatim: In celestial mechanics, an orbital resonance occurs when two orbiting bodies exert a regular, periodic gravitational influence on each other, usually due to their orbital periods being related by a ratio of two small integers.
mechanism_atoms: When two bodies' orbital periods are in a simple integer ratio (e.g., 1:2 or 2:3), they experience periodic, regularly spaced gravitational kicks that can reinforce each other over many orbits.
Mean-motion resonances (MMRs) are the most common type; the Laplace resonance of Io–Europa–Ganymede (1:2:4) is a prominent three-body example.

Resonances can be stabilizing (trapping bodies in resonant configurations and maintaining orbit stability) or destabilizing (driving chaotic orbital evolution and clearing resonance gaps such as the Kirkwood gaps in the asteroid belt).
Conjunctions between resonant bodies always recur at the same orbital locations, causing orbital eccentricities to be pumped up and maintained against tidal dissipation.
Tidal heating of Io results from eccentricity forced by the Laplace resonance, demonstrating how orbital resonance converts gravitational perturbations into internal geologic energy.

concepts.name: Density wave theory
concepts.branch: earth & space science / astronomy / galactic dynamics
concepts.summary_verbatim: Density wave theory or the Lin–Shu density wave theory is a theory proposed by C.C. Lin and Frank Shu in the mid-1960s to explain the spiral arm structure of spiral galaxies.
mechanism_atoms: Spiral arms in galaxies are not fixed material structures but quasi-stationary density waves—regions of temporarily enhanced density that rotate with a characteristic pattern speed.
Stars and gas in the galactic disk orbit at varying speeds that depend on their distance from the galactic center; the spiral pattern rotates more slowly than most of the disk material.
As stars orbit through the slower-moving density wave, they linger in the arm region, producing a visible overdensity even though the stellar membership of the arm constantly changes.
Gas clouds entering the compression zone of a spiral arm experience shocks that trigger star formation, explaining why spiral arms are bright with young, hot stars and HII regions.

Differential rotation that would otherwise wind up any material arm into oblivion within a few galactic rotations is overcome because the density wave pattern is maintained by self-gravity of the disk.

concepts.name: Dark matter halo
concepts.summary_verbatim: In modern models of physical cosmology, a dark matter halo is a basic unit of cosmological structure.
mechanism_atoms: Dark matter halos form when primordial density fluctuations in the early universe grow under gravity, decouple from the Hubble expansion, and collapse into gravitationally bound structures.
The halo extends far beyond the visible disk of a galaxy, roughly spherically distributed, and constitutes the majority (~95%) of the galaxy's total mass.

Observational evidence comes from galaxy rotation curves: without a massive dark matter halo the circular velocity of disk stars would decrease with distance from the center, but it is observed to remain flat or rise.
The NFW (Navarro–Frenk–White) profile from N-body simulations describes the density distribution of dark matter halos as cuspy in the center and falling as r^{-3} at large radii.
Halos serve as gravitational scaffolds within which baryonic matter accumulates to form galaxies; the mass of the halo strongly correlates with the properties of its central galaxy.

concepts.name: Atmospheric circulation
concepts.summary_verbatim: Atmospheric circulation is the large-scale movement of air and together with ocean circulation is the means by which thermal energy is redistributed on the surface of Earth.
mechanism_atoms: Differential solar heating between equatorial and polar regions creates temperature and pressure gradients that drive large-scale atmospheric flow.
The atmosphere is organized into three meridional circulation cells in each hemisphere: the Hadley cell (0–30°), Ferrel cell (30–60°), and Polar cell (60–90°).
Earth's rotation deflects moving air via the Coriolis effect, converting poleward pressure-gradient-driven flow into predominantly zonal (east–west) winds.
Jet streams—narrow, fast-flowing air currents at the tropopause—mark the boundaries between circulation cells and steer mid-latitude weather systems.
The general circulation transports latent heat poleward through moisture, sensible heat through temperature advection, and potential energy through the movement of air masses.

concepts.name: Hadley cell
concepts.summary_verbatim: A Hadley cell is a thermally direct circulation within the troposphere that emerges due to differences in insolation and heating between the tropics and the subtropics.
mechanism_atoms: Intense solar heating at the equator warms surface air, causing it to rise in the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ), releasing latent heat from condensation of tropical moisture.
Ascending air spreads poleward at the upper troposphere, cools radiatively, and subsides at around 30° latitude, creating the subtropical high-pressure belts and associated deserts.
Descending dry air at ~30° flows back equatorward along the surface as the trade winds, which are deflected westward by the Coriolis effect.
The upper-level poleward branch is accelerated by conservation of angular momentum and the Coriolis effect, producing the subtropical jet stream at the Hadley cell's poleward boundary.

The Hadley cell controls the distribution of the world's tropical rainforests (at the ITCZ) and subtropical deserts (at the descending limb), and its width has been expanding poleward in recent decades.

concepts.name: Jet stream
concepts.summary_verbatim: A jet stream is a fast flowing, relatively narrow air current found at the tropopause, the transition between the troposphere (where temperature decreases with height) and the stratosphere (where temperature increases with height).
mechanism_atoms: Jet streams form at the boundaries of adjacent air masses with strong horizontal temperature contrasts; the thermal wind relation requires increasing westerly wind shear with altitude where horizontal temperature gradients exist.

The polar jet (50–60°) forms at the Polar/Ferrel cell boundary and is strongest in winter when the equator-to-pole temperature gradient is largest; the subtropical jet (~30°) forms at the Hadley/Ferrel boundary.
Wind speeds in jet streams commonly exceed 90 km/h and can surpass 400 km/h; the highest speeds occur where temperature gradients are most intense.
Jet streams steer extratropical cyclones and anticyclones, controlling the track, speed, and development of mid-latitude weather systems.
Meandering of the polar jet stream (Rossby waves) creates persistent blocks and troughs that cause extended periods of anomalous weather in affected regions.

concepts.name: Weather front
concepts.summary_verbatim: A weather front is a boundary separating air masses for which several characteristics differ, such as air density, wind, temperature, and humidity.
mechanism_atoms: A front forms where two air masses with contrasting temperature and moisture properties converge; the denser (colder) air undercuts the warmer air, producing a sloping boundary layer.
At a warm front, warm air rises gradually over cold air along a gentle slope (~1:150 ratio), producing a wide band of stratiform cloud and steady precipitation.
At a cold front, cold air advances rapidly and undercuts warm air more steeply (~1:50 ratio), lifting it sharply to produce intense, narrow bands of convective cloud and heavy precipitation.
Occluded fronts form when a faster-moving cold front overtakes a warm front, cutting the warm air sector off from the surface and lifting it entirely above the ground.
Frontogenesis (front intensification) occurs when deformation flow in the atmosphere enhances horizontal temperature gradients, tightening the frontal zone.

concepts.name: Thunderstorm
concepts.summary_verbatim: A thunderstorm, also known as an electrical storm or a lightning storm, is a storm characterized by the presence of lightning and thunder.
mechanism_atoms: Three conditions are required: atmospheric moisture (fuel), an unstable temperature lapse rate (lifting), and a trigger mechanism (surface heating, frontal lifting, or orographic uplift).
Warm, moist surface air rises in a convective updraft; water vapor condenses, releasing latent heat that makes the updraft buoyant and drives further ascent—a self-reinforcing process.
In the mature stage, ice crystals in the upper anvil and graupel in the middle levels separate charge via collisions (non-inductive charging), building a strong electric dipole.
When the electric field exceeds the air's dielectric strength (~1 MV/m), a stepped leader propagates downward and a return stroke (lightning bolt) neutralizes the charge.

Downdrafts initiated by precipitation drag and evaporative cooling eventually undercut the updraft, ending the storm unless wind shear tilts the updraft so it is separated from the rain-cooled outflow (supercell organization).

concepts.name: Thermohaline circulation
concepts.summary_verbatim: Thermohaline circulation (THC) is a part of the large-scale ocean circulation driven by global density gradients formed by surface heat and freshwater fluxes.
mechanism_atoms: Seawater density depends on both temperature (thermo) and salinity (haline); cold, salty water is densest and sinks to drive deep-water circulation.

In polar regions (especially the North Atlantic and Southern Ocean), surface cooling and sea-ice formation increase the salinity and density of surface water, causing it to sink to form deep water masses (NADW and AABW).
Deep water flows equatorward along the ocean floor, gradually mixing with surrounding water and upwelling in the Indian and Pacific Oceans, completing a circuit taking ~1,000 years.

The return flow of warm, relatively fresh surface water toward the poles (e.g., the Gulf Stream system as part of AMOC) transports significant amounts of heat poleward, moderating high-latitude climates.
Freshwater influx (e.g., from melting ice sheets) can reduce surface density in deep-water formation regions, potentially weakening or collapsing the circulation—a major climate tipping point.

concepts.name: Atlantic meridional overturning circulation
concepts.summary_verbatim: The Atlantic meridional overturning circulation (AMOC) is the main ocean current system in the Atlantic Ocean.
mechanism_atoms: AMOC consists of a northward surface flow of warm, saltier water in the upper Atlantic (including the Gulf Stream) and a compensating southward flow of cold, denser deep water.
Deep water formation occurs primarily in the Labrador Sea and the Nordic Seas, where intense winter cooling and brine rejection (during sea-ice formation) drive convection and sinking.
The density contrast between the sinking high-latitude water and the warmer, lighter subtropical water provides the pressure gradient that sustains the overturning circulation.
AMOC transports roughly 1.3 petawatts of heat northward across 26°N, keeping northern Europe significantly warmer than it would otherwise be at its latitude.
Paleoclimate evidence shows that AMOC has weakened or collapsed during past cold events (e.g., Younger Dryas), causing abrupt regional and global climate shifts.

concepts.name: Glacier mass balance
concepts.summary_verbatim: A glacier's mass balance or surface mass balance (SMB)—the difference between accumulation and ablation (sublimation and melting)—is crucial to the survival of the glacier.
mechanism_atoms: Accumulation occurs in the upper glacier where snowfall, wind-blown snow, and avalanche inputs add mass; compression of snow through firn into glacial ice stores accumulated mass.

Ablation occurs in the lower glacier via surface melting (dominant), sublimation, calving of icebergs, and basal melt; the equilibrium line altitude (ELA) separates the accumulation and ablation zones.
When annual accumulation exceeds ablation the glacier gains mass and advances; when ablation exceeds accumulation it thins and retreats.

Ice flows from the accumulation zone toward the ablation zone under gravity, driven by internal deformation (creep) and basal sliding; this flow transfers mass from where it accumulates to where it melts.
Glacier mass balance is a sensitive indicator of climate change; global glacier mass loss contributes to sea-level rise, with the cryosphere losing mass at an accelerating rate.

concepts.name: Ice-sheet dynamics
concepts.summary_verbatim: In glaciology, an ice sheet, also known as a continental glacier, is a mass of glacial ice that covers surrounding terrain and is greater than 50,000 km² (19,000 sq mi).
mechanism_atoms: Ice flows outward from the central plateau toward the margins driven by the difference in surface slope between the high-accumulation interior and the lower-accumulation, higher-ablation edges.
Ice deforms internally by viscous creep (Glen's flow law) in response to shear stress; deformation rate increases nonlinearly with stress.
Basal sliding occurs where the ice-bed interface is at the pressure melting point, lubricated by a thin film of meltwater or deformable subglacial sediment, dramatically accelerating ice flow.
Ice streams are fast-flowing channels (tens to hundreds of km/year) within the ice sheet that drain the interior through topographic troughs, responsible for most mass loss from ice sheets.

Marine ice sheets grounded below sea level are vulnerable to marine ice sheet instability: once the grounding line retreats into deeper water, ice discharge accelerates in a self-reinforcing feedback (MISI).

concepts.name: Carbon cycle
concepts.branch: earth & space science / climatology / earth systems
concepts.summary_verbatim: The carbon cycle is a part of the biogeochemical cycle where carbon is exchanged among the biosphere, pedosphere, geosphere, hydrosphere, and atmosphere of Earth.
mechanism_atoms: Photosynthesis removes CO₂ from the atmosphere, fixing it into organic biomass; cellular respiration and decomposition return it to the atmosphere as CO₂.
The ocean absorbs roughly 2.9 Pg C/year from the atmosphere via dissolution (solubility pump) and biological uptake (biological pump), which exports organic carbon to depth.
Chemical weathering of silicate rocks consumes CO₂ to form bicarbonate ions, which rivers carry to the ocean where they precipitate as carbonate sediments—a long-term (million-year) carbon sink.
Volcanic and metamorphic outgassing returns CO₂ from the geosphere to the atmosphere, balancing the weathering sink over geological timescales (Urey reaction / GEOCARB cycle).

Climate–carbon feedbacks are important: warming reduces ocean and terrestrial carbon uptake efficiency, amplifying greenhouse warming (positive climate–carbon feedback); conversely, higher CO₂ stimulates plant growth (concentration–carbon negative feedback).

concepts.name: Climate change feedbacks
concepts.summary_verbatim: A feedback that amplifies an initial change is called a positive feedback while a feedback that reduces an initial change is called a negative feedback.
mechanism_atoms: Water-vapor feedback: warming increases atmospheric water vapor (a greenhouse gas), amplifying initial warming—the largest positive climate feedback (~1.8 W m⁻² K⁻¹).
Ice–albedo feedback: warming melts reflective ice and snow, exposing darker ocean or land surfaces that absorb more solar energy, further warming the climate.
Planck (blackbody) feedback is the dominant negative feedback: a warmer planet radiates more longwave energy to space, acting as a restoring force toward equilibrium.
Cloud feedbacks remain the largest source of uncertainty: low-level clouds decrease under warming (net positive feedback), while high-altitude cirrus changes are complex.
Carbon-cycle feedbacks include permafrost thaw releasing stored methane and CO₂ (positive), reduced ocean CO₂ solubility at higher temperatures (positive), and enhanced vegetation uptake (negative).

concepts.name: PID controller
concepts.summary_verbatim: A proportional–integral–derivative controller (PID controller or three-term controller) is a control loop mechanism employing feedback that is widely used in industrial control systems and a variety of other applications requiring continuously modulated control.
mechanism_atoms: The controller continuously calculates an error value as the difference between a desired setpoint and a measured process variable.
A proportional term applies a correction scaled directly to the current error magnitude.
An integral term sums past errors over time to eliminate steady-state offset.
A derivative term predicts future error by acting on the rate of change of the error signal.
The three terms are summed to produce a single output that drives the actuator toward the setpoint.

concepts.name: Centrifugal governor
concepts.summary_verbatim: A centrifugal governor is a specific type of governor with a feedback system that controls the speed of an engine by regulating the flow of fuel or working fluid, so as to maintain a near-constant speed.
mechanism_atoms: Two weighted balls are mounted on arms linked to a rotating spindle driven by the engine output shaft.
As rotational speed increases, centrifugal force causes the balls to fly outward and upward.
The outward displacement of the balls mechanically closes a throttle or fuel valve via linkages.
Reduced fuel or steam flow slows the engine, causing balls to drop back down and reopen the valve.
This forms a closed proportional-control feedback loop that maintains near-constant speed.

concepts.name: Phase-locked loop
concepts.summary_verbatim: A phase-locked loop or phase lock loop (PLL) is a control system that generates an output signal with a frequency that is locked to the frequency of an input signal, using phase differences between the two to lock them to each other.
mechanism_atoms: A phase detector compares the phase of the input reference signal to the phase of the voltage-controlled oscillator (VCO) output.
The phase detector outputs a voltage proportional to the phase difference between the two signals.
This error voltage is low-pass filtered to remove high-frequency components and fed back to the VCO.
The filtered error voltage adjusts the VCO frequency until phase error approaches zero (locked state).
In locked state, the output frequency tracks the input reference frequency with minimal phase offset.

concepts.name: Transformer (electrical device)
concepts.summary_verbatim: In electrical engineering, a transformer is a passive component that transfers electrical energy from one electrical circuit to another circuit, or multiple circuits.
mechanism_atoms: A varying current in the primary coil produces a varying magnetic flux in the transformer core.
By Faraday's law, the changing flux induces a varying electromotive force (EMF) in secondary coils wound on the same core.
The ratio of primary to secondary turns determines the voltage step-up or step-down ratio.
Energy is transferred magnetically with no direct electrical connection between primary and secondary circuits.
Transformers operate only on alternating current because a steady DC produces no changing flux.

concepts.name: Distillation
concepts.summary_verbatim: Distillation is a method of separation of substances based on differences in their volatilities.
mechanism_atoms: A liquid mixture is heated until the more volatile component preferentially vaporizes.
The vapor, enriched in the lower-boiling-point component, rises and is conducted away from the boiling flask.
The vapor is cooled in a condenser, causing it to re-liquefy as a distillate with altered composition.
Multiple theoretical plates (repeated vaporization-condensation stages) increase separation purity.
The less volatile component accumulates as residue in the still pot.

concepts.name: Truss
concepts.summary_verbatim: A truss is an assembly of members such as beams, connected by nodes, that creates a rigid structure.
mechanism_atoms: In a truss, all members are two-force members, meaning they carry only axial tension or compression, not bending.
External loads applied at nodes are distributed as axial forces through individual members along their lengths.
The triangulated geometry of members makes the truss rigid and prevents mechanism-like collapse.
Top chord members typically act in compression while bottom chord members act in tension under typical loading.
The arrangement converts bending action (which would occur in a beam) into pure axial forces, allowing lightweight structures.

concepts.name: Prestressed concrete
concepts.summary_verbatim: In a prestressed concrete member, the internal stresses are introduced in a planned manner so that the stresses resulting from the imposed loads are counteracted to the desired degree.
mechanism_atoms: High-tensile steel tendons or wires are placed within or alongside the concrete member.
In pre-tensioning, tendons are tensioned before concrete is cast; after curing, tension is released, transferring compressive stress into the concrete via bond.
In post-tensioning, tendons are tensioned after concrete has hardened and then anchored at the ends, compressing the concrete.
The induced pre-compression offsets the tensile stresses that applied loads would create, preventing cracking.
This allows concrete, which is weak in tension, to carry larger tensile loads without failing.

concepts.name: Fluidized bed
concepts.summary_verbatim: A fluidized bed is a physical phenomenon that occurs when a solid particulate substance (usually present in a holding vessel) is under the right conditions so that it behaves like a fluid.
mechanism_atoms: Pressurized gas or liquid is pumped upward through a bed of solid particles from below.
At a critical fluid velocity (the minimum fluidization velocity), drag forces on particles equal gravity, suspending them.
Above this velocity, the bed expands and particles mix freely, giving the bed fluid-like properties.
Enhanced particle–fluid contact dramatically improves heat and mass transfer rates versus fixed beds.
Used in catalytic cracking, combustion, and coating processes where uniform temperature and intimate contact are required.

concepts.name: Arch (structure)
concepts.summary_verbatim: An arch is a curved vertical structure spanning an open space underneath it.
mechanism_atoms: Vertical loads on the arch are resolved into horizontal and vertical reaction forces at the abutments (arch action).
The curved geometry causes the structure to carry loads primarily in compression rather than bending.
The inward horizontal thrust from abutments provides a counterbalancing moment, greatly reducing bending stresses.
Arch action allows spans far greater than those possible with a simply supported beam of the same material.
Masonry arches exploit the fact that stone and brick are strong in compression but weak in tension.

concepts.name: Rectifier
concepts.summary_verbatim: A rectifier is an electrical device that converts alternating current (AC), which periodically reverses direction, to direct current (DC), which flows in only one direction.
mechanism_atoms: Diodes (or other unidirectional devices) allow current to pass in only one direction, blocking the reverse half-cycle.
A half-wave rectifier passes only one polarity of the AC waveform, producing pulsating DC.
A full-wave bridge rectifier uses four diodes arranged so both half-cycles are conducted in the same direction through the load.
A smoothing capacitor in parallel with the load stores charge during voltage peaks and releases it during troughs, reducing ripple.
Filter inductors further reduce ripple by opposing rapid changes in current.

concepts.name: Error correction code
concepts.domain: information theory / error detection and correction
concepts.summary_verbatim: In computing, telecommunication, information theory, and coding theory, forward error correction (FEC) or channel coding is a technique used for controlling errors in data transmission over unreliable or noisy communication channels.
mechanism_atoms: The sender adds redundant (parity or check) bits to the data according to a mathematical code structure.
The receiver uses the redundant bits to detect whether errors occurred during transmission.
Codes with sufficient redundancy allow the receiver to locate and correct errors without requesting retransmission.
Block codes (e.g., Reed-Solomon) group data into fixed-size blocks and append check symbols.
Convolutional codes encode data as a continuous stream using sliding-window convolution with a generator polynomial.

concepts.name: Hydraulic accumulator
concepts.domain: hydraulics / energy storage and pressure regulation
concepts.summary_verbatim: A compressed gas accumulator consists of a cylinder with two chambers that are separated by an elastic diaphragm, a totally enclosed bladder, or a floating piston.
mechanism_atoms: One chamber is connected to the hydraulic circuit and contains pressurized fluid.
The other chamber contains pre-charged inert gas (typically nitrogen) that acts as a compressible spring.
When system pressure rises, fluid compresses the gas, storing energy in the compressed gas.
When system pressure drops or flow demand peaks, the compressed gas expands, forcing fluid back into the circuit.
This buffers pressure spikes, maintains system pressure during pump off-cycles, and delivers emergency actuation energy.

concepts.name: Annealing (materials science)
concepts.domain: materials / microstructure control via heat treatment
concepts.summary_verbatim: In metallurgy and materials science, annealing is a heat treatment that alters the physical and sometimes chemical properties of a material to increase its ductility and reduce its hardness, making it more workable.
mechanism_atoms: The material is heated above its recrystallization temperature and held there for a sufficient time.
At elevated temperature, atomic diffusion allows dislocations to rearrange or annihilate (recovery stage).
New, strain-free grains nucleate and grow to replace deformed grains (recrystallization stage).
Continued heating causes grain growth, further reducing internal boundary area and residual stress.
Controlled slow cooling prevents re-introduction of thermal stresses and locks in the softened microstructure.

concepts.name: Sintering
concepts.summary_verbatim: Sintering or frittage is the process of compacting and forming a solid mass of material by pressure or heat without melting it to the point of liquefaction.
mechanism_atoms: Powdered material is compacted into a desired shape (green body) under pressure.
The green body is heated to a temperature below the melting point of the material.
Atoms diffuse across particle boundaries, driven by the reduction of surface energy.
Necks form and grow between adjacent particles, bonding them together and reducing porosity.
The result is a dense, solid part with mechanical properties superior to the loose powder starting material.

concepts.name: Gear
concepts.domain: mechanical transmission / torque and speed conversion
concepts.summary_verbatim: A gear or gearwheel, also called a toothed wheel, is a rotating machine part typically used to transmit rotational motion or torque by means of a series of 'teeth' that engage with compatible teeth of another gear or other part.
mechanism_atoms: Interlocking teeth on mating gears enforce a fixed velocity ratio equal to the inverse ratio of tooth counts.
Force is transmitted at the pitch point where teeth mesh, converting torque at the cost of inverse speed change.
A larger driven gear relative to the driver gear reduces output speed and multiplies output torque (gear reduction).
Helical gears have angled teeth that gradually engage, reducing noise and impact loading compared to spur gears.
A gear train combining multiple gear pairs multiplies the individual stage ratios for large overall transmission ratios.

concepts.name: Rankine cycle
concepts.summary_verbatim: The Rankine cycle is an idealized thermodynamic cycle describing the process by which certain heat engines, such as steam turbines or reciprocating steam engines, allow mechanical work to be extracted from a fluid as it moves between a heat source and heat sink.
mechanism_atoms: A pump raises the pressure of liquid water (working fluid) from condenser pressure to boiler pressure.
The high-pressure water is heated in a boiler by an external heat source, converting it to high-pressure steam.
Steam expands through a turbine, doing work by pushing turbine blades and dropping in pressure and temperature.
Spent low-pressure steam enters a condenser, where a heat sink (cooling water) removes latent heat and returns it to liquid.
The cycle efficiency is limited by the temperature ratio between heat source and heat sink (Carnot bound).

concepts.name: Damper (mechanical)
concepts.summary_verbatim: In mechanical engineering, a damper is a device for suppressing vibrations in a mechanical system by dissipating energy.
mechanism_atoms: A viscous damper forces fluid through an orifice as a piston moves; viscous drag converts kinetic energy into heat.
Damping force is proportional to the velocity of relative motion between the damper's two ends.
By absorbing kinetic energy from oscillating structures, the damper reduces amplitude over successive cycles.
Critical damping is the minimum damping that prevents oscillation; overdamping slows return to equilibrium without oscillation.
Tuned mass dampers add a secondary oscillating mass tuned to the structure's natural frequency to cancel resonant motion.

concepts.name: Fault tolerance
concepts.summary_verbatim: In engineering and systems theory, redundancy is the intentional duplication of critical components or functions of a system with the goal of increasing reliability of the system, usually in the form of a backup or fail-safe, or to improve actual system performance.
mechanism_atoms: Critical subsystems are duplicated (or triplicated) so that failure of one copy does not cause system failure.
A monitoring or voting mechanism detects discrepancies between redundant units.
Upon detecting a fault, the system switches automatically to the backup component (failover).
Active redundancy keeps backup units running in parallel so switchover is instantaneous; standby redundancy activates backups on demand.
Triple modular redundancy (TMR) uses majority voting among three independent units to mask single faults in real time.

concepts.name: Low-pass filter
concepts.summary_verbatim: A low-pass filter is a filter that passes signals with a frequency lower than a selected cutoff frequency and attenuates signals with frequencies higher than the cutoff frequency.
mechanism_atoms: In an RC low-pass filter, the capacitor charges slowly relative to high-frequency signals, shunting them to ground.
At frequencies below the cutoff (f_c = 1/2πRC), the capacitor's impedance is high, so signal passes to the output largely unattenuated.
At frequencies above cutoff, capacitor impedance drops, diverting signal energy away from the output (attenuation).
The −3 dB cutoff frequency marks the boundary where output power is halved relative to input.
Higher-order filters (Butterworth, Chebyshev) cascade multiple poles to achieve sharper roll-off beyond cutoff.

concepts.name: Catalysis
concepts.summary_verbatim: Catalysis is the increase in rate of a chemical reaction due to an added substance known as a catalyst.
mechanism_atoms: A catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy than the uncatalyzed route.
Reactant molecules adsorb onto the catalyst surface (heterogeneous catalysis) or form intermediate complexes (homogeneous catalysis).
The intermediate species reacts more readily to form products than the direct reactant–product pathway.
After products desorb, the catalyst is regenerated and available for further reaction cycles.
Catalyst selectivity steers reactions toward desired products by stabilizing specific transition states.

concepts.name: Hydraulic press
concepts.summary_verbatim: A hydraulic press is a machine press using a hydraulic cylinder to generate a compressive force.
mechanism_atoms: Pascal's law states that pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted equally in all directions.
A small input force on a small-area piston generates high fluid pressure throughout the hydraulic circuit.
The same pressure acting on a much larger output piston produces a proportionally multiplied output force.
Force multiplication ratio equals the ratio of the output piston area to the input piston area.
Used for forging, clinching, punching, blanking, deep drawing, and metal forming operations.

concepts.name: Modulation (signal)
concepts.summary_verbatim: In electronics and telecommunications, modulation is the process of varying one or more properties of a periodic waveform, called the carrier signal, with a separate signal called the modulation signal that typically contains information to be transmitted.
mechanism_atoms: A high-frequency carrier wave (sinusoid) is selected whose frequency can propagate efficiently over the channel.
The information signal varies one property of the carrier: amplitude (AM), frequency (FM), or phase (PM).
Impressed variations in the carrier property encode the information for transmission.
At the receiver, a demodulator extracts the information signal by reversing the modulation process.
Modulation allows multiple signals to coexist on the same medium by assigning different carrier frequencies (frequency-division multiplexing).

concepts.name: Cam (mechanism)
concepts.summary_verbatim: A cam is a rotating or sliding piece in a mechanical linkage used especially in transforming rotary motion into linear motion.
mechanism_atoms: The cam has an irregular or eccentric profile that contacts a follower (lever or rod) riding against its surface.
As the cam rotates, the changing radial distance from the cam axis to the contact surface drives the follower in a prescribed displacement profile.
The follower may be a flat-faced plate, roller, or knife-edge, each affecting contact stress and motion fidelity.
Return springs or conjugate cams maintain contact between cam and follower during the return stroke.
Cam profiles are engineered to produce specific displacement, velocity, and acceleration curves in the follower (e.g., constant velocity, harmonic, cycloidal).

concepts.name: Heat exchanger
concepts.summary_verbatim: A heat exchanger is a system used to transfer heat between a source and a working fluid.
mechanism_atoms: Hot and cold fluids flow on opposite sides of a thermally conductive wall (or in direct contact) so heat conducts from hotter to cooler.
Counter-flow arrangements maximize temperature gradient along the heat transfer surface, improving efficiency.
Shell-and-tube designs route one fluid through tubes and the other fluid around the tubes inside a shell.
The rate of heat transfer is governed by Q = U·A·ΔT_lm, where U is overall heat transfer coefficient and ΔT_lm is the log-mean temperature difference.
Fins or corrugations extend the surface area to enhance heat transfer without increasing equipment volume.

concepts.name: Wheatstone bridge
concepts.summary_verbatim: A Wheatstone bridge is an electrical circuit used to measure an unknown electrical resistance by balancing two legs of a bridge circuit, one leg of which includes the unknown component.
mechanism_atoms: Four resistors are arranged in a diamond (bridge) circuit with a voltage source across one diagonal.
A galvanometer or null detector is connected across the other diagonal to measure bridge imbalance.
When the ratio of resistances in each leg is equal, no current flows through the galvanometer (balanced/null condition).
The unknown resistance is determined from the known resistor values that produce the null balance.
Small changes in the unknown resistance (e.g., from a strain gauge or thermistor) produce a measurable output voltage proportional to the change.

concepts.name: Redundancy (engineering)
concepts.summary_verbatim: In engineering and systems theory, redundancy is the intentional duplication of critical components or functions of a system with the goal of increasing reliability of the system, usually in the form of a backup or fail-safe, or to improve actual system performance, such as in the case of GNSS.
mechanism_atoms: Critical components are replicated so a single failure leaves at least one functioning copy in service.
Active (parallel) redundancy keeps all copies running simultaneously; any surviving copy sustains system operation.
Standby (cold/warm) redundancy activates dormant backup units only upon detecting primary unit failure.
Majority-vote logic (as in TMR) compares outputs of parallel units and accepts the majority result, masking errors.
System reliability with N redundant components is calculated as 1 minus the probability that all N units fail simultaneously.

concepts.name: Flywheel
concepts.summary_verbatim: A flywheel is a mechanical device that uses the conservation of angular momentum to store rotational energy, a form of kinetic energy proportional to the product of its moment of inertia and the square of its rotational speed.
mechanism_atoms: Energy is stored by accelerating the flywheel mass to a high rotational speed against its rotational inertia.
Stored kinetic energy equals ½·I·ω², where I is moment of inertia (related to mass and radius) and ω is angular velocity.
When demand exceeds supply, the flywheel decelerates, releasing stored energy to the connected load.
A flywheel smooths out torque pulsations in reciprocating engines by absorbing excess energy during power strokes and releasing it between strokes.
High rotational speed and large radius (for greater I) maximize energy density; modern flywheels use carbon fiber to tolerate centrifugal stresses.

concepts.name: Feedback (engineering)
concepts.summary_verbatim: Feedback occurs when outputs of a system are routed back as inputs as part of a chain of cause and effect that forms a circuit or loop.
mechanism_atoms: A sensor measures the actual output of the system and converts it into a comparable signal.
The measured output is subtracted from the desired setpoint to form an error signal.
A controller processes the error and generates a corrective action applied to the system's input.
Negative feedback reduces the error by driving the output toward the setpoint, providing stability.
Positive feedback amplifies deviations from the setpoint, useful for switching circuits but destabilizing in linear systems.

concepts.name: Carnot cycle
concepts.summary_verbatim: A Carnot cycle is an ideal thermodynamic cycle proposed by French physicist Sadi Carnot in 1824 and expanded upon by others in the 1830s and 1840s.
mechanism_atoms: The cycle consists of four reversible processes: isothermal expansion, adiabatic expansion, isothermal compression, and adiabatic compression.
During isothermal expansion, the working gas absorbs heat from the hot reservoir at constant temperature.
During adiabatic expansion, the gas expands without heat exchange, doing work and dropping in temperature.
During isothermal compression, waste heat is rejected to the cold reservoir at constant temperature.
Carnot's theorem states that no heat engine operating between two given temperatures can be more efficient than the Carnot efficiency η = 1 − T_cold/T_hot.

concepts.name: Hooke's law
concepts.summary_verbatim: In physics, Hooke's law is an empirical law which states that the force (F) needed to extend or compress a spring by some distance (x) scales linearly with respect to that distance—that is, Fs = kx, where k is a constant factor characteristic of the spring (i.e., its stiffness).
mechanism_atoms: A spring (or elastic solid) stores energy by deforming when an external force is applied.
The restoring force is directly proportional to displacement from equilibrium: F = −kx.
The spring constant k (stiffness) depends on material elastic modulus and geometry.
Linear elasticity holds only within the elastic limit; beyond it, permanent deformation (plastic behavior) occurs.
Hooke's law generalizes to three-dimensional solids via the stress-strain relationship σ = E·ε, where E is Young's modulus.

concepts.name: Triple modular redundancy
