concepts.summary_verbatim: In computing, triple modular redundancy, sometimes called triple-mode redundancy, (TMR) is a fault-tolerant form of N-modular redundancy, in which three systems perform a process and that result is processed by a majority-voting system to produce a single output.
mechanism_atoms: Three independent modules execute the same computation in parallel.
A majority voter compares the three outputs and selects the result agreed upon by at least two of the three.
A single module failure is masked because the two healthy modules outvote the faulty one.
TMR can tolerate one fault per voting interval without any output error reaching the system.
Used in spacecraft, nuclear plant controls, and aviation systems where single-event upsets could be catastrophic.

concepts.name: Solenoid valve
concepts.summary_verbatim: A solenoid valve is an electromechanically operated valve used in heating systems, fuel pipelines, and industrial automation to regulate the flow of liquids or gases.
mechanism_atoms: An electrical coil (solenoid) surrounds a movable ferromagnetic plunger inside a tube.
Energizing the coil generates a magnetic field that pulls the plunger inward against a return spring.
The plunger's movement opens or closes the valve orifice, controlling fluid flow.
De-energizing the coil allows the return spring to restore the plunger and valve to its default position.
Two-way, three-way, and four-way configurations allow directional control of fluid paths in pneumatic and hydraulic circuits.

concepts.name: Sourdough fermentation
concepts.summary_verbatim: Sourdough is a stable culture of lactic acid bacteria and yeast in a mixture of flour and water.
mechanism_atoms: Wild yeasts (Saccharomyces and related species) ferment sugars in flour to produce carbon dioxide, leavening the dough.
Lactic acid bacteria (LAB) produce lactic acid and acetic acid through heterolactic fermentation, creating sourness and imposing acidic stress that favors niche-specific microorganisms.
LAB metabolize maltose, a sugar released from starch; the maltose-LAB interaction enables yeasts to enter and establish in the community.
Dough acidification by LAB inhibits spoilage organisms and drives a microbial succession toward acid-tolerant strains.
Sustained co-culture is maintained by each partner metabolizing substrates the other cannot, creating metabolic interdependence.

concepts.name: Miso fermentation (koji-based)
concepts.domain: enzymatic proteolysis / starch hydrolysis / salt-tolerant aging
concepts.summary_verbatim: Miso consists of a starter culture called kōji, soybeans, and usually a grain (either rice, barley, or rye), and goes through a two-step process: first creating the kōji, and second the kōji is combined with the other components, and the mixture is left to be enzymatically digested, fermented and aged.
mechanism_atoms: Aspergillus oryzae is grown aerobically on steamed grain to produce kōji, secreting large quantities of amylolytic enzymes (amylase, glucoamylase) and proteolytic enzymes (protease, peptidase).
Amylases hydrolyze starch in the grain to glucose and dextrin, supplying fermentable sugars.
Proteases and peptidases cleave soy proteins into smaller peptides and free amino acids including glutamic acid, producing umami flavor.
A. oryzae secretes salt-tolerant alkaline proteases, allowing enzymatic activity to continue in the high-sodium environment required for miso.
Leucine aminopeptidase cleaves glutamic acid from polypeptides, directly driving the characteristic umami taste of the finished product.

concepts.name: Fish sauce fermentation (autolysis)
concepts.summary_verbatim: Fish sauce is a liquid condiment made from fish or krill that have been coated in salt and fermented for up to two years.
mechanism_atoms: High salt concentration (typically 20-25%) creates a selective brine that prevents putrefaction while allowing halophilic enzymatic activity.
Autolysis is the primary mechanism: endogenous digestive enzymes in the fish intestines and flesh break down protein into peptides and amino acids.
Fermentation starts from lactic acid enzymes in the spine of the fish, which begin protein decomposition.
Over weeks to years, enzymatic hydrolysis progressively releases glutamate and other free amino acids responsible for umami flavor.
The resulting liquid is rich in glutamate content, which is the chemical basis of its intense savory character.

concepts.name: Kimchi microbial succession
concepts.domain: lactic acid fermentation / anaerobic microbial succession
concepts.summary_verbatim: Kimchi is a traditional Korean side dish of salted and fermented vegetables, most often napa cabbage or Korean radishes, made with a widely varying selection of seasonings.
mechanism_atoms: Salt draws water from the vegetables via osmosis, creating a brine that selects for salt-tolerant lactic acid bacteria already present on raw vegetables.
Early fermentation is dominated by Leuconostoc species because of their lower acid tolerance and preference for low-salt, microaerophilic conditions.
As acidity rises and salt concentration increases, Leuconostoc populations decline and Lactobacillus species become dominant due to their higher acid and salt tolerance.
Glucose and fructose liberated from plant cell walls serve as the primary carbon source for lactic acid bacteria throughout fermentation.
Lactic acid (produced by both homo- and hetero-fermentative LAB) is the most abundant organic acid, driving pH drop and flavor development.

concepts.name: Sauerkraut lacto-fermentation
concepts.summary_verbatim: Sauerkraut is finely cut raw cabbage that has been fermented by various lactic acid bacteria.
mechanism_atoms: Salt is mixed with shredded cabbage; osmotic pressure draws out cabbage juice to form an anaerobic brine in which LAB already present on the vegetable proliferate.
In the first phase, anaerobic bacteria such as Klebsiella and Enterobacter lead fermentation and begin producing an acidic environment.
Rising acidity eliminates less acid-tolerant bacteria, selecting for more acid-tolerant LAB that continue converting sugars to lactic acid.
The oxygen-poor brine environment created by the salt selects against aerobic spoilage organisms, allowing LAB dominance.
The finished product is stable at low pH because the lactic acid concentration inhibits further microbial activity.

concepts.name: Tempeh mycelium binding
concepts.domain: solid-state fungal fermentation / mycelial mat formation
concepts.summary_verbatim: Tempeh is a traditional Indonesian food made by a controlled fermentation process that binds soybeans into a cake form, using a Rhizopus mold.
mechanism_atoms: Cooked soybeans are inoculated with spores of Rhizopus oligosporus or Rhizopus oryzae, filamentous fungi that grow on solid substrate.
Fermentation proceeds at ~30°C for 24–48 hours under aerobic conditions, with the mold growing through and between the beans.
The mold produces fluffy white mycelia that physically bind the beans into a solid, sliceable cake through interlocking hyphal networks.
Rhizopus secretes proteases and amylases that partially catabolize soy proteins and starches, improving digestibility.
As mold growth declines after 48 hours, the beans remain knitted together by the hardened mycelial mat, giving tempeh its characteristic firm texture.

concepts.name: Vinegar production (acetification)
concepts.domain: aerobic oxidative fermentation / ethanol to acetic acid
concepts.summary_verbatim: Acetobacter is a genus of acetic acid bacteria characterized by the ability to convert ethanol to acetic acid in the presence of oxygen.
mechanism_atoms: Acetic acid bacteria (AAB), primarily Acetobacter species, oxidize ethanol to acetic acid in a two-step aerobic oxidative process.
Unlike typical anaerobic fermentations, acetification requires continuous oxygen supply; industrial production bubbles air through the solution.
AAB use ethanol as the electron donor and oxygen as the electron acceptor, generating acetic acid as the metabolic byproduct.
A. oryzae can also oxidize lactate and acetate further into carbon dioxide and water if ethanol is exhausted.
Modern continuous stirred-tank reactors with aeration can produce vinegar of 15% acetic acid in only 24 hours.

concepts.name: Malolactic fermentation in winemaking
concepts.summary_verbatim: Malolactic conversion (also known as malolactic fermentation or MLF) is a process in winemaking in which tart-tasting malic acid, naturally present in grape must, is converted to softer-tasting lactic acid.
mechanism_atoms: Lactic acid bacteria (primarily Oenococcus oeni) convert dicarboxylic malic acid into monocarboxylic lactic acid plus CO2.
The conversion is driven indirectly by chemiosmosis: the pH gradient between inside the bacterial cell and the acidic wine generates ATP for the bacteria.
Malic acid has two carboxyl groups producing a harsher, more sour taste; lactic acid has one, producing a softer, creamier mouthfeel.
MLF reduces the total titratable acidity of wine, which is desirable for wines with excessive malic acid from cool-climate grapes.
Winemakers control whether MLF occurs by regulating sulfur dioxide levels, temperature, and bacterial inoculation timing.

concepts.name: Maillard reaction
concepts.summary_verbatim: The Maillard reaction is a chemical reaction between amino acids and reducing sugars to create melanoidins, the compounds that give browned food its distinctive flavor.
mechanism_atoms: The reaction occurs between the amine group of a free amino acid and the carbonyl group of a reducing sugar, typically with the addition of heat.
The condensation product rearranges (Amadori rearrangement) and undergoes further reactions to produce hundreds of volatile and non-volatile flavor and color compounds.
Melanoidins—brown, high molecular weight heterogeneous polymers—are the final colored products formed when sugars and amino acids combine at high temperatures and low water activity.
The reaction is distinct from caramelization (which involves only sugars): the Maillard reaction requires both an amino acid and a reducing sugar.
It is responsible for browning in seared meats, coffee roasting, toasted bread crusts, and fried onions.

concepts.name: Gluten network formation
concepts.summary_verbatim: Gluten is an elastic network of wheat grain's proteins, gliadin and glutenin primarily, which forms readily with the addition of water and often kneading in the case of bread dough.
mechanism_atoms: When flour is hydrated, glutenin (high- and low-molecular-weight subunits) and gliadin proteins absorb water and align to form a continuous protein network.
Intermolecular interactions include hydrogen bonding, hydrophobic interactions, and covalent disulfide bonds formed between cysteine residues in glutenin subunits.
Kneading promotes disulfide crosslinking by aligning protein chains and oxidizing free sulfhydryl groups, strengthening the network.
Glutenins primarily control dough elasticity (proportional to low-molecular-weight glutenin sulfur content), while gliadins contribute extensibility and viscous flow.
During baking, gluten proteins coagulate irreversibly, trapping CO2 bubbles and setting the bread's porous crumb structure.

concepts.name: Bread leavening by yeast
concepts.domain: biological gas production / foam structure stabilization
concepts.summary_verbatim: Many breads are leavened by yeast, with Saccharomyces cerevisiae being the most commonly used species.
mechanism_atoms: Baker's yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) ferments simple sugars (glucose, fructose, maltose) in flour under anaerobic conditions, producing CO2 and ethanol.
CO2 gas is trapped by the viscoelastic gluten network, forming a foam of microscopic gas cells that expand during proofing.
If dough lacks sufficient gluten strands, it cannot retain CO2 pockets and collapses, producing a dense loaf.
During baking, the ethanol evaporates, CO2 further expands, and the gluten network coagulates, fixing the open crumb structure permanently.
Bread is thermodynamically classified as a gas-in-solid foam, with gluten providing the solid continuous phase.

concepts.name: Food curing with salt and nitrite
concepts.summary_verbatim: Curing is any of various food preservation and flavoring processes of foods such as meat, fish and vegetables, by the addition of salt, with the aim of drawing moisture out of the food by the process of osmosis.
mechanism_atoms: Salt induces osmosis, drawing water out of food cells and reducing water activity, which inhibits microbial growth.
Salt dehydrates food by pulling excess moisture from proteins and also denatures proteins, altering their structure similarly to heat.
Sodium nitrite bonds to myoglobin in meat, acting as a substitute for oxygen and maintaining a stable red color in cured products.
Nitrites inhibit growth of Clostridium botulinum, the bacterium causing botulism, providing a critical safety function.
Nitrates serve as a slow-release reservoir: bacteria convert nitrate to nitrite over time, extending the antimicrobial effect in long-cured products.

concepts.name: Smoking (food preservation)
concepts.summary_verbatim: Smoking is the process of flavoring, browning, cooking, or preserving food by exposing it to smoke from burning or smoldering material, most often wood.
mechanism_atoms: Wood smoke contains phenolic compounds that are both antioxidants (slowing rancidification of fats) and antimicrobials (inhibiting bacterial growth).
Other antimicrobial compounds in smoke include formaldehyde, acetic acid, and other organic acids, giving wood smoke a low pH of about 2.5.
Smoke deposits a surface layer of antimicrobial chemicals that penetrate only superficially into meat or fish, limiting its standalone preservation effect.
Cold smoking also dehydrates the food surface, further reducing water activity and creating an unfavorable environment for microbial growth.
Effective preservation requires combining smoking with salt-curing or drying, as smoke alone cannot penetrate deeply enough to sterilize the interior.

concepts.name: Pressure canning (botulinum sterilization)
concepts.domain: thermal sterilization / spore destruction under pressure
concepts.summary_verbatim: Canning is a method of food preservation in which food is processed and sealed in an airtight container.
mechanism_atoms: Clostridium botulinum spores can only be destroyed at temperatures above the boiling point of water (>100°C), requiring pressurized equipment.
A pressure canner converts water to steam and raises pressure to achieve 116-130°C inside sealed jars.
The target sterilization standard is a 'botulinum cook' of 121°C for 3 minutes throughout the entire product volume.
Low-acid foods (pH > 4.6) including most vegetables, meats, and dairy require pressure canning because C. botulinum thrives in anaerobic, neutral-pH environments.
High-acid foods (pH < 4.6) can be safely water-bath canned at 100°C because the acidity itself prevents C. botulinum germination.

concepts.name: Honey production (sucrose inversion)
concepts.summary_verbatim: Honey is a sweet and viscous substance made by several bees, the best-known of which are honey bees, which store honey as food.
mechanism_atoms: Forager bees collect flower nectar (primarily sucrose) and store it in their honey stomach, where salivary enzymes from the hypopharyngeal gland begin hydrolysis.
Invertase (sucrase) cleaves the alpha-1,2-glycosidic bond of sucrose, producing glucose and fructose; this is completed as house bees pass nectar between each other and into cells.
Glucose oxidase added by bees reacts with glucose to produce gluconic acid (lowering pH) and hydrogen peroxide (an antimicrobial agent), both partially responsible for honey's stability.
Bees fan the honey in open cells to evaporate water, concentrating sugars until water activity falls below the threshold for microbial growth (typically <17-20% moisture).
Once sufficiently dehydrated, bees cap the cells with beeswax; the result is a supersaturated sugar solution that resists fermentation and spoilage indefinitely.

concepts.name: Cheesemaking (rennet coagulation)
concepts.summary_verbatim: Cheesemaking (or caseiculture) is the craft of making cheese.
mechanism_atoms: Milk is acidified (by starter bacteria or direct acidification) to lower pH, destabilizing casein micelles and promoting coagulation.

Rennet (or microbial equivalents) is added; its key enzyme chymosin cleaves kappa-casein at a specific peptide bond (Phe-Met), removing the hydrophilic macropeptide that normally keeps micelles in suspension.
Destabilized casein micelles aggregate in the presence of calcium ions, forming a gel (curd).
The solid curd is cut, stirred, and heated, causing syneresis—the expulsion of liquid whey from the protein matrix.
Further pressing, salting, and aging concentrate and transform the curd into finished cheese through continued enzymatic and microbial activity.

concepts.name: Crop rotation (nitrogen cycling)
concepts.domain: biological nitrogen fixation / soil fertility maintenance
concepts.summary_verbatim: Crop rotation is the practice of growing a series of different types of crops in the same area across a sequence of growing seasons.
mechanism_atoms: Legume crops host symbiotic rhizobia bacteria in root nodules that fix atmospheric N2 into ammonium compounds usable by plants.
When legume plants die and decompose, fixed nitrogen is released into the soil, fertilizing it for subsequent nitrogen-demanding crops.
Rotating cereal crops (which deplete soil nitrogen) with nitrogen-fixing legumes replenishes soil fertility without synthetic fertilizer input.
Rotation also disrupts pest and disease cycles by removing host plants before pathogen populations become established in the soil.
A nitrogen-fixing crop (legume) should always precede a nitrogen-depleting crop (cereal) to maximize the soil fertility benefit of the rotation.

concepts.name: Companion planting and allelopathy
concepts.domain: chemical plant-plant inhibition / ecological pest suppression
concepts.summary_verbatim: Companion planting in gardening and agriculture is the planting of different crops in proximity for any of a number of different reasons, including pest control, pollination, providing habitat for beneficial insects, maximizing use of space, and to otherwise increase crop productivity.
mechanism_atoms: Allelopathy is a verified mechanism: certain plants release chemical compounds (allelochemicals) into soil or air that inhibit the germination or growth of neighboring species.
Strongly aromatic plants deter pests through volatile chemical signals that mask or repel pest-attracting cues from crop plants.
Companion plants can hide crops from pest insects by providing a physical and olfactory barrier (masking effect).
Some companion plants act as nursery habitat for beneficial insects including predators and parasitoids that naturally suppress pest populations.
Trap cropping deliberately draws pest insects to a sacrificial companion plant away from the main crop, concentrating pests for removal.

concepts.name: Grafting (vascular cambium union)
concepts.summary_verbatim: Grafting or graftage is a horticultural technique whereby tissues of plants are joined so as to continue their growth together.
mechanism_atoms: Successful grafting requires precise alignment of the vascular cambium (a layer of meristematic cells) between rootstock and scion.
The wound healing response generates callus tissue at the interface, forming a callus bridge that physically connects the two cut surfaces.
New vascular cambium differentiates within the callus bridge, and secondary xylem and phloem then develop, restoring water and nutrient transport.
Auxin signaling in the cambium promotes cell division and vascular cell differentiation, driving the reconnection of the transport system.
Taxonomic proximity between rootstock and scion is a general prerequisite for long-term graft success and survival.

concepts.name: Irrigation scheduling (evapotranspiration-based)
concepts.domain: crop water demand modeling / deficit irrigation
concepts.summary_verbatim: Irrigation scheduling is the process of deciding when to irrigate and how much water to apply, based upon measurements or estimates of soil moisture or crop water use.
mechanism_atoms: Evapotranspiration (ET) combines evaporation from soil surface and transpiration from plant leaves; ET controllers measure local weather to calculate daily crop water demand.
Irrigation is applied when the soil moisture deficit reaches a threshold that would begin to stress the crop, matching water input to plant uptake rate.
Reference ET (ETo) is calculated from meteorological variables (temperature, humidity, wind, radiation), then adjusted by a crop coefficient for the specific plant and growth stage.
Drip irrigation delivers water directly to the root zone at low volumes and high frequency, minimizing surface evaporation and runoff losses.
Modern systems use soil moisture sensors combined with ET models to dynamically adapt irrigation duration and frequency in real time.

concepts.name: Integrated pest management (economic threshold)
concepts.summary_verbatim: Integrated pest management (IPM), also known as integrated pest control (IPC), is a broad-based approach that integrates practices for economic control of pests.
mechanism_atoms: The economic threshold (ET) is the pest density at which the cost of a control action equals the economic damage prevented; intervention is only triggered when the pest population reaches this level.
Regular monitoring tracks pest population density to determine whether the ET has been reached before deciding on action.
Biological controls—natural predators, parasitoids, and pathogens—are deployed or conserved to keep pest populations below damaging levels without chemical inputs.
Cultural controls (crop rotation, sanitation, resistant varieties) reduce pest habitat and population buildup.
Chemical pesticides are used as a last resort, only after monitoring indicates the ET has been exceeded, minimizing pesticide use and resistance development.

concepts.name: No-till farming (soil biology preservation)
concepts.domain: soil structure maintenance / mycorrhizal network preservation
concepts.summary_verbatim: No-till farming (also known as zero tillage or direct drilling) is an agricultural technique for growing crops or pasture without disturbing the soil through tillage.
mechanism_atoms: Conventional tillage physically disrupts soil macro-aggregates and destroys the extraradical hyphal network of arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, rendering them non-infective.
No-till preserves intact hyphal networks that connect plant roots to soil phosphorus and water resources otherwise unreachable.
Undisturbed soil builds macro-aggregate structure: no-till soils with straw returned show 9.1-12.2% higher macro-aggregate content and 10% more bulk soil organic carbon than tilled soils.
Mycorrhizal fungi provide carbohydrates to host plants in exchange for nutrients (nitrogen, phosphorus) and moisture from the broader soil volume.
Preservation of earthworm and arthropod populations in no-till soils further improves aeration, water infiltration, and organic matter decomposition.

concepts.name: Selective breeding (artificial selection)
concepts.domain: controlled genetic selection / trait amplification over generations
concepts.summary_verbatim: Selective breeding (also called artificial selection) is the process by which humans use animal or plant breeding to selectively develop particular phenotypic traits (characteristics) by choosing which typical animals or plants will sexually reproduce and have offspring together.
mechanism_atoms: Humans select breeding pairs based on desired phenotypic traits (growth rate, milk yield, meat quality, disease resistance), preventing unselected individuals from reproducing.
Over successive generations, alleles associated with favored traits increase in frequency in the population while disfavored alleles decrease.
Selection generally reduces overall genetic variation in the population as favorable allele combinations are fixed.
Systematic pedigree and performance recording, developed in 18th-century England, enabled rigorous artificial selection by tracking heritable trait performance across generations.
The process differs from natural selection in that the selection pressure is applied by humans toward human economic goals rather than environmental survival.

concepts.name: Composting (thermophilic decomposition)
concepts.summary_verbatim: Compost is a mixture of ingredients used as plant fertilizer and to improve soil's physical, chemical, and biological properties.
mechanism_atoms: Composting proceeds in sequential microbial phases: mesophilic bacteria begin decomposition, then thermophilic bacteria take over as heat builds (60-70°C), and finally mesophiles return during curing.
The optimal carbon-to-nitrogen ratio is approximately 25-30:1; materials too rich in carbon decompose slowly while excess nitrogen causes ammonia volatilization.
Thermophilic microorganisms including Bacillus and Streptomyces species efficiently decompose complex organic polymers (cellulose, hemicellulose) at elevated temperatures.
Aerobic bacteria are most efficient; regular turning of compost piles replenishes oxygen to maintain aerobic conditions and prevent anaerobic, odor-producing fermentation.
Decomposition releases plant-available nutrients: bacteria process carbon and nitrogen and excrete nitrogen, phosphorus, and magnesium in mineral forms usable by plants.

concepts.name: Brewing (wort fermentation)
concepts.domain: yeast fermentation / alcohol and flavor compound production
concepts.summary_verbatim: Brewing is the production of beer by steeping a starch source (commonly cereal grains, the most popular of which is barley) in water and fermenting the resulting sweet liquid with yeast.
mechanism_atoms: Malted barley is mashed in hot water; amylase enzymes convert starch to fermentable sugars (primarily maltose) forming wort.
Saccharomyces cerevisiae (ale yeast) ferments maltose and glucose anaerobically to produce ethanol and CO2, consuming the wort sugars.
Ale yeasts are top-fermenting: their hydrophobic surface causes cells to adhere to CO2 bubbles and rise to the fermentation vessel surface.
Lager yeasts (Saccharomyces pastorianus) are bottom-fermenting hybrids that work at lower temperatures and settle to the bottom of the vessel.
Hop compounds added during boiling contribute bitterness (iso-alpha acids) and antimicrobial properties that stabilize the beer against bacterial spoilage.

concepts.name: Fractional distillation of ethanol
concepts.summary_verbatim: Fractional distillation is the separation of a mixture into its component parts, or fractions, by heating them to a temperature at which one or more fractions will vaporize.
mechanism_atoms: A fermented liquid is heated in a still; vapor rises through a fractionating column containing multiple theoretical plates (trays or packing).
Each plate allows vapor and liquid to reach equilibrium: the more volatile component (ethanol, bp 78.4°C) concentrates in the rising vapor phase while water (bp 100°C) condenses and returns.
A temperature gradient exists from hot at the bottom to cool at the top, with each tray representing one equilibration step enriching the vapor in ethanol.
Only the most volatile vapors remain gaseous all the way to the top and pass through the condenser to be collected as distillate.
The ethanol-water azeotrope (95.6% ethanol) sets the theoretical maximum for simple fractional distillation without special techniques.

concepts.name: Steam distillation of essential oils
concepts.domain: co-distillation of immiscible volatiles / azeotropic depression
concepts.summary_verbatim: Steam distillation is a separation process that consists of distilling water together with other immiscible compounds.
mechanism_atoms: Steam is passed through plant material (flowers, leaves, bark, roots); heat causes volatile aromatic compounds to vaporize at temperatures below their individual boiling points.

Because essential oil compounds are immiscible with water, they co-distill with steam via Dalton's law—the total vapor pressure is the sum of both components' pressures, lowering the distillation temperature.
This allows volatile compounds with boiling points well above 100°C to be distilled without decomposing the heat-sensitive aromatic molecules.
The vapor mixture (steam + essential oil vapors) passes through a condenser; the two liquid phases separate in the florentine flask due to their immiscibility and density difference.
Steam distillation is the primary industrial method for isolating eucalyptus, camphor, and citrus oils on a large scale.

concepts.name: Mortise and tenon joinery
concepts.domain: mechanical interlocking joint / structural wood connection
concepts.summary_verbatim: A mortise and tenon joint is a type of joint that connects two pieces of wood or other material.
mechanism_atoms: The tenon is a projecting tongue cut to precise dimensions at the end of one member; it fits exactly into the mortise, a matching rectangular hole cut into the receiving member.
Shoulders on the tenon seat against the face of the mortised member, preventing racking and providing bearing surface for compression loads.
The tight mechanical fit distributes shear and bending loads across the shoulder area, while the tenon inside the mortise resists tensile (pull-apart) forces.
Gluing the tenon inside the mortise adds shear strength; the joint can also be locked with a drawbore pin or wedge driven through the tenon, creating a permanent mechanical lock.
In traditional Chinese timber-frame construction, mortise-and-tenon joints were precision-cut to interlock without fasteners or glue, allowing slight movement under seismic loads.

concepts.name: Dovetail joint (tensile interlock)
concepts.summary_verbatim: A dovetail joint or simply dovetail is a joinery technique most commonly used in woodworking joinery (carpentry), including furniture, cabinets, log buildings, and timber framing.
mechanism_atoms: Trapezoidal pins on one board interlock with matching trapezoidal tails cut into the adjoining board; the widening geometry prevents the joint from pulling apart under tension.
The interlocking trapezoidal shape converts tensile (pull-apart) force into compressive force on the angled surfaces, mechanically resisting separation.
Once glued, a dovetail joint requires no additional mechanical fasteners; the geometry alone provides resistance to racking and tensile loads.
Sliding dovetail joints connect two boards at right angles mid-field (not at ends), providing interlocking strength without glue.
The joint requires precise measurement and cutting—any gap reduces the mechanical lock—making it a high-skill traditional woodworking technique.

concepts.name: C4 carbon fixation
concepts.summary_verbatim: C4 carbon fixation or the Hatch–Slack pathway is a photosynthetic process in some plants that increases the concentration of CO2 around the enzyme RuBisCO, thereby increasing photosynthetic efficiency.
mechanism_atoms: In C4 plants, CO2 is initially fixed by PEP carboxylase in mesophyll cells to form a 4-carbon compound (oxaloacetate), which is converted to malate or aspartate.
These 4-carbon acids are shuttled to bundle-sheath cells, where they are decarboxylated, releasing CO2 directly around RuBisCO.
The high local CO2 concentration around RuBisCO in the bundle sheath suppresses photorespiration (oxygenase activity of RuBisCO), which would otherwise waste fixed carbon.
This CO2-concentrating mechanism allows C4 plants to photosynthesize efficiently at high temperatures, high light, and under drought or salinity stress.
Though only ~3% of flowering plant species use C4 fixation, they account for ~23% of global terrestrial primary production (examples: maize, sugarcane, sorghum).

concepts.name: Layering (vegetative plant propagation)
concepts.summary_verbatim: Layering is a form of plant propagation in which a stem or branch is induced to grow roots while still attached to the parent plant, then separated to create a new plant.
mechanism_atoms: A stem section is wounded or girdled while still attached to the parent plant; wounding disrupts the flow of auxin and carbohydrates downward, causing them to accumulate above the wound site.
Auxin (IAA) accumulation at the wound triggers adventitious root initiation from cells in the stem cortex or cambium region.
The stem remains photosynthetically active and receives water and nutrients from the parent until roots are established, providing a reliable resource supply during root development.
In air layering, moist sphagnum moss wrapped around the wounded stem provides humidity and oxygen for root emergence without burying the stem in soil.
Once adventitious roots are visible and robust, the rooted section is severed and transplanted as a genetically identical clone of the parent.

concepts.name: Koji (Aspergillus oryzae) enzyme production
concepts.domain: filamentous fungal solid-state fermentation / umami enzyme cascade
concepts.summary_verbatim: Kōji mold, Aspergillus oryzae, is a filamentous fungus used in East Asia to saccharify rice, sweet potato, and barley in the making of alcoholic beverages such as sake and shōchū, and also to ferment soybeans for making soy sauce and miso.
mechanism_atoms: A. oryzae grows aerobically on steamed grain substrate in solid-state fermentation, secreting high concentrations of extracellular amylases and proteases into the substrate.
Amylases (alpha-amylase and glucoamylase) hydrolyze starch chains into glucose and dextrin, producing fermentable sugars and sweet flavor.
Proteases (including leucine aminopeptidase) cleave proteins into peptides and free amino acids; glutamic acid released this way directly produces umami taste.
Pectinase breaks down plant cell wall pectin, improving substrate penetration and releasing additional sugars and proteins.
Due to amino acids split off from proteins, koji results in a strong umami taste; this enzyme-rich substrate is then used as the enzymatic engine for sake, miso, and soy sauce production.

concepts.name: Elo rating system
concepts.summary_verbatim: The Elo rating system is a method for calculating the relative skill levels of players, originally designed for rating chess players.
mechanism_atoms: Each player is assigned a numerical rating; the difference in ratings predicts the expected outcome of a match.
After a game, ratings are updated: if the higher-rated player wins, only a few points transfer; if the lower-rated player wins (an upset), many points transfer.
The update formula uses an expected score based on the logistic curve, so the actual score minus expected score (scaled by a K-factor) is added to the winner's rating.
A draw yields a small gain for the lower-rated player and a small loss for the higher-rated player.
The K-factor controls the maximum rating change per game; provisional players use higher K values than established ones.

concepts.name: Swiss-system tournament
concepts.summary_verbatim: A Swiss-system tournament is a competition format in which contestants are paired using rules designed to ensure that each competitor plays opponents with a similar running score without playing the same opponent more than once.
mechanism_atoms: In round 1, players are paired randomly or by initial seeding.
In subsequent rounds, players with equal or similar cumulative scores are paired together.
No player faces the same opponent twice, even if scores converge.
After the final round, players are ranked by total score; ties are resolved by Buchholz (sum of opponents' scores) or similar tie-break systems.
The system finds a clear winner within relatively few rounds even among a large field, avoiding the knockout problem of a good player being eliminated by a single loss.

concepts.name: Handicap (golf)
concepts.summary_verbatim: A golf handicap is a numerical measure of a golfer's demonstrated ability, or potential ability, that is used to enable players of different abilities to compete against one another.
mechanism_atoms: A player's handicap index is calculated from the best recent differentials (adjusted gross score minus course rating, scaled by slope rating).
The course handicap converts the index for a specific course using: Handicap Index × Slope Rating / 113.
In stroke play, each player subtracts their course handicap from their gross score to get a net score.
The World Handicap System (WHS), launched in 2020, uses the best 8 of the most recent 20 score differentials to compute the index.
Equitable Stroke Control caps the maximum score on any hole to prevent one bad hole from distorting the handicap.

concepts.name: Seeding (sports)
concepts.summary_verbatim: In sport, seeding is the practice of separating the most skilled competitors from each other in the early rounds of a tournament.
mechanism_atoms: Competitors are assigned seed numbers based on prior ranking or performance; the best player receives seed 1.
Seedings are placed in the draw bracket so that the top two seeds cannot meet before the final, top four cannot meet before the semi-finals, and so on.
Lower-seeded players are matched against higher-seeded opponents in early rounds, protecting top seeds from early upsets statistically.
In some formats, re-seeding occurs after each round so that the highest remaining seeds always face the lowest remaining seeds.
Unseeded players are drawn randomly into remaining bracket slots.

concepts.name: Zugzwang
concepts.summary_verbatim: Zugzwang (from German 'compulsion to move'; pronounced [ˈtsuːktsvaŋ]) is a situation found in chess and other turn-based games wherein one player is put at a disadvantage because of their obligation to make a move; a player is said to be 'in zugzwang' when any legal move will worsen their position.
mechanism_atoms: In a zugzwang position, the player to move would prefer to pass, but passing is illegal in chess.
Any legal move the player in zugzwang makes weakens their position, allowing the opponent to achieve a decisive advantage.
Zugzwang most commonly arises in endgames where piece count is reduced and every move commitment is critical.
Opposition (two kings directly facing each other with one square between them) is a common zugzwang motif: the player to move must cede ground.
Players can engineer zugzwang for the opponent by using triangulation—moving a piece in a three-move detour to 'waste' a tempo and transfer the obligation to move.

concepts.name: Tempo (chess)
concepts.summary_verbatim: In chess and other chess-like games, a tempo (from Italian: tempo, lit. 'time') is a 'turn' or single move (a half-move or ply made either by White or Black).
mechanism_atoms: Gaining a tempo means forcing the opponent to react in a way that lets you accomplish your plans in fewer moves.
Losing a tempo (losing a move) means making a move that does not improve your position, effectively giving the opponent an extra turn's worth of initiative.
A 'zwischenzug' (intermediate move) gains a tempo by interpolating an unexpected move before the expected reply.
In endgames, a spare tempo (an available pawn move that does not change the key balance) can be used to put the opponent in zugzwang.
Material is often sacrificed to gain tempos in the opening (gambits), since rapid development can outweigh the lost material.

concepts.name: Ko fight
concepts.domain: indefinite repetition prevention / strategic threat exchange
concepts.summary_verbatim: A ko fight (Japanese: コウ, 劫, kō, from the translation of the Sanskrit term kalpa) is a tactical and strategic phase that can arise in the game of Go.
mechanism_atoms: Ko arises when a single stone can be captured and recaptured indefinitely, cycling the board position—which the ko rule forbids.
After one player captures a ko stone, the opponent may not immediately recapture; they must play elsewhere first (the 'ko threat').
A ko threat is a move elsewhere that demands a response; if the opponent ignores it to recapture the ko, they suffer a loss on the board.
Players accumulate or invent ko threats throughout the game; the player with more useful ko threats typically wins the ko fight.
Ko fights can be sente (forcing) or gote (non-forcing) depending on the value of the threats relative to the ko itself.

concepts.name: Pot odds (poker)
concepts.summary_verbatim: In poker, pot odds are the ratio of the current size of the pot to the cost of a contemplated call.
mechanism_atoms: A player computes pot odds as: pot size divided by call size (e.g., $90 pot, $10 call = 9:1 odds).
The player then estimates their 'equity' (probability of winning the hand with remaining cards).
If equity exceeds the pot-odds threshold (e.g., equity > 10% for 9:1 odds), calling has positive expected value.
Implied odds extend pot odds by considering future bets that will likely be won if the player hits their draw.
Reverse implied odds penalize calls where hitting the draw may still lose to a better hand, reducing actual EV.

concepts.name: Bluff (poker)
concepts.summary_verbatim: In the card game of poker, a bluff is a bet or raise made with a hand which is not thought to be the best hand.
mechanism_atoms: The objective of a bluff is to induce at least one opponent holding a better hand to fold.
According to game-theoretic optimal (GTO) play, a player should bluff at a frequency equal to the pot odds they give opponents: e.g., if pot odds are 2-to-1, bluff 1/3 of the time on that bet size.
A 'semi-bluff' is a bluff with a drawing hand that has equity if called—combining fold equity with draw equity.
Bluffing frequency must be balanced so that opponents cannot profitably always call or always fold.
Blockers (holding cards that reduce the number of strong hands an opponent can hold) increase the effectiveness of bluffs.

concepts.name: Drafting (aerodynamics)
concepts.summary_verbatim: Drafting, or slipstreaming, is an aerodynamic technique where two moving objects are aligning in a close group to exploit the lead object's slipstream and thus reduce the overall effect of drag.
mechanism_atoms: The lead object pushes air aside, creating a lower-pressure wake behind it; the trailing object moves into this wake and experiences reduced drag.
In cycling, a rider directly behind a lead rider can reduce aerodynamic drag by 20–40%, significantly lowering energy expenditure.
Drafting benefit diminishes with lateral offset; optimal position is directly behind or slightly to the side in the slipstream cone.
The lead object also benefits slightly from reduced pressure differential at its rear ('pushing' effect from the follower).
In motor racing, drafting allows the trailing car to slingshot past the leader by using saved momentum to accelerate out of the draft at high speed.

concepts.name: Sports periodization
concepts.domain: training load management / peak performance timing
concepts.summary_verbatim: Periodization is a cyclical method of planning and managing athletic or physical training and involves progressive cycling of various aspects of a training program during a specific period.
mechanism_atoms: Training is divided into macrocycles (season), mesocycles (weeks to months), and microcycles (days to one week), each with distinct goals.
Load is progressively increased then intentionally reduced in a taper phase to allow supercompensation—recovery that exceeds the original fitness level.
Different mesocycles focus on different attributes: hypertrophy, strength, power, or sport-specific skill, in a sequenced order.
Overreaching (short-term overload) is deliberately planned but followed by recovery to avoid overtraining syndrome.
Periodization aims to ensure peak physical condition coincides with the most important competition dates.

concepts.name: Pacing strategies in track and field
concepts.summary_verbatim: Pacing strategies in track and field are the varied strategies which runners use to distribute their energy throughout a race.
mechanism_atoms: Even pacing (constant speed) minimizes total anaerobic energy cost and is theoretically optimal for time trials over middle and long distances.
Positive split (faster first half) risks premature lactate accumulation and a steep fade in the second half.
Negative split (faster second half) conserves glycogen early; many world marathon records have been set with slight negative splits.
In championship races where relative place matters more than time, runners may run slowly early to save a finishing sprint.
Pacemakers (rabbits) are hired to lead at a predetermined pace for world-record attempts, then drop out before the finish.

concepts.name: Fair cake-cutting
concepts.summary_verbatim: Fair cake-cutting is a kind of fair division problem.
mechanism_atoms: The 'cake' represents a heterogeneous, divisible resource (e.g., land, time) with different values at different locations for different agents.
A division is proportional if each of n players receives a piece they value at at least 1/n of the total.
A division is envy-free if no player prefers another player's piece to their own.
The classic two-person procedure is 'divide and choose': one player cuts, the other selects first—guaranteeing proportionality but not envy-freeness in general.
The Selfridge–Conway procedure achieves envy-free division for three players using a trimming technique so each player believes they received a largest piece.

concepts.name: Divide and choose
concepts.summary_verbatim: Divide and choose (also cut and choose or I cut, you choose) is a procedure for fair division of a continuous resource between two parties.
mechanism_atoms: One player (the 'divider') cuts the resource into two pieces they consider equal in value.
The other player (the 'chooser') selects whichever piece they prefer.
The divider receives the remaining piece; rational dividers will cut exactly in half by their own valuation, guaranteeing themselves at least 50%.
The chooser always receives at least 50% by their own valuation since they pick first.
The procedure is strategy-proof for the divider but gives the chooser an information advantage, making it not fully envy-free if valuations differ.

concepts.name: Pomodoro Technique
concepts.summary_verbatim: The Pomodoro Technique is a time management method developed by Francesco Cirillo in the late 1980s.
mechanism_atoms: Work is broken into fixed 25-minute intervals called 'pomodori', each dedicated to a single task without interruption.
After each pomodoro, a short break (5 minutes) is taken; after four pomodori, a longer break (15–30 minutes) is taken.
Interruptions during a pomodoro either abort it (requiring a restart) or are noted and deferred to after the interval.
Completed pomodori are recorded, providing a visible tally of productive intervals and a sense of accomplishment.
The technique reduces the psychological friction of starting tasks by framing them as short, bounded commitments rather than open-ended efforts.

concepts.name: Queueing theory
concepts.summary_verbatim: Queueing theory is the mathematical study of waiting lines, or queues.
mechanism_atoms: A queue is modeled by arrival rate (λ), service rate (μ), and number of servers; system utilization ρ = λ/μ.
When ρ < 1, the queue is stable (finite expected wait); when ρ ≥ 1, the queue grows without bound.
Little's Law states: average number in system L = arrival rate λ × average time in system W (L = λW).
Different queue disciplines (FIFO, LIFO, priority, shortest-job-first) affect average wait times and fairness differently.
The M/M/1 model (Poisson arrivals, exponential service, single server) gives closed-form formulas for average queue length and wait time.

concepts.name: Little's law
concepts.summary_verbatim: In mathematical queueing theory, Little's law is a theorem by John Little which states that the long-term average number of customers (L) in a stationary system is equal to the long-term average effective arrival rate (λ) multiplied by the average time that a customer spends in the system (W).
mechanism_atoms: The law is expressed as L = λW, where L is average items in the system, λ is average arrival rate, and W is average time per item in the system.
Little's Law applies to any stable system (arrivals = departures over time) regardless of arrival distribution, service distribution, or queue discipline.
Practically: if a supermarket checkout sees 60 customers/hour and each spends 5 minutes, then on average 5 customers are in the checkout zone at any moment.
The law enables managers to compute any one of L, λ, W from the other two without full distributional knowledge.
It is used in manufacturing, software performance analysis, and hospital capacity planning to diagnose bottlenecks.

concepts.name: Maze-solving algorithm
concepts.summary_verbatim: A maze-solving algorithm is an automated method for solving a maze.
mechanism_atoms: The wall-follower (hand-on-wall) rule works for simply-connected mazes: keep one hand on a wall and follow it until the exit is reached.
Trémaux's algorithm marks passages as visited (once or twice) and refuses to enter twice-marked passages, guaranteeing termination in all connected mazes.
Dead-end filling removes all dead-end passages iteratively, leaving only through-routes; the remaining passages contain the solution.
For mazes viewed from above, Dijkstra's or A* algorithms find the shortest path by expanding nodes in order of increasing cost.
The Pledge algorithm extends wall-following to handle multiple disconnected components by tracking cumulative rotation angle.

concepts.name: Multi-armed bandit
concepts.summary_verbatim: In probability theory and machine learning, the multi-armed bandit problem (sometimes called the K- or N-armed bandit problem) is a problem in which a decision maker iteratively selects one of multiple fixed choices (i.e., arms or actions) when the properties of each choice are only partially known at the time of allocation, and may become better understood as time passes.
mechanism_atoms: Each 'arm' has an unknown reward distribution; the agent must choose which arm to pull on each trial.
Exploitation uses the arm with the highest estimated mean so far; exploration tries less-sampled arms to improve estimates.
The epsilon-greedy strategy exploits the best known arm with probability 1−ε and explores randomly with probability ε.
Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) algorithms add a confidence bonus to rarely-tried arms, balancing exploration and exploitation optimally.
Thompson sampling maintains a probability distribution over each arm's reward and samples from those distributions to select the arm to pull.

concepts.name: Prisoner's dilemma
concepts.summary_verbatim: The prisoner's dilemma is a standard example in game theory.
mechanism_atoms: Two players simultaneously choose to cooperate (C) or defect (D); payoffs are: mutual cooperation > one-sided defection win > mutual defection > one-sided cooperation loss.
Defection is a dominant strategy: regardless of the other player's choice, each player receives a higher payoff by defecting.
Mutual defection (the Nash equilibrium) is Pareto-suboptimal—both would be better off if both cooperated.
In the iterated (repeated) prisoner's dilemma, cooperation can emerge because future retaliation changes the incentive structure.
Tit-for-tat (cooperate first, then copy opponent's last move) won Robert Axelrod's 1980 computer tournaments as the most effective iterated strategy.

concepts.name: Tit for tat
concepts.summary_verbatim: Tit for tat is an English saying meaning 'equivalent retaliation' and is a highly effective strategy in game theory.
mechanism_atoms: On the first move, the agent cooperates (nice/non-exploitative opening).
On every subsequent move, the agent copies exactly what the opponent did on the previous move.
The strategy is retaliatory (punishes defection immediately), forgiving (returns to cooperation as soon as the opponent does), and clear (simple enough for opponents to recognize and adapt to).
Tit-for-tat won both of Robert Axelrod's 1980 computer tournaments of the iterated prisoner's dilemma.
A known weakness: a single miscommunication can trigger a 'death spiral' of mutual defection; 'generous tit-for-tat' occasionally forgives defections to break cycles.

concepts.name: Nim
concepts.summary_verbatim: Nim is a mathematical combinatorial game in which two players take turns removing (or "nimming") objects from distinct heaps or piles.
mechanism_atoms: On each turn, a player must remove at least one object from exactly one pile; they may remove any number from that pile.
Under normal play convention, the player who takes the last object wins; under misère play, they lose.
The winning strategy depends on the nim-sum: compute the XOR (bitwise exclusive-or) of all pile sizes; if the nim-sum is 0, the position is losing for the player to move.
A winning move always leaves a position with nim-sum = 0; the player can always achieve this when the nim-sum is non-zero.
Nim is foundational via the Sprague–Grundy theorem: every finite impartial game is equivalent to a single nim pile of some size (its Grundy value).

concepts.name: Sprague–Grundy theorem
concepts.summary_verbatim: In combinatorial game theory, the Sprague–Grundy theorem states that every impartial game under the normal play convention is equivalent to a one-heap game of nim, or to an infinite generalization of nim.
mechanism_atoms: Every position in a finite impartial game is assigned a Grundy number (nimber): 0 for losing positions, and the minimum excludant (mex) of the Grundy numbers of all reachable positions.
A position with Grundy number 0 is a P-position (previous player wins, i.e., the player who just moved wins); any non-zero Grundy number is an N-position.
When multiple impartial games are played simultaneously, the combined Grundy number is the XOR of individual Grundy numbers.
This allows any sum of impartial games to be reduced to a single Nim game of equivalent size, enabling exact solution.
The theorem applies only to impartial games (both players have identical move sets from any position), not to partisan games like chess.

concepts.name: Minimax
concepts.summary_verbatim: Minimax (sometimes Minmax, MM or saddle point) is a decision rule used in artificial intelligence, decision theory, combinatorial game theory, statistics, and philosophy for minimizing the possible loss for a worst case (maximum loss) scenario.
mechanism_atoms: A game tree is built by expanding all possible moves for both players to a given search depth.
Leaf nodes are assigned static evaluation scores from the perspective of the maximizing player.
MAX nodes (maximizing player's turns) propagate the maximum child score upward; MIN nodes propagate the minimum child score upward.
The root node's value determines the best move for the current player; the algorithm assumes the opponent always plays optimally.
Alpha-beta pruning optimizes minimax by discarding branches that cannot affect the final decision, reducing worst-case node evaluations from O(b^d) to O(b^(d/2)).

concepts.name: Alpha–beta pruning
concepts.summary_verbatim: Alpha–beta pruning is a search algorithm that seeks to decrease the number of nodes that are evaluated by the minimax algorithm in its search tree.
mechanism_atoms: Two bounds are maintained: alpha (the best score the maximizer can guarantee) and beta (the best score the minimizer can guarantee).
When a node's value falls outside [alpha, beta], the subtree is pruned (cut off) because it cannot influence the final result.
Alpha-beta prunes 'fail-low' subtrees at MAX nodes (already worse than alpha) and 'fail-high' subtrees at MIN nodes (already worse than beta).
With perfect move ordering (best moves searched first), alpha-beta reduces effective branching factor from b to √b, doubling searchable depth.
A chess program searching 4 plies with ~36 branches/node evaluates 1M+ nodes naively; optimal alpha-beta reduces this to ~2,000 nodes.

concepts.name: Nash equilibrium
concepts.summary_verbatim: In game theory, a Nash equilibrium is a situation where no player could gain more by changing their own strategy (holding all other players' strategies fixed) in a game.
mechanism_atoms: Each player chooses a strategy that is a best response to the strategies chosen by all other players.
A Nash equilibrium is stable in the sense that no unilateral deviation is profitable; it is self-enforcing.
Pure strategy Nash equilibria involve deterministic choices; mixed strategy equilibria involve randomization over actions with specific probabilities.
John Nash proved that every finite n-player non-cooperative game has at least one Nash equilibrium in mixed strategies.
Nash equilibria need not be Pareto-optimal: the prisoner's dilemma's mutual defection is a Nash equilibrium but worse for both players than mutual cooperation.

concepts.name: Vickrey auction
concepts.summary_verbatim: A Vickrey auction or sealed-bid second-price auction (SBSPA) is a type of sealed-bid auction.
mechanism_atoms: Bidders submit sealed bids without knowing others' bids; the highest bidder wins the item.
The winner pays not their own bid but the second-highest bid submitted.
Bidding one's true valuation is a weakly dominant strategy: underbidding risks losing a profitable auction; overbidding risks paying more than the item is worth.
The second-price rule makes truthful revelation incentive-compatible—no bidder can gain by misreporting their value.
The Vickrey-Clarke-Groves (VCG) mechanism generalizes this to multiple items, charging each winner the externality they impose on others.

concepts.name: Card counting
concepts.summary_verbatim: Card counting is a strategy in blackjack used to determine whether the player or the dealer has an advantage on the next hand.
mechanism_atoms: Counters assign point values to cards: low cards (2–6) are +1 (benefit dealer when removed), high cards (10–Ace) are −1 (benefit player when removed), mid cards are 0.
A running count is maintained across dealt cards; a positive count means the remaining deck is rich in high cards, favoring the player.
The true count adjusts for deck depth: running count divided by number of decks remaining.
When the true count is high, players increase their bets (and alter strategy decisions like doubling or splitting) to exploit the advantage.
Card counting shifts the house edge from approximately −0.5% (basic strategy) to a small positive expected value for the player.

concepts.name: Polynesian navigation
concepts.summary_verbatim: Navigators travelled to small inhabited islands using wayfinding techniques and knowledge passed by oral tradition from master to apprentice, often in the form of song.
mechanism_atoms: Navigators memorized the rising and setting points of key stars on the horizon to form a mental star compass orienting direction across open ocean.
Ocean swell direction and shape were read by body feel; island chains predictably refract and reflect swells, allowing course correction.
Bioluminescence patterns in the water and cloud formations over land provided proximity cues to unseen islands.
Land-based birds sighted at dawn or dusk indicated nearby islands, because these species do not stray far from shore.
Knowledge was guild-held and transmitted orally through song, chant, and structured apprenticeship; navigators held high social status and could broker aid between islands.

concepts.name: Micronesian navigation
concepts.summary_verbatim: Micronesian navigation techniques are those navigation skills used for thousands of years by the navigators who voyaged between the thousands of small islands in the western Pacific Ocean in the subregion of Oceania, that is commonly known as Micronesia.
mechanism_atoms: A sidereal (star) compass divides the horizon into ~32 points by the rising and setting positions of 15 principal stars, providing directional reference without instruments.
Navigators tracked star paths (wofanu) as memorized routes connecting specific islands, switching between stars as they crossed the sky.
Ocean swells were used as a straight-line bearing when stars were obscured; each swell direction corresponded to a named compass point.
The etak cognitive framework treats the canoe as stationary and the reference island as moving, enabling triangulation of position relative to a third island.
Dances, chants (rong), and tactile coral-fragment diagrams encoded complex island-star relationships for apprentice memorization.

concepts.name: Etak (navigation)
concepts.summary_verbatim: etak is a word of Micronesian origin for a distinctive cognitive and mnemonic approach to oceanic navigation and orientation involving a notional reference point or "island", called etak, and triangulation based on it.
mechanism_atoms: The canoe is conceptualized as stationary; the destination and reference islands are mentally 'moving' past the canoe during the voyage.
A third island (the etak island) not on the direct route is used as a bearing reference; navigators track its apparent movement against the star compass.
The position along the voyage is judged by which star the etak island lies beneath at any moment.
This inversion reduces cumulative dead-reckoning error by anchoring relative position to a fixed external landmark rather than integrating speed and time.
The system is entirely mnemonic, requiring years of training to internalize the star-island-bearing relationships.

concepts.name: Dead reckoning
concepts.summary_verbatim: In navigation, dead reckoning is the process of calculating the current position of a moving object by using a previously determined position, or fix, and incorporating estimates of speed, heading (or direction or course), and elapsed time.
mechanism_atoms: A known starting fix is advanced forward mathematically using recorded heading, speed, and elapsed time.
Speed was historically measured by chip log (floating wood timed over a measured distance); modern sensors use accelerometers or pitot tubes.
Heading is maintained by compass (magnetic or gyroscopic) and corrected for magnetic variation.
Errors accumulate with each update cycle; the method is subject to compounding inaccuracies from current, wind drift, and instrument error.
Periodic external fixes (celestial observations, coastal landmarks, GPS) are used to reset accumulated error and restart the reckoning chain.

concepts.name: Fire-stick farming
concepts.summary_verbatim: Fire-stick farming, also known as cool burning, is a cultural burning practice whereby Aboriginal Australians regularly use fire to burn vegetation, a management technique which has been utilized for thousands of years.
mechanism_atoms: Low-intensity 'cool' fires are lit at specific seasons to clear undergrowth without destroying mature trees, creating a patchy mosaic of habitat at different successional stages.
Burning releases nutrients from biomass as ash, prompting resprouting of nitrogen-rich grasses and edible plants such as yams, which are harvested post-fire.
Mosaic burning reduces fuel loads across the landscape, preventing catastrophic high-intensity wildfires by removing continuous dense undergrowth.
Nutrient-flush grasslands attract grazing animals (kangaroos, wallabies, emus) to burned patches, concentrating prey for easier hunting.
Over millennia, repeated burning converted dry forest to savanna, permanently altering Australian biomes; European explorers mistook this anthropogenic landscape for natural wilderness.

concepts.name: Terra preta
concepts.summary_verbatim: Terra preta (Portuguese pronunciation: [ˈtɛʁɐ ˈpɾetɐ], literally "black earth" in Portuguese), also known as Amazonian dark earth or Indian black earth, is a type of very dark, fertile anthropogenic soil (anthrosol) found in the Amazon Basin.
mechanism_atoms: Indigenous communities added a mixture of charcoal, bones, broken pottery, compost, and manure to low-fertility Amazonian oxisols over centuries.
The charcoal (biochar) component is chemically stable and resists decomposition, persisting for thousands of years and providing a porous matrix that binds and retains nutrients.
Charcoal's high surface area hosts soil microbial communities that mineralize organic matter and fix nitrogen, boosting long-term fertility.
Terra preta soils self-regenerate at approximately 1 cm per year through ongoing microbial and organic activity, unlike surrounding infertile soils.
Depths can reach 2 meters, indicating sustained multi-generational soil-building practice; the soils date to 450 BCE–950 CE.

concepts.name: Songline
concepts.summary_verbatim: A songline has been called a "dreaming track", as it marks a route across the land or sky followed by one of the creator-beings or ancestors in the Dreaming.
mechanism_atoms: Geographic features (hills, waterholes, rock formations) are encoded as lyrics in a song sequence; singing the song in order navigates the physical landscape.
Songlines cross-connect into a continental network; travellers fluent in one song transfer to another at known junction sites, analogous to a subway interchange.
Songs are shared across linguistically distinct Aboriginal groups, enabling cross-cultural navigation and trade without a common spoken language.
Knowledge is transmitted through ceremony, dance, and visual art (paintings on rock or bark), providing multi-modal redundancy for retention.
The system is estimated to predate writing by tens of thousands of years and encodes ecological, seasonal, and social information alongside geography.

concepts.name: Traditional ecological knowledge
concepts.summary_verbatim: Traditional ecological knowledge (TEK) is a cumulative body of knowledge, practice, and belief, evolving by adaptive processes and handed down through generations by cultural transmission, about the relationship of living beings (including humans) with one another and with their environment.
mechanism_atoms: Knowledge accumulates through multigenerational direct observation and is updated adaptively as environmental conditions change.
Transmission occurs via oral tradition, ceremony, and apprenticeship (learning-by-doing), embedding ecological cues in cultural memory structures.
TEK practices include resource rotation, succession management, and maintaining landscape patchiness to sustain biodiversity.
Social institutions (elders, taboos, councils) regulate resource use and enforce conservation rules embedded in cultural norms.
Integration with local governance gives TEK adaptive management properties comparable to formal scientific monitoring, but operating at finer spatial and temporal scales.

concepts.name: Transhumance
concepts.summary_verbatim: Transhumance is a type of pastoralism or nomadism, a seasonal movement of livestock between fixed summer and winter pastures.
mechanism_atoms: Herds are moved vertically (mountain–valley) or horizontally (wet–dry zones) to track seasonal grass growth, matching livestock to peak forage availability.
Fixed seasonal pastures (alpages in summer, valleys in winter) are used on regular annual cycles, distinguishing transhumance from true nomadism's irregular movement.
Established drove roads or corridors (e.g., Alpine paths used since the Neolithic, documented from 3000 BCE) encode accumulated route knowledge.
Timing of each move is calibrated to snowmelt, rainfall, and grass condition rather than calendar date, requiring experienced judgment.
The practice avoids overgrazing by distributing pressure across altitudinal zones and allowing each pasture to recover during the opposite season.

concepts.name: Nomadic pastoralism
concepts.summary_verbatim: Nomadic pastoralism, also known as nomadic herding or pastoral nomadism, is a form of pastoralism in which livestock are herded in order to seek for fresh pastures on which to graze.
mechanism_atoms: Movement patterns are irregular and responsive to rainfall and pasture conditions, unlike transhumance's fixed seasonal routes.
Herders maintain large, flexible herd compositions to buffer against drought-induced mortality, spreading risk across species (camels, goats, cattle).
Mobility requires portable dwellings (yurts, tents) and minimal fixed property, enabling rapid redeployment to new grazing areas.
Social networks between groups facilitate information sharing about distant water and pasture availability, functioning as a distributed sensing system.
Pastoralists exchange animal products (hides, dairy, meat) with settled agriculturalists, creating interdependent economic relationships.

concepts.name: Central place theory
concepts.summary_verbatim: Central place theory is an urban geographical theory that seeks to explain the number, size and range of market services in a commercial system or human settlements in a residential system.
mechanism_atoms: Each good or service requires a minimum 'threshold' population to be economically viable; high-order goods need larger thresholds and appear only in larger centers.
Consumers travel up to a maximum 'range' distance to acquire goods; beyond this, the cost outweighs benefit, limiting each center's effective market area.
Settlements self-organize into a nested hierarchy of hexagonal market areas, because hexagons tesselate without overlap and minimize total travel distance.
Higher-order centers (cities) are spaced farther apart, lower-order centers (villages) are more numerous and closely spaced.
Three spatial principles (market, transport, administrative) produce K=3, K=4, K=7 hierarchies depending on which optimization dominates.

concepts.name: Map projection
concepts.summary_verbatim: In cartography, a map projection is any of a broad set of transformations employed to represent the curved two-dimensional surface of a globe on a plane.
mechanism_atoms: All projections introduce distortion; a sphere cannot be flattened without stretching or tearing, as proven by Euler (1775): no single projection can be both conformal and equal-area.
Conformal (orthomorphic) projections preserve local angles and shapes but distort area (e.g., Mercator makes polar regions appear vast).
Equal-area projections preserve relative surface areas but distort shapes (e.g., Mollweide).
Compromise projections (e.g., Robinson, Winkel Tripel) balance shape and area distortion without perfectly preserving either.
Projection surface geometry (cylindrical, conic, azimuthal) determines which regions have least distortion; standard parallels or the tangent point are zones of near-accuracy.

concepts.name: Early human migrations
concepts.summary_verbatim: Early human migrations are the earliest migrations and expansions of archaic and modern humans across continents.
mechanism_atoms: Homo erectus began expanding out of Africa approximately 2 million years ago, colonizing Eurasia in multiple dispersal waves.
Modern Homo sapiens originated in Africa ~300,000 years ago and dispersed globally; genetic evidence supports a primary Out-of-Africa wave ~70,000–50,000 BP.
Coastal migration routes along shorelines ('Beachcomber' hypothesis) enabled rapid spread by providing reliable shellfish and marine food sources.
Climate oscillations (glacial advances/retreats) opened and closed corridors (e.g., the Green Sahara, Bering land bridge) that gated migration timing.
Population genetic bottlenecks in non-African populations reflect founding effects from small pioneering groups crossing geographic barriers.

concepts.name: Austronesian peoples
concepts.summary_verbatim: The Austronesian peoples, sometimes referred to as Austronesian-speaking peoples, are a large group of peoples who speak Austronesian languages, having settled in Taiwan, maritime Southeast Asia, parts of mainland Southeast Asia, Micronesia, coastal New Guinea, Island Melanesia, Polynesia, and Madagascar.
mechanism_atoms: The Austronesian expansion originated in Taiwan circa 3000–1500 BCE, spreading outrigger canoe and sail technology enabling open-ocean crossings.
Staged island-hopping colonization used each newly settled island as a platform for further voyaging, enabling rapid geographic spread.
Linguistic differentiation traces dispersal routes; Austronesian languages share structural features allowing reconstruction of migration sequences.
Portable agriculture (breadfruit, taro, pigs, chickens) was carried on canoes, enabling settlers to establish food systems on uninhabited islands.
The expansion reached Madagascar (~1,500 years ago) by traversing the entire Indian Ocean, the widest maritime dispersal of any pre-industrial people.

concepts.name: Oral tradition
concepts.summary_verbatim: Oral tradition, or oral lore, is a form of human communication in which knowledge, art, beliefs, ideas and culture are received, preserved, and transmitted orally from one generation to another.
mechanism_atoms: Formulaic composition uses repeated metrical phrases and epithets that fit standard rhythmic slots, reducing the cognitive load of composition during live performance.
Ring composition (chiastic structure) mirrors the beginning and end of a narrative passage around a central point, aiding memory and providing coherent structure.
Poetic meter and rhyme constrain word choice, making unauthorized alterations immediately detectable and resisting drift over generations.
Multi-modal encoding (song, dance, visual art, gesture) provides redundant storage of the same information in different sensory channels.
Master-apprentice transmission with error correction by the community maintains fidelity; deviation is socially sanctioned.

concepts.name: Oral-formulaic composition
concepts.summary_verbatim: Oral-formulaic composition (also known as the oral-formulaic theory or the Parry-Lord theory) is a theory that was developed in the second quarter of the 20th century to explain the way in which epic poets compose and perform their poetry.
mechanism_atoms: Poets maintain a repertoire of formulae—fixed metrical phrases expressing a single idea—that can be slotted into verse lines without conscious composition.
Higher-order 'type-scenes' (arming a warrior, feasting, a ship's departure) are stock narrative blocks that can be expanded or compressed to fit context.
Improvisation recombines formula and type-scene in real time, producing unique performance text from reusable components.
The system enables illiterate performers to compose thousands of lines of verse extemporaneously while maintaining thematic coherence.
Each performance is a novel recombination rather than memorized verbatim text, explaining why oral epics exist in multiple variants.

concepts.name: Shifting cultivation
concepts.summary_verbatim: Shifting cultivation is an agricultural system in which plots of land are cultivated temporarily, then abandoned while post-disturbance fallow vegetation is allowed to freely grow while the cultivator moves on to another plot.
mechanism_atoms: Forest is cleared and burned; ash releases phosphorus, potassium, calcium, and magnesium into the soil, providing a short-term fertility pulse.
Crops are grown for 2–5 years until declining yields signal nutrient depletion and weed/pest pressure, then the plot is abandoned.
During a fallow period of 5–20+ years, secondary forest regenerates, restoring organic matter, soil structure, and nutrient stocks.
The system harvests stored solar energy from the standing forest biomass, with soil fertility effectively subsidized by accumulated forest capital.
Viable only at low population density; shorter fallow cycles (from land pressure) reduce recovery time and cause long-term soil degradation.

concepts.name: Slash-and-burn agriculture
concepts.summary_verbatim: Slash-and-burn agriculture is a form of shifting cultivation in agriculture that involves the cutting and burning of plants in a forest or woodland to create a field called a swidden.
mechanism_atoms: Vegetation is felled and left to dry, then burned just before the rainy season so ash is incorporated into soil by first rains.
The burn temporarily eliminates weeds and soil-borne pests while simultaneously depositing mineral nutrients.
Fields are productive for 2–5 seasons until soil nutrient depletion and weed reinvasion force abandonment.
Abandoned swidden is left fallow to regenerate; repeated burning cycles on the same plot are possible only after full forest recovery.
In its traditional form, this system is sustainable for small populations over large areas; European colonial population increases and commercial pressures disrupted its ecological balance.

concepts.name: Vernacular architecture
concepts.summary_verbatim: Vernacular architecture (also folk architecture) is building done outside any academic tradition, and without the involvement of professional designers and architects.
mechanism_atoms: Design is driven by locally available materials (mud, stone, timber, thatch) whose thermal and structural properties directly shape building form.

Climate adaptation is achieved through accumulated trial-and-error over generations: thick earthen walls in hot-arid climates buffer diurnal temperature swings; steeply pitched roofs in wet climates shed rain.
Passive ventilation systems (courtyards, wind towers, raised floors) use convection and evaporation to cool interiors without mechanical energy.
Knowledge is transmitted through apprenticeship and imitation rather than written plans; builders internalize regional 'rules' as tacit craft knowledge.
Vernacular forms are culturally legible, encoding social structure (e.g., gender separation, status hierarchies) in room layout and orientation.

concepts.name: Wayfinding
concepts.summary_verbatim: Wayfinding (or way-finding) encompasses all of the ways in which people (and animals) orient themselves in physical space and navigate from place to place.
mechanism_atoms: Landmark-based navigation anchors position to distinctive environmental features; landmarks are hierarchically organized by salience and uniqueness.
Route knowledge (sequential path segments between landmarks) is the most basic learned spatial representation, requiring minimal cognitive overhead.
Survey knowledge (a configural 'map') emerges from accumulated route experience and allows flexible detour and shortcut planning.
Environmental signage (signs, color-coding, architecture) externalizes wayfinding knowledge, reducing cognitive load for unfamiliar users.
Multi-sensory cues (proprioception, sound, smell) supplement vision and provide redundancy when visual cues are absent (night, fog).

concepts.name: Kinship
concepts.summary_verbatim: In anthropology, kinship is the web of social relationships that form an important part of the lives of all humans in all societies, although its exact meanings even within this discipline are often debated.
mechanism_atoms: Descent rules (patrilineal, matrilineal, bilateral) assign individuals to kin groups, regulating inheritance of property, titles, and obligations.
Alliance theory (Lévi-Strauss) holds that marriage rules between groups create durable social alliances and circulate resources across kinship networks.
Kinship terminology systems (Omaha, Crow, Iroquois, Hawaiian, Eskimo) reflect underlying social structure, classifying relatives in ways that encode descent ideology.
Exogamy rules (prohibition on intra-group marriage) force alliances outward, expanding social networks and reducing genetic inbreeding.
Fictive kinship (adoption, ritual kinship) extends network benefits to non-biological relationships, enabling social incorporation of outsiders.

concepts.name: Exogamy
concepts.summary_verbatim: Exogamy is a custom enjoining marriage outside one's own group.
