mechanism_atoms: Marriage outside the group is enforced through social taboos (incest prohibitions) and legal rules that define prohibited degrees of relatedness.
Exogamy is most commonly defined through kinship group (clan or moiety) membership rather than geography, religion, or ethnicity.
By compelling marriage alliances with outsiders, exogamy builds inter-group bonds and reduces conflict between neighboring social units.
In patrilineal systems, women marry out (virilocal residence), enabling men to maintain residential solidarity; the pattern reverses in matrilineal systems.
Prescriptive marriage rules (e.g., cross-cousin marriage) specify not just who is forbidden but who is preferred, structuring alliance networks predictably.

concepts.name: Alliance theory (kinship)
concepts.summary_verbatim: Alliance theory, also known as the general theory of exchanges, is a structuralist method of studying kinship relations.
mechanism_atoms: The incest taboo's primary social function is to force groups to exchange spouses outward rather than retaining women internally, creating inter-group alliances.
Elementary structures prescribe or prefer a specific marriage partner (e.g., mother's brother's daughter), producing determinate cycles of exchange.
Direct exchange (moiety systems) alternates wives between two groups; delayed exchange (section systems) creates longer cycles through three or more groups.
Each marriage creates reciprocal obligations (bride-price, bride-service, counter-gifts) that sustain multi-generational alliances.
Complex structures merely prohibit certain kin categories without prescribing alternatives, leaving partner choice to other social or economic factors.

concepts.name: Tragedy of the commons
concepts.summary_verbatim: The tragedy of the commons is the concept that, in a system where individuals benefit from the use of a shared resource while the cost of that use is shared by all users, it is rational for individuals to overuse the resource, even though collectively this will likely lead to the depletion of the resource.
mechanism_atoms: Each individual gains full benefit from adding one more unit of use but bears only a 1/N share of the resulting common cost, creating a systematic incentive to over-exploit.
The tragedy arises from divergence between individual rationality and collective rationality; what is optimal for each actor is destructive for the group.
Hardin (1968) proposed privatization or state regulation as the only remedies; Elinor Ostrom (2009 Nobel laureate) empirically refuted this by documenting successful community self-governance.
Ostrom's design principles for sustainable commons include clear group boundaries, proportional allocation rules, collective monitoring, and graduated sanctions.
The model applies to any rivalrous, non-excludable resource (fisheries, groundwater, atmosphere) where property rights are absent or unenforceable.

concepts.name: Quipu
concepts.summary_verbatim: Quipu (/ˈkiːpuː/ KEE-poo), also spelled khipu (Ayacucho Quechua: kipu, [ˈkipu]; Cusco Quechua: khipu, [kʰipu]), are record-keeping devices fashioned from knotted cords.
mechanism_atoms: A main cord bears pendant strings whose knot positions encode numbers in a decimal positional system (knot type and position = ones, tens, hundreds, etc.).
Color of the cord encodes data category (population, tax, crop type, military); cord color combinations extend the information space multiplicatively.
Knot handedness (S-twist vs Z-twist), attachment direction, and cord ply carry additional semantic dimensions beyond number.
Nested pendant cords allow hierarchical data structures (a summary cord with detail sub-cords), enabling complex accounting trees.
Specialist readers (quipucamayocs) were trained imperial officials who could encode and decode census data, tax obligations, and agricultural inventories.

concepts.name: Pastoralism
concepts.summary_verbatim: Pastoralism is a form of animal husbandry where domesticated animals (known as "livestock") are released onto large vegetated outdoor lands (pastures) for grazing, historically by nomadic people who moved around with their herds.
mechanism_atoms: Livestock convert non-arable vegetation (grass, shrubs) into animal protein and draft power, extending human subsistence into environments unsuitable for crop agriculture.
Seasonal grazing rotation prevents overgrazing by moving animals before forage is depleted, allowing vegetation to recover.
Herders exploit spatial heterogeneity in rainfall and pasture quality by moving across the landscape rather than intensifying a fixed location.
Manure from grazing animals fertilizes pastures and maintains soil organic matter, sustaining long-term productivity.
Exchange relations with sedentary farmers (animal products for grain) create economic complementarity that stabilizes both food systems.

concepts.name: Common-pool resource
concepts.summary_verbatim: A common-pool resource (CPR) is a type of good consisting of a natural or human-made resource system (e.g. an irrigation system or fishing ground), the size or characteristics of which makes it costly, but not impossible, to exclude potential beneficiaries from obtaining benefits from its use.
mechanism_atoms: CPRs are simultaneously rivalrous (one person's use diminishes availability) and costly-to-exclude, creating conditions for overexploitation.
Elinor Ostrom documented >800 cases of successful community self-governance without privatization or state control, refuting Hardin's dichotomy.
Effective CPR institutions define clear group boundaries (who has rights), monitor resource condition, and impose graduated sanctions on rule-breakers.
Nested governance (local rules embedded within regional and national frameworks) allows CPR management to scale across jurisdictional levels.
Resource users participate in modifying rules over time; adaptive co-management responds to changing ecological and social conditions.

concepts.name: Alpine transhumance
concepts.summary_verbatim: Alpine transhumance is a seasonal droving of grazing livestock between the valleys in winter and the high mountain pastures in summer.
mechanism_atoms: Herds are driven upward in spring as snowmelt exposes high pastures (alpages), typically above 1500 m in the Alps, reaching up to 2400–2800 m.
Vertical migration exploits the asynchronous growth seasons of low-altitude winter pastures and high-altitude summer pastures, doubling effective grazing area.
Established drove roads (Alpwege, drailles) encode centuries of route knowledge; the same paths have been used since at least the High Middle Ages (documented 1204 CE).
Dairying at altitude (cheese-making in mountain huts) transforms perishable milk into storable products (alpine cheese) that can be carried back to valleys in autumn.
Archaeological evidence (pollen records, animal bone assemblages) traces Alpine transhumance to the later Neolithic, ~3000 BCE.

concepts.name: Stratigraphy (archaeology)
concepts.summary_verbatim: Stratigraphy is a key concept to modern archaeological theory and practice.
mechanism_atoms: Excavators record discrete stratigraphic units (contexts) deposited through human activity or natural processes at a site.
Layers are ordered by superposition: earlier deposits lie beneath later ones, so objects in lower strata predate those above.
Each context is assigned a unique number and its relationship to adjacent contexts is recorded, building a Harris Matrix of relative sequence.
Datable finds within a layer (coins, ceramics with known typologies) anchor the relative sequence to calendar time.
Disturbances such as pits or robber trenches cut through earlier layers and are therefore dated later than the contexts they intrude.

concepts.name: Seriation (archaeology)
concepts.summary_verbatim: In archaeology, seriation is a relative dating method in which assemblages or artifacts from numerous sites in the same culture are placed in chronological order.
mechanism_atoms: Contextual seriation orders assemblages by presence or absence of a design style, grouping those sharing the most styles as contemporaneous.
Frequency seriation ranks assemblages by the proportional abundance of a design style, assuming styles follow a battleship-curve of popularity (rising, peaking, then declining).
Assemblages sharing many stylistic traits are placed adjacent; those sharing few traits are placed further apart in the sequence.
The resulting sequence is taken to indicate time but yields no absolute dates without independent calibration.
William Flinders Petrie applied the method to Egyptian pre-dynastic pottery; Oscar Montelius independently refined it for Scandinavian Bronze Age artefacts.

concepts.name: Dendrochronology
concepts.summary_verbatim: Dendrochronology or tree-ring dating is the scientific method of dating tree rings (also called growth rings) to the exact year they were formed in a tree.
mechanism_atoms: A tree adds one growth ring per year; ring width varies predictably with climate so each year produces a distinctive pattern.
Cross-dating matches the ring-width pattern of an undated sample against a reference chronology of overlapping, dated samples to identify the calendar years of the rings.
Reference chronologies extend back millennia by chaining together overlapping ring sequences from living trees, dead wood, and ancient timbers.
Once a wood sample is dated by cross-dating, the outermost ring gives the felling year of the timber to a precision of one year.
Dendrochronology also calibrates radiocarbon dates by providing wood of known calendar age for comparison against radiocarbon measurements.

concepts.name: Radiocarbon dating
concepts.summary_verbatim: Radiocarbon dating (also referred to as carbon dating or carbon-14 dating) is a method for determining the age of an object containing organic material by using the properties of radiocarbon, a radioactive isotope of carbon.
mechanism_atoms: Cosmic rays produce carbon-14 in the upper atmosphere; living organisms continuously absorb C-14 and maintain a near-constant ratio of C-14 to C-12.
When an organism dies it stops exchanging carbon; C-14 decays at a fixed half-life of approximately 5,700 years, so the surviving ratio decreases predictably.
Measuring the residual C-14 activity (by decay counting or accelerator mass spectrometry) yields the elapsed time since death.
Raw radiocarbon years are converted to calendar years using a calibration curve derived from tree-ring-dated samples and other archives.
The method dates organic material up to about 50,000 years old; Willard Libby developed it in 1949 and received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1960.

concepts.name: Roman roads
concepts.summary_verbatim: At the peak of Rome's development, no fewer than 29 great military highways radiated from the capital, and the empire's 113 provinces were interconnected by 372 great roads.
mechanism_atoms: Construction began by digging a trench to bedrock, which was filled with compacted rubble (statumen) to form a stable, well-drained foundation.
Successive layers of rammed concrete, finer gravel (nucleus), and fitted stone paving (pavimentum) were added above the foundation to create a durable all-weather surface.
A raised central embankment (agger) and flanking drainage ditches kept the roadbed dry and elevated above surrounding terrain.
Way stations (mutationes) provided relay horses at regular intervals; dispatches could travel up to 800 km in 24 hours using a relay of horses.
The network totaled more than 400,000 km of roads, of which 80,500 km were stone-paved, primarily built to move armies but also enabling commerce and administration.

concepts.name: Cursus publicus
concepts.summary_verbatim: The cursus publicus (Latin: 'the public way') was the state mandated and supervised courier and transportation service of the Roman Empire, the use of which continued into the Eastern Roman Empire and the Ostrogothic Kingdom.
mechanism_atoms: Smaller relay posts called mutationes, spaced every 8–12 Roman miles (12–18 km), supplied fresh horses, mules, or vehicles to couriers, preventing animal exhaustion.
Larger posting inns called mansiones, spaced every 20–30 Roman miles (29–44 km), provided lodging, meals, and administrative services for traveling officials.
Access required official passes (diplomata) issued by the emperor or high-ranking officials; unauthorized use was illegal.
Emperor Diocletian later divided the system into two parallel services: one for urgent correspondence (fast horses) and one for bulk shipments (oxen).
Urgent imperial dispatches could achieve relay speeds of up to approximately 160 miles per day; routine traffic moved at about 50 miles per day.

concepts.name: Chapar Khaneh
concepts.summary_verbatim: A Chapar Khaneh (Persian: چاپارخانه, transl. 'courier house') was a postal service station in the Achaemenid Empire.
mechanism_atoms: Relay stations were spaced approximately every 20–25 km along the Royal Road and other key routes of the Persian Empire.
A courier rode each stage at full speed then handed dispatches to the next mounted courier at the station, who rode the next stage — a torch-race metaphor used by Herodotus.
Each station kept fresh horses and provisions so incoming riders could immediately re-mount without delay.
The network allowed messages to travel from Susa to Sardis (approximately 2,700 km) in about nine days, versus roughly 90 days on foot.
Couriers were known as angaros (Greek: ἄγγαρος); the system was later adapted by the Romans as the cursus publicus and by the Mongols as the yam.

concepts.name: Yam (route)
concepts.summary_verbatim: The yam or jam (Russian: ям), also called the örtöö (Mongolian: өртөө, lit. 'checkpoint'), was a Mongol postal system or supply point route messenger system.
mechanism_atoms: Relay stations (örtöö) were placed at intervals of roughly 14–40 miles apart across the Mongol Empire, providing food, shelter, and spare horses to messengers.
Messengers rode at full speed to the next station, handed over dispatches to a fresh messenger, then rested — enabling continuous relay day and night.
Mongol messengers could cover 200–300 km per day using this relay method.
By the late 13th century the network in China alone comprised over 1,400 postal stations supported by approximately 50,000 horses and thousands of other draft animals.
The system was expanded by Ögedei Khan and required local populations to supply horses, fodder, and provisions to stations as a tax obligation.

concepts.name: Silk Road
concepts.summary_verbatim: The Silk Road was a network of Asian trade routes active from the second century BCE until the mid-15th century.
mechanism_atoms: Goods moved via relay trade: individual merchants traveled defined segments between relay stations; no single merchant typically traversed the entire route from China to the Mediterranean.
At each major station merchants sold their goods to the next merchant, who carried them to the following station, repeating until the goods reached their destination — analogous to a relay race.
The overland route divided into northern and southern branches bypassing the Taklamakan Desert, merging and diverging around mountain and desert obstacles.
Caravanserais spaced roughly a day's travel apart provided water, fodder, storage, and security for caravans between major nodes.
The maritime Silk Road allowed ships to carry far larger cargoes over the entire distance without regional relay, but overland relay remained dominant for luxury goods.

concepts.name: Caravanserai
concepts.summary_verbatim: A caravanserai (or caravansary) was an inn that provided lodging for travelers, merchants, and caravans.
mechanism_atoms: Caravanserais were spaced approximately one day's camel-march (25–35 km) apart along trade routes, so a caravan always reached shelter before nightfall.
The standard layout included a central courtyard for animals, surrounding rooms or alcoves for merchants and goods, storage for fodder and supplies, and a water source (well or cistern).
Achaemenid Persia built staging posts along the Royal Road as early as the 6th–4th centuries BCE; Herodotus documented their existence.
Caravanserais provided water for human and animal consumption, fodder, and shops where travellers could replenish supplies, reducing the risk and cost of long-distance transport.
By supporting continuous flow of goods and people, caravanserais enabled the Silk Road and other routes to function as integrated logistical systems rather than isolated journeys.

concepts.name: Horreum (Roman granary)
concepts.summary_verbatim: A horreum (plural: horrea) was a type of public warehouse used during the ancient Roman period.
mechanism_atoms: Horrea used raised floors (suspensurae) on dwarf walls or piers to allow air circulation beneath stored grain, reducing moisture, mold, and pest infestation.
Thick masonry walls (60–90 cm, often with buttresses) and narrow slit windows maintained stable temperatures and provided security.
Interior wall surfaces were coated with olive oil lees (amurca) and plaster for waterproofing and insecticide effect.
By the end of the imperial period Rome had nearly 300 horrea; the largest, the Horrea Galbae, contained 140 ground-floor rooms covering some 21,000 m².
Grain was transported by sea from Egypt or the Black Sea region to port granaries, then redistributed by river barge to legionary fortress granaries farther inland.

concepts.name: Roman aqueduct
concepts.summary_verbatim: Rome's first aqueduct was built in 312 BC, and supplied a water fountain at the city's cattle market.
mechanism_atoms: Water flowed entirely by gravity along a continuous, gently sloping channel (specus), lined with waterproof opus signinum mortar; no pumps were required.
Engineers maintained a precise, shallow gradient (typically 1:4,800) over many kilometers so flow remained steady without erosion or stagnation.
Where valleys were shallow, multi-tiered masonry arcades carried the channel at the correct elevation across the gap using semicircular arches on stone piers.

Where deep valleys had to be crossed, inverted siphons — lead pipes descending into and rising out of the valley — used hydrostatic pressure to push water across, discharging into a receiving tank at a slightly lower elevation.

Settling tanks (piscinae limariae) at intervals trapped sediment to keep the channel clear, and the water was distributed to fountains, baths, and private pipes through a castellum divisorium (distribution basin).

concepts.name: Qanat
concepts.summary_verbatim: A qanāt (Persian: قَنَات) or kārīz (کَارِیز) is a water supply system that was developed in ancient Iran for the purpose of transporting usable water to the surface from an aquifer or a well through an underground aqueduct.
mechanism_atoms: Builders excavated a 'mother well' (mādar chāh) into a hillside aquifer to reach the water table, then dug a gently sloping underground tunnel downhill toward the settlement.
The slope of the tunnel was calibrated to be just steep enough for flow by gravity but too gentle to cause erosion — entirely pump-free.
Vertical access shafts (like a chain of wells) were dug at intervals along the tunnel route to remove spoil during construction and to allow later maintenance and ventilation.
By keeping water underground the qanat prevented evaporation losses severe enough to make surface canals impractical in arid Iran and neighboring regions.
Tens of thousands of qanats still function in approximately 35 countries; the technology is approximately 3,000 years old and originated in Iron Age Iran.

concepts.name: Siege (warfare)
concepts.summary_verbatim: A siege occurs when an attacker encounters a city or fortress that cannot be easily taken by a quick assault, and which refuses to surrender.
mechanism_atoms: In a passive siege (blockade) attackers encircled the target with a line of circumvallation — earthen ramparts and trenches — cutting off food, water, and reinforcements until defenders surrendered or starved.
An outer contravallation line protected besiegers from relief armies attempting to break the blockade from outside.

Active assault tactics included battering rams and siege hooks to breach gates or walls, siege towers to overcome height advantage, and mining (sapping) — tunneling under walls to collapse foundations.
Catapults, ballistae, and other siege engines projected missiles over or against walls to suppress defenders and breach defenses.
Sieges could be decided by starvation, thirst, or disease afflicting either the defender or — if supply lines failed — the besieger.

concepts.name: Debasement (currency)
concepts.summary_verbatim: Debasement lowers the intrinsic value of the coinage and so more coins can be made with the same quantity of precious metal.
mechanism_atoms: The mint reduced the proportion of gold or silver in each coin while issuing it at the same face value, allowing the government to produce more coins from the same bullion stock.
Recipients initially accepted debased coins at face value, but as debasement continued and more coins circulated, prices rose (inflation), eroding purchasing power.
Gresham's Law operated: people hoarded or exported full-weight older coins and spent the debased ones, driving good money out of circulation.
Roman Emperor Nero began reducing the denarius's silver content from ~98% in 64 CE; by the reign of Claudius II (269 CE) the antoninianus contained only ~2% silver.
Governments resorted to debasement to fund wars or deficits without direct taxation, but repeated debasement typically led to economic instability and loss of confidence in the currency.

concepts.name: Tally stick
concepts.summary_verbatim: A tally stick (or simply a tally) was an ancient memory aid used to record and document numbers, quantities, and messages.
mechanism_atoms: Notches of different sizes were carved into a squared hazelwood stick to represent different monetary denominations or quantities; a deep notch might equal a pound, a shallower notch a shilling, etc.
The stick was split lengthwise after notching; each party retained one half bearing identical notches — the longer 'stock' went to the lender/creditor, the shorter 'foil' to the debtor.
Because the grain patterns and notch positions matched perfectly only when the two halves were re-joined, splitting made forgery nearly impossible.
In medieval England from about 1100 CE, tally stocks circulated in a secondary market, being accepted as payment at a discount — functioning as a form of government debt instrument ('wooden money').
The system was abolished by the Receipt of the Exchequer Act 1783; when accumulated tallies were incinerated in 1834, the resulting fire destroyed the Palace of Westminster.

concepts.name: Domesday Book
concepts.summary_verbatim: Domesday Book is a manuscript record of the Great Survey of much of England and parts of Wales completed in 1086 at the behest of William the Conqueror.
mechanism_atoms: Seven or eight panels of royal commissioners fanned out across separate groups of counties, each compiling accounts of the king's and tenants-in-chief's estates.
Each panel convened sworn inquests in county and hundred courts; local juries of free men, village priests, reeves, and subtenants testified under oath to standardized questions.
Questions established who held each manor before the Conquest (1066, tempore regis Edwardi) and who held it in 1086, plus its acreage, ploughlands, meadows, mills, and taxable value.
Cross-examination among the different jury groups reconciled conflicting accounts to produce verified, agreed records.
The survey's data, used for fiscal and tenurial enforcement, was compiled into two volumes; entries were organized by county then by landholder for rapid reference.

concepts.name: Cadastre
concepts.summary_verbatim: A cadastre or cadaster is a comprehensive recording of the real estate or real property's metes-and-bounds of a country.
mechanism_atoms: A cadastre records the boundaries, ownership, and value of every parcel of land in a jurisdiction, enabling taxation proportional to holdings.
Surveyors delineate each parcel using metes-and-bounds descriptions (bearings and distances) or, in later systems, coordinate-based maps.
Roman censors maintained land registers (tabulae censuales) listing property owners, acreage, and estimated values as the basis for the tributum land tax.
Cadastral registers were updated periodically: changes in ownership through sale, inheritance, or confiscation required re-registration to keep the fiscal record current.
The Aragonese catastro (1715), French cadastre napoléonien (1807), and similar systems institutionalized parcel-level mapping as the foundation of state revenue systems across Europe.

concepts.name: Double-entry bookkeeping
concepts.summary_verbatim: Double-entry bookkeeping, also known as double-entry accounting, is a method of bookkeeping in which every financial transaction is recorded with equal and opposite entries (debits and credits) - thus 'balancing the books'.
mechanism_atoms: Every transaction is entered twice: as a debit in one account and an equal credit in at least one other account, so total debits always equal total credits across the ledger.
The accounting equation (Assets = Liabilities + Equity) is preserved by every transaction, enabling detection of arithmetic errors — any imbalance signals a mistake.
Credits and debits are posted on opposite sides of a T-account (credit right, debit left); the net balance of all accounts can be read from a trial balance.
The method was codified and published by Luca Pacioli in 1494 in Venice, systematizing practices already used by Italian merchants for approximately two centuries.
By recording both the source and the destination of every transfer of value, double-entry makes fraud and omission easier to detect than single-entry systems.

concepts.name: Plague of Justinian
concepts.summary_verbatim: The Antonine Plague of AD 165 to 180 (named for the emperors Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus of the Antonine dynasty), also known as the Plague of Galen (after Galen, the Greek physician who described it), was a prolonged and destructive epidemic, which affected the Roman Empire.
mechanism_atoms: The plague was caused by Yersinia pestis bacteria, transmitted via flea bites; infected fleas regurgitated bacteria into the bite wound of a new rodent or human host.
Grain ships from Egypt introduced infected rats to Constantinople circa 541 CE, providing a reservoir in the densely populated capital.
Trade routes and military supply trains spread infected rats and their fleas along established corridors throughout the Byzantine Empire and beyond.
The disease caused swelling of the lymph nodes (buboes), septicemia, and pneumonia, killing rapidly; contemporary sources reported 5,000–10,000 deaths per day at the Constantinople peak.
The first pandemic lasted from approximately 541 to 750 CE in recurrent waves, killing an estimated 25–50 million people across the Mediterranean and Near East.

concepts.name: Black Death
concepts.summary_verbatim: The Black Death was a plague pandemic that occurred in Europe from 1346 to 1353.
mechanism_atoms: Bubonic plague (Yersinia pestis) spread primarily through bites of infected rat fleas (Xenopsylla cheopis), with secondary pneumonic spread person-to-person via respiratory droplets.
The disease traveled along established trade routes — Silk Road, Black Sea, and Mediterranean maritime networks — carried by rats in merchant ships and caravans.
Symptoms included fever, chills, and painful swollen lymph nodes (buboes) in the groin, armpits, or neck; pneumonic form produced bloody sputum and was almost invariably fatal.
The pandemic killed approximately one-third to one-half of Europe's population between 1346 and 1353, with mortality rates in cities often exceeding 50%.
Recurrent waves continued after 1353; the epidemiological pattern of explosive urban outbreaks followed by rural spread and subsidence matched the dynamics of a rodent-flea-human transmission cycle.

concepts.name: Late Bronze Age collapse
concepts.summary_verbatim: The Late Bronze Age collapse was a period of societal collapse in the Mediterranean basin during the late 13th to early 12th century BC.
mechanism_atoms: A multi-causal 'perfect storm' is the leading theory: overlapping drought, famine, Sea People invasions, internal rebellions, and disruption of long-distance trade networks interacted to overwhelm interconnected Bronze Age kingdoms.

Dendrochronological and isotopic evidence points to a prolonged drought (approximately 300 years) in the Eastern Mediterranean beginning circa 1200 BCE, triggering agricultural failure and population movements.

Bronze Age palatial economies depended on long-distance exchange of tin (from Central Asia/Afghanistan) and copper (Cyprus) to produce bronze; collapse of trade routes cut off weapon and tool production.
The high interdependence of the palace-based city-states meant collapse in one region (Hittites, Mycenae) cascaded to destabilize trading partners across the system.

Most affected civilizations — Mycenaean Greece, Hittite Empire, Ugarit — never recovered; Egypt survived in weakened form; the Iron Age that followed relied on more locally available iron rather than long-distance bronze supply chains.

concepts.name: Societal collapse
concepts.summary_verbatim: Societal collapse (also known as civilizational collapse or systems collapse) is the fall of a complex human society characterized by the loss of cultural identity and of social complexity as an adaptive system, the downfall of government, and the rise of violence.
mechanism_atoms: Joseph Tainter's model holds that societies invest increasing resources in complexity (administration, military, infrastructure) to solve problems; returns on complexity eventually diminish while costs keep rising.
When the marginal return on added complexity falls below subsistence level, collapse — rapid simplification — becomes economically rational as a collective outcome.
Collapse manifests as loss of stratification, specialization, and long-distance exchange; population declines, trade contracts, and literacy may disappear as complex institutions fail.
Climate shifts, epidemics, invasion, and internal revolt can each trigger or accelerate collapse but typically interact: they reduce the resource surplus that maintains complexity.
Virtually all civilizations have suffered societal collapse; most never recovered their prior complexity — exceptions include Rome in the West (collapsed ~476 CE) and Maya civilization.

concepts.name: Smoke signal
concepts.summary_verbatim: The smoke signal is one of the oldest forms of long-distance communication.
mechanism_atoms: Fires were lit on elevated points (hilltops, towers) to maximize visibility; dry fuel produced flame and light; damp fuel such as green grass or dung added to the fire produced thick, visible smoke columns.
Blankets, hides, or shields were used to interrupt smoke columns, generating distinct puffs that encoded pre-arranged meanings.
Relay chains of beacon fires transmitted a binary signal (fire/no-fire) across hundreds of kilometers almost instantaneously — faster than any courier.
Chinese soldiers along the Great Wall used smoke signals from beacon towers to warn of enemy invasion; the color or volume of smoke could indicate the size of the invading force.
The Greek historian Polybius (2nd century BCE) described a polybius fire-signaling system that could transmit alphabetic messages by using combinations of torches arranged in grids.

concepts.name: Heliograph
concepts.summary_verbatim: A heliograph (from Ancient Greek ἥλιος (hḗlios) 'sun' and γράφειν (gráphein) 'to write') is a solar telegraph system that signals by flashes of sunlight (generally using Morse code from the 1840s) reflected by a mirror.
mechanism_atoms: An operator aimed a polished mirror to reflect sunlight toward a distant station, then interrupted the beam using a shutter or by tilting the mirror to produce dots and dashes of Morse code.
The flashing light was visible up to 50–80 km in clear weather, requiring no fuel, wire infrastructure, or electrical power.
Relay stations re-transmitted received signals, enabling messages to traverse mountain ranges and deserts without any physical connection.
The British Army used heliographs extensively in India and southern Africa (1870s–1900s) as a tactical communication system requiring only sunlight and trained operators.

Limitations included dependency on sunshine and clear line-of-sight, making the system useless at night or in cloud cover — the same constraint that had limited all pre-electric optical telegraph systems.

concepts.name: Census
concepts.summary_verbatim: A census is often construed as the opposite of a sample as it intends to count everyone in a population, rather than a fraction.
mechanism_atoms: Ancient Roman censors conducted the census every five years (lustrum): adult male citizens declared their name, age, family, property value, and tribe before designated officials (censors).
Data were collected by ward (vicus) and tribe (tribus) at the Field of Mars in Rome; provincial governors submitted returns for non-citizen populations.
Declared information was used to assign military obligations (based on property class), determine voting weight (comitia centuriata), and calculate tax liability.
Enumerators recorded individual-level data on tabulae (tablets); totals were inscribed on public monuments and stored in the aerarium (treasury).
False declaration was a criminal offense (capitis deminutio); verification was achieved by cross-checking declarations across household members and witnesses.

concepts.name: History of military logistics
concepts.summary_verbatim: The history of military logistics goes back to Neolithic times.
mechanism_atoms: Ancient armies typically foraged (living off the land) or exacted food from civilian populations along their line of march; systematic supply depots emerged as armies grew too large to be fed by local foraging alone.
Roman legions relied on a combination of pre-positioned supply caches, purchasing agents (frumentarii), river and sea transport, and road networks to sustain campaigns far from Italy.
Sea and river transport was far cheaper than overland carriage: it was estimated cheaper to ship grain across the entire Mediterranean than to cart it 120 km overland.
Granaries (horrea) at legionary fortresses stored typically a year's supply of grain, enabling operations through winter or during prolonged sieges without dependence on seasonal harvest.
Logistical failure — running out of food, fodder, or transport animals — was a primary cause of campaign failure; armies that could not feed themselves disintegrated through desertion or starvation.

concepts.name: Roman currency (debasement)
concepts.summary_verbatim: Roman currency for most of Roman history consisted of gold, silver, bronze, orichalcum (brass), and copper coinage.
mechanism_atoms: The silver denarius, introduced c. 211 BCE at ~4.5 g of near-pure silver, was progressively reduced in silver content by successive emperors to cover military and administrative costs.
Nero (64 CE) began formal debasement, reducing silver content from ~98% to ~93% and shaving coin weight; the process accelerated under 3rd-century military emperors.
By 269 CE the antoninianus (double denarius) contained only about 2% silver, effectively becoming a bronze coin with a silver wash — triggering severe inflation.
Diocletian's currency reform (301 CE) attempted to stabilize coinage by issuing a new high-silver argenteus and fixing prices by edict, but the Edict on Maximum Prices largely failed.
The repeated debasement cycle — reduce silver → increase money supply → inflation → loss of confidence → further reduction — contributed to the fiscal crisis of the 3rd century CE.

concepts.name: Vowel harmony
concepts.summary_verbatim: In phonology, vowel harmony is a phonological process in which vowels assimilate ("harmonize") to share certain distinctive features.
mechanism_atoms: One vowel (the trigger) causes other vowels within the phonological domain (typically the word) to shift so they match its feature value.
The constraint operates long-distance: affected vowels need not be adjacent to the trigger; intervening consonants are transparent.
Common harmonizing features include backness, height, nasalization, roundedness, and advanced/retracted tongue root.
The vowel that causes the assimilation is called the trigger; vowels that must match it are called targets.
Harmony is confined to the phonological word domain but may extend across word boundaries in some languages.

concepts.name: Phonological assimilation
concepts.summary_verbatim: In phonology, assimilation is a sound change in which some phonemes (typically consonants or vowels) change to become more similar to other nearby sounds.
mechanism_atoms: A segment acquires one or more phonetic features from an adjacent or nearby segment, reducing articulatory distance between them.
Changes triggered by a following segment (anticipatory/regressive assimilation) are far more frequent than those triggered by a preceding segment (perseverative/progressive assimilation).
Regular assimilation is conditioned purely by phonological environment, not by word meaning.
Assimilation to a nonadjacent segment is possible but far less common than assimilation to an immediately adjacent one.
The physiological mechanism involves coarticulation—overlapping articulatory gestures for adjacent sounds.

concepts.name: Tone sandhi
concepts.summary_verbatim: Tone sandhi is a phonological change that occurs in tonal languages, involving changes to the tones assigned to individual words or morphemes, based on the pronunciation of adjacent words or morphemes.
mechanism_atoms: Tone sandhi is a compulsory change that occurs when certain tones are juxtaposed in connected speech.
In East/Southeast Asian languages, paradigmatic replacement is common: one tone changes to another in a given environment regardless of whether the new tone already exists in surrounding morphemes.
In North American and African tonal languages, syntagmatic displacement is typical: one tone is replaced by another already present in adjacent tones.
In Mandarin, Tone 3 before another Tone 3 shifts to Tone 2 (rising), and before any other tone it surfaces as a low falling tone.
The change typically simplifies bidirectional tone sequences into one-directional ones, reducing articulatory complexity.

concepts.name: Agglutinative language
concepts.summary_verbatim: An agglutinative language is a type of language that primarily forms words by stringing together morphemes (word parts)—each typically representing a single grammatical meaning—without significant modification to their forms.
mechanism_atoms: Affixes (prefixes, suffixes, infixes, circumfixes) are added linearly to a root, each affix carrying exactly one grammatical meaning.
Morpheme boundaries are transparent: the form of each affix is consistent and does not fuse with adjacent morphemes.
This contrasts with fusional languages where a single affix encodes multiple grammatical categories simultaneously.
The term derives from Latin agglutinare ('to glue together'), coined by Wilhelm von Humboldt.
Example: Japanese kaku + masu + ta = kakimashita ('wrote'), where each morpheme retains its identity.

concepts.name: Reduplication
concepts.summary_verbatim: In linguistics, reduplication is a morphological process in which the root or stem of a word, part of that, or the whole word is repeated exactly or with a slight change.
mechanism_atoms: Reduplication can be described phonologically as repetition of segments (consonants/vowels) or prosodic units (syllables, moras).
It can also be described morphologically as repetition of linguistic constituents—words, stems, or roots.
Functions include encoding plurality, intensification, repetition, distribution, or habituality (Sapir's 'self-evident symbolism').
Reduplication is theoretically significant as an interface phenomenon between phonology and morphology.
It is used both for inflection (grammatical categories) and for lexical derivation (creating new words).

concepts.name: Recursive grammar
concepts.summary_verbatim: A recursive grammar is one that contains production rules that are recursive, meaning that expanding a non-terminal according to these rules can eventually lead to a string that includes the same non-terminal again.
mechanism_atoms: A non-terminal symbol in a grammar rule can reappear as input to the same rule, enabling infinite embedding of structures within structures.
Recursion allows a finite set of rules to generate an infinite set of sentences.
A non-recursive grammar can produce only a finite language; all finite languages can be expressed without recursion.
Chomsky argued that unbounded sentence length in natural language follows directly from recursive rules in the grammar.
The faculty of language in the narrow sense (FLn) is hypothesized to consist primarily of the computational mechanism of recursion, unique to humans.

concepts.name: Agreement (linguistics)
concepts.summary_verbatim: In linguistics, agreement or concord (abbreviated agr) occurs when a word changes form depending on the other words to which it relates.
mechanism_atoms: Agreement is an instance of inflection: a word's form is determined by the grammatical feature values (person, number, gender, case) of another word in the clause.
The agreeing word (the controller) imposes its feature values on the target word, which must inflect accordingly.
Agreement typically holds between a verb and its subject (subject-verb agreement) or between a noun and its modifier.
It is a redundancy mechanism: the same semantic information (e.g., plurality) is encoded on multiple words in the phrase.
The same principle applies across sentences in pronoun-antecedent agreement, a case of long-distance feature matching.

concepts.name: Dependency grammar
concepts.summary_verbatim: Dependency is the notion that linguistic units, such as words, are connected to each other by directed links.
mechanism_atoms: The finite verb is the structural center (root) of the clause; all other words depend on it directly or transitively.
Every word (except the root) has exactly one head, giving the structure a tree topology with directed arcs from head to dependent.
Each head-dependent arc carries a syntactic function label (e.g., SUBJ, OBJ, DET, ATTR).
Unlike phrase-structure grammar, dependency grammar does not posit intermediate phrase nodes—only word-to-word relations.
Lucien Tesnière (1893–1954) formalized modern dependency grammar, positioning the verb as the root of all clause structure.

concepts.name: Sound change
concepts.summary_verbatim: In historical linguistics, a sound change is a change in the pronunciation of a language.
mechanism_atoms: Sound change operates under the working assumption of regularity: it applies mechanically whenever its structural (phonological) conditions are met, irrespective of word meaning.
A sound change may be conditioned (occurring only in specific phonological environments) or unconditioned (applying to all instances of the sound).
Types include phonetic replacement, phoneme merger (two sounds collapse into one), and phoneme split (one sound diverges into two).
The Neogrammarians coined the term 'sound law' in the 19th century, codifying specific changes as Grimm's law, Verner's law, etc.
Exceptions to regular sound change are attributed to analogy, dialect borrowing, or lexical diffusion.

concepts.name: Grammaticalization
concepts.summary_verbatim: Grammaticalization is a continuous historical process in which free-standing words develop into grammatical appendages, while these in turn become ever more specialized and grammatical.
mechanism_atoms: The process is consistently unidirectional: words move from concrete to abstract meaning, not the reverse.
A formerly autonomous lexical item (e.g., a verb of motion or possession) gradually loses semantic content and acquires grammatical function (e.g., tense marker, auxiliary).
As a word grammaticalizes it typically undergoes phonological reduction (erosion) and becomes phonologically dependent on adjacent words.
The term was coined by Antoine Meillet in 1912 as 'the attribution of a grammatical nature to a formerly autonomous word'.
Grammaticalization is a subtype of semantic change and feeds morphological paradigm-building over generations.

concepts.name: Comparative method (linguistics)
concepts.summary_verbatim: Comparative reconstruction, usually referred to just as reconstruction, establishes features of the ancestor of two or more related languages, belonging to the same language family, by means of the comparative method.
mechanism_atoms: Linguists identify cognate sets—sets of words in different related languages that descend from a common ancestral form.
Regular sound correspondences across cognates are identified; a sequence of sound laws (regular changes) is postulated to explain the correspondences.
Reconstructed ancestral forms (protoforms) are written with an asterisk (*) to indicate they are hypothetical, not attested.
The method emerged in the early 19th century with Indo-European studies and was formalized by the Neogrammarians.
Key contributors include Rasmus Rask, Jacob Grimm, and August Schleicher, who produced the first systematic proto-language reconstruction in 1861.

concepts.name: Abjad
concepts.summary_verbatim: An abjad is a segmental script containing symbols for consonants only, or where vowels are optionally written with diacritics ("pointing") or only written word-initially.
mechanism_atoms: Basic graphemes represent only consonants; vowel sounds are implied by the reader from phonological context and lexical knowledge.
Where vowel diacritics exist (Hebrew niqqud, Arabic harakat), their use is optional and not the dominant literate form.
This script type is distinguished from alphabets (which require vowel graphemes) by Peter T. Daniels's typology.
The name 'abjad' comes from the first four letters of the original Arabic alphabetical order: alef, ba, jim, dal.
Examples: Arabic, Hebrew, Syriac—all Semitic languages whose phonology supports consonantal ambiguity resolution.

concepts.name: Logogram
concepts.summary_verbatim: A logogram (also logograph or lexigraph) is a written character that represents a semantic component of a language, such as a word or morpheme.
mechanism_atoms: The grapheme maps to a unit of meaning (word or morpheme) rather than to a sound; there is no direct phonetic link in the basic character.
In practice, all known logographic systems include a phonetic dimension via the rebus principle—characters are borrowed for their sound to represent new meanings.
Adding a phonetic component to ideographs is considered the key innovation enabling writing to fully encode human language.
Logographic systems require hundreds to thousands of distinct symbols, contrasting with alphabets' fewer than 100.
Examples: Chinese characters, Egyptian hieroglyphs, cuneiform script all combine logographic and phonetic elements.

concepts.name: Syllabary
concepts.summary_verbatim: In the linguistic study of written languages, a syllabary is a set of written symbols that represent the syllables or (more frequently) morae which make up words.
mechanism_atoms: Each symbol (syllabogram) typically represents a consonant + vowel (CV) unit, or a vowel alone, encoding a full syllable in one grapheme.
Syllabaries require hundreds of symbols, versus fewer than 100 for alphabets and thousands for logographies.
Languages using syllabaries tend to have simple phonotactics dominated by CV syllables, which map cleanly to syllabogram inventory.
Japanese kana (hiragana and katakana), developed around 800 CE, are the best-known living syllabaries.
Syllabaries occupy a typological middle ground between alphabets (sub-syllabic) and logographies (supra-syllabic).

concepts.name: Boustrophedon
concepts.summary_verbatim: Boustrophedon is a style of writing in which alternate lines of writing are reversed, with letters also written in reverse, mirror-style.
mechanism_atoms: Writing proceeds in one horizontal direction on the first line, then the direction reverses on the next line (and letters are mirrored), continuing to alternate.
The name derives from Greek for 'as the ox turns (in plowing)'—the writer's hand turns at each end like a plowman.
Early alphabetic writing (including early Greek) commonly used boustrophedon before settling on left-to-right convention.
A variant ('reverse boustrophedon') in Rongorongo rotates the entire tablet 180° between lines rather than mirroring characters.
Modern writing systems universally adopt a fixed direction per line; boustrophedon survives only in ancient inscriptions.

concepts.name: Poverty of the stimulus
concepts.summary_verbatim: In linguistics, the poverty of the stimulus is the claim that children are not exposed to rich enough data within their linguistic environments to acquire every feature of their language without innate language-specific cognitive biases.
mechanism_atoms: Children receive only positive evidence: they hear grammatical sentences but are not corrected on what is ungrammatical.
Some grammatical generalizations require distinguishing between hypotheses that could only be differentiated by negative evidence (ungrammatical forms), which children never receive.
Children nonetheless converge on the correct adult grammar, suggesting innate constraints guide hypothesis selection.
This convergence is used as evidence for Universal Grammar—innate aspects of linguistic competence.
The term was coined by Noam Chomsky in Rules and Representations (1980).

concepts.name: Critical period hypothesis
concepts.summary_verbatim: The critical period hypothesis is a hypothesis within the field of linguistics and second language acquisition that claims a person can achieve native-like fluency in a language only before a certain age.
mechanism_atoms: The first few years of life constitute a window during which first-language acquisition occurs readily, supported by high neuroplasticity.
Syntactic aspects of language are based on computational mechanisms operable only during certain developmental periods.
Semantic aspects rely on associative learning mechanisms, which allow lifelong learning beyond the critical period.
After the critical period (somewhere between age 5 and puberty), language acquisition becomes significantly harder and typically less successful.
First proposed by Wilder Penfield and Lamar Roberts (1959) and popularized by Eric Lenneberg in Biological Foundations of Language (1967).

concepts.name: Cooperative principle (Gricean maxims)
concepts.summary_verbatim: The cooperative principle is a norm governing all cooperative interactions among humans.
mechanism_atoms: Grice's principle states: make your contribution as required by the accepted purpose of the conversation.
Four maxims operationalize it: Quantity (be sufficiently informative), Quality (be truthful), Relation (be relevant), Manner (be clear and orderly).
By adhering to or deliberately flouting these maxims, speakers imply additional meanings beyond literal content.
Listeners infer conversational implicatures by assuming the speaker is following (or purposefully violating) the maxims.
The principle was formulated by H. P. Grice and became foundational to the linguistic field of pragmatics.

concepts.name: Deixis
concepts.summary_verbatim: Deixis refers to context-bound reference words, and more specifically, the phenomenon whereby contextual features of the speech event are encoded by lexical and grammatical means.
mechanism_atoms: Deictic expressions derive their meaning from the deictic center (origo): the originating source point, typically the speaker in the speech event.
Person deixis encodes speaker ('I'), addressee ('you'), and other ('he/she/they') relative to the origo.
Spatial deixis ('here', 'there') and temporal deixis ('now', 'then') also radiate from the speaker's position in space and time.
Without access to the deictic center, deictic expressions cannot be resolved to referents—they are context-dependent by design.
Deixis and indexicality are near-synonyms; deixis is associated with linguistics, indexicality with philosophy and semiotics.

concepts.name: Implicature
concepts.summary_verbatim: In pragmatics, a subdiscipline of linguistics, an implicature is something the speaker suggests or implies with an utterance, even though it is not literally expressed.
mechanism_atoms: Conversational implicatures arise because hearers assume speakers are following Grice's cooperative principle and maxims.
When a speaker appears to violate a maxim (e.g., says something uninformative), the hearer seeks an interpretation that restores cooperation.
Conventional implicatures are tied to specific lexical items ('but', 'therefore') and do not depend on conversational context.
Implicatures are defeasible: they can be cancelled without contradiction, unlike entailments.
The term was coined by H. P. Grice in 1975 as a cover term for 'imply', 'suggest', 'indicate', and 'mean'.

concepts.name: Sign language (linguistic structure)
concepts.summary_verbatim: Sign languages have capability and complexity equal to spoken languages; their study as part of the field of linguistics has demonstrated that they exhibit the fundamental properties that exist in all languages.
mechanism_atoms: Sign languages exhibit duality of patterning: meaningless sub-units (handshapes, movements, locations) combine into meaningful signs.
They exhibit full recursion: grammatical rules can feed back into themselves, enabling unbounded clause embedding.
Signs are conventional and often arbitrary—they lack direct visual resemblance to their referents, like words in spoken language.
The spatial modality enables simultaneous expression: classifiers allow spatial representation of a referent's type, size, shape, movement, and extent at once.
Visual perception allows processing of simultaneous information, exploiting the spatial channel in ways impossible for the serial acoustic channel.

concepts.name: Creole language
concepts.summary_verbatim: A creole language is a stable natural language developed from a mixture of different languages.
mechanism_atoms: Creoles arise when adult learners of a target language receive only fragmentary input due to social/physical separation from native speakers, producing a pidgin.
Children of pidgin speakers then nativize this system—acquiring it as a first language—and expand it into a full creole with stable grammar.
The adult pidgin-formation stage involves reduction of overt grammatical apparatus due to imperfect L2 learning.
The child nativization stage adds grammar, vocabulary, and regularity beyond what the pidgin input contained.
McWhorter proposes that creoles characteristically lack contextual inflection, functional tone, and semantically opaque word formation.

concepts.name: Pidgin
concepts.summary_verbatim: Pidgins are simplified versions of their lexifier languages with limited lexicons, and words from the lexifier language may acquire completely new meanings in the pidgin.
mechanism_atoms: Pidgins form through contact between groups lacking a common language; they draw vocabulary primarily from a superstrate (lexifier) language.
Grammar comes largely from the substrate (native) languages of the speakers, not from the lexifier—a process called relexification.
Pidgin genesis involves gradual borrowing of lexifier vocabulary onto a substrate grammatical scaffold.
Pidgins have no native speakers; when children acquire one as a first language, it expands into a creole.
Unlike creoles, pidgins have restricted vocabulary, simplified phonology, and lack the full grammatical range of a natural language.

concepts.name: Semantic change
concepts.summary_verbatim: In diachronic (or historical) linguistics, semantic change is a change in one of the meanings of a word.
mechanism_atoms: Every word has multiple senses; semantic change adds, removes, or alters senses over time, sometimes producing meanings radically different from the original.
Semantic chaining: new meanings link to existing ones when they are proximal in semantic space, forming chain-like structures of incremental extension.
Grammaticalization is a prominent mechanism: concrete lexical items gradually shift to abstract grammatical function words.
Frequency of use and polysemy are correlated with rate of semantic change; high-frequency words undergo change more readily.
Semantic change is regular enough that cognates across related languages can diverge in meaning while remaining etymologically traceable.

concepts.name: Zipf's law
concepts.summary_verbatim: Zipf's law states that if words of language are ranked in the order of decreasing frequency in texts, the frequency of a word is inversely proportional to its rank.
mechanism_atoms: The frequency of the nth most common word is approximately 1/n of the most common word's frequency, producing a power-law distribution.
This pattern is hypothesized to arise from a mediation between two pressures: minimizing production cost (speaker) and maximizing transmission success (hearer).
Information-theoretically, Zipf's law is the expected outcome of a communicative system under a rigorous definition of communicative tension.
A computer simulation using dual-process theory replicates the structural pattern, suggesting common cognitive mechanisms drive the distribution.
Named after George Kingsley Zipf; it applies broadly across languages, genres, and even non-linguistic ranked data.

concepts.name: Nonconcatenative morphology
concepts.summary_verbatim: Nonconcatenative morphology, also called discontinuous morphology and introflection, is a form of word formation and inflection in which the root is modified and which does not involve stringing morphemes together sequentially.
mechanism_atoms: A Semitic stem comprises a consonantal root (encoding the semantic domain) and a vowel melody (encoding grammatical category), arranged by a canonical CV-pattern template.
The root, vowel melody, and pattern morphemes are assigned to separate tiers; association rules map them onto a single phonological string.
Example: Arabic root k-t-b 'writing' + vowel patterns produces kataba 'he wrote', kitaab 'book', kaatib 'writer', etc.
This is called transfixation: the vowel morpheme is interdigitated through the consonantal root rather than appended.
McCarthy's autosegmental account assigns consonantal root and vowel pattern to parallel tiers, enabling independent manipulation of each.

concepts.name: Language transfer
concepts.summary_verbatim: Language transfer is the application of linguistic features from one language to another by a bilingual or multilingual speaker, and is also known as L1 interference, linguistic interference, and crosslinguistic influence.
mechanism_atoms: Positive transfer occurs when L1 and L2 structures coincide, facilitating acquisition; negative transfer (interference) occurs when they diverge, producing errors.
Transfer is more likely early in L2 acquisition when the learner's L2 grammar and lexicon are underdeveloped.
Typological distance matters: transfer is more probable between closely related languages sharing features.
Transfer can affect phonology, grammar, vocabulary, discourse structure, and reading processes.
The source need not be the native language; transfer also occurs from a previously learned L2 or L3.

concepts.name: Lexical diffusion
concepts.summary_verbatim: Lexical diffusion is the hypothesis that a sound change is an abrupt change that spreads gradually across the words in a language to which it is applicable.
mechanism_atoms: A sound change begins by affecting a few words and then spreads incrementally through the vocabulary over time.
The phonetic change itself is discrete and abrupt within any given word (phonetically abrupt), but the spread across lexical items is gradual (lexically gradual).
This contrasts with the Neogrammarian view that sound change applies simultaneously to all qualifying words as an articulatory drift.
Lexical diffusion was reformulated and named by William Wang studying Chinese dialects in the 1960s–1970s.
Word frequency and lexical connectivity influence the order in which words are affected by the spreading change.

concepts.name: Phonological rule
concepts.summary_verbatim: A phonological rule is a formal way of expressing a systematic phonological or morphophonological process in linguistics.
mechanism_atoms: Rules are written as formal rewrite rules specifying: what sound changes, what it changes to, and the phonological environment triggering the change.
Rules are commonly expressed using distinctive features—natural, articulatory/acoustic characteristics—allowing generalization over classes of sounds.
Example: intervocalic alveolar flapping in American English changes /t/ and /d/ to a flap between vowels (as in 'butter').
Phonological rules are used in generative phonology to model the brain's computations in producing and perceiving speech.
Rules interact: their ordering (feeding vs. bleeding relations) determines the surface output when multiple rules could apply.

concepts.name: Adaptive immune system
concepts.summary_verbatim: Adaptive immunity creates immunological memory after an initial response to a specific pathogen, and leads to an enhanced response to future encounters with that pathogen.
mechanism_atoms: Lymphocytes (T and B cells) recognise specific antigens via antigen receptors, unlike the innate immune system which responds non-specifically.
Upon first antigen exposure, clonal expansion produces effector cells that mount the primary immune response and memory cells that persist.
On re-exposure, memory cells enable a faster and stronger secondary response, conferring immunological memory.
B cells differentiate into plasma cells that secrete antibodies; T cells differentiate into helper, cytotoxic, or regulatory subsets.
Clonal selection ensures only lymphocytes bearing receptors matching the invading antigen are activated and amplified.

concepts.name: Clonal selection
concepts.summary_verbatim: In immunology, clonal selection theory explains the functions of cells of the immune system (lymphocytes) in response to specific antigens invading the body.
mechanism_atoms: When B or T cells encounter their matched antigen they multiply, producing many clones all targeting the same antigen.
B cells that respond most avidly to antigen are preferentially selected to proliferate and mature.
Clonal expansion amplifies rare antigen-specific lymphocytes into a large pool of effector cells.
Selected clones include both short-lived effector cells and long-lived memory cells.
The process underpins both primary immune responses and immunological memory.

concepts.name: Immunological memory
concepts.summary_verbatim: Immunological memory is the ability of the immune system to respond more rapidly and effectively to a pathogen that has been encountered previously.
mechanism_atoms: After the primary immune response, antigen-specific T and B memory cells persist in blood circulation in a resting state for up to several decades.
On re-encounter with the same antigen, memory cells are reactivated immediately and respond faster and more strongly than naive cells.
Memory B cells produce antibodies upon reactivation, effectively protecting the organism from disease.
Vaccination exploits this mechanism by injecting non-pathogenic antigen to generate durable memory without causing disease.
Immunity to some diseases (e.g. chickenpox, measles) lasts a lifetime, while immunity to others wanes over time.

concepts.name: Complement system
concepts.summary_verbatim: The complement system triggers phagocytosis by opsonizing antigens; the alternative complement pathway is one element of innate immunity.
mechanism_atoms: Complement proteins circulate as inactive precursors; sequential activation creates a cascade that amplifies the response.
Opsonization: complement fragments (C4b, C3b, iC3b) coat pathogens, marking them for phagocytosis by macrophages and neutrophils.
The membrane attack complex (MAC) formed by terminal complement components lyses target cells directly.
Complement can act independently of adaptive immunity, providing immediate innate opsonization.
Three activation pathways (classical, lectin, alternative) converge on cleavage of C3, the central amplification step.

concepts.name: Dose-response relationship
concepts.summary_verbatim: A dose–response relationship is a function or curve that describes the change in effect on an organism caused by different levels of exposure to a stressor after a certain exposure time.
mechanism_atoms: The adage 'the dose makes the poison' captures how a small amount of a toxin may have no effect while a large amount is lethal.
The curve is typically sigmoidal; key parameters include EC50 (concentration producing 50% maximal effect), Hill coefficient (nH, steepness), and Emax (maximal effect).
Pharmacodynamics emphasises dose-response relationships: drug concentration drives biological effect via receptor binding.
A threshold dose must be exceeded before any measurable effect occurs; below threshold, homeostatic mechanisms compensate.
Factors modulating the curve include physicochemical drug properties, route and duration of administration, species, sex, and age.

concepts.name: Pharmacokinetics
concepts.summary_verbatim: Pharmacokinetics is the study of the bodily absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion of drugs.
mechanism_atoms: Absorption: drug moves from site of administration into systemic circulation, governed by bioavailability.
Distribution: drug disperses through body fluids and tissues, influenced by plasma protein binding and lipophilicity.
Metabolism: cytochrome P450 and glucuronosyltransferase enzymes chemically transform the drug, often reducing activity and increasing polarity for excretion.
Excretion: kidneys filter drug metabolites from blood into urine; hepatic biliary excretion also contributes.
Clearance kinetics determine plasma half-life and dosing interval needed to maintain therapeutic concentrations.

concepts.name: Basic reproduction number (R0)
concepts.summary_verbatim: The basic reproduction number, R0, of an infection is the expected number of cases directly generated by one case in a population where all individuals are susceptible to infection.
mechanism_atoms: R0 is calculated by multiplying the average number of contacts by the probability that a susceptible contact becomes infected (the shedding potential).
When R0 > 1 the infection spreads exponentially through a wholly susceptible population; when R0 < 1 it dies out.
R0 is not a biological constant: it depends on social behaviour, contact rates, and environment, not just pathogen biology.
R0 cannot itself be modified by vaccination, but the effective reproduction number Re is reduced as population immunity increases.
R0 determines the herd immunity threshold: the fraction of the population that must be immune to halt spread equals 1 − 1/R0.

concepts.name: Herd immunity
concepts.summary_verbatim: When a critical proportion of the population becomes immune, called the herd immunity threshold (HIT) or herd immunity level (HIL), the disease may no longer persist in the population, ceasing to be endemic.
mechanism_atoms: The herd immunity threshold (HIT) = 1 − 1/R0; above this fraction of immune individuals, each case generates fewer than one secondary case and the chain of transmission breaks.
Both natural infection and vaccination can confer immunity that contributes to the population threshold.
Even individuals who cannot be immunised are protected indirectly once the threshold is exceeded, because transmission chains collapse.
Heterogeneous contact rates mean some sub-populations reach threshold earlier than others, creating pockets of vulnerability.
Loss of immunity over time (waning) or entry of naive individuals can push the population back below the threshold and allow re-emergence.

concepts.name: Blood sugar regulation
concepts.summary_verbatim: Blood sugar regulation is the process by which the body maintains blood glucose within a narrow range, and it is composed of several interacting systems, of which hormone regulation is the most important.
mechanism_atoms: Pancreatic beta cells sense elevated blood glucose and secrete insulin; insulin causes liver cells to convert glucose to glycogen and drives uptake by muscle and fat cells, lowering blood glucose.
Pancreatic alpha cells sense low blood glucose and secrete glucagon; glucagon stimulates glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis in the liver, raising blood glucose.
Insulin and glucagon form a bidirectional negative-feedback loop that keeps glucose in a narrow homeostatic range.
Beta cells inhibit insulin secretion when glucose falls low, removing the corrective signal when it is no longer needed.
Additional hormones (cortisol, epinephrine, growth hormone) provide secondary counter-regulatory mechanisms during prolonged hypoglycaemia.

concepts.name: Insulin
concepts.summary_verbatim: Insulin is a peptide hormone produced by beta cells of the pancreatic islets encoded in humans by the insulin (INS) gene.
mechanism_atoms: Beta cells secrete insulin in response to rising blood glucose; secretion is inhibited when glucose is low.
Insulin binds its receptor on target cells (liver, muscle, adipose), triggering a tyrosine kinase signalling cascade.
In liver: promotes glycogen synthesis (glycogenesis) and suppresses gluconeogenesis.
In muscle and fat: induces translocation of GLUT4 glucose transporters to the cell surface, increasing glucose uptake.
Insulin resistance—reduced cellular response to insulin—underlies type 2 diabetes mellitus.

concepts.name: Hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis
concepts.summary_verbatim: The hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis is a central neuroendocrine system that modulates the body's response to stress.
mechanism_atoms: Stress signals reach the hypothalamus, which secretes corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) into the portal circulation.
CRH stimulates the anterior pituitary to release adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) into the bloodstream.
ACTH travels to the adrenal cortex and stimulates synthesis and release of cortisol (a glucocorticoid).
Elevated cortisol feeds back negatively onto both the hypothalamus and pituitary, suppressing further CRH and ACTH release (negative feedback loop).
Cortisol mobilises glucose, suppresses immune responses, and modulates other physiological systems to cope with stress.

concepts.name: Thermoregulation
concepts.summary_verbatim: Thermoregulation is the ability of an organism to keep its body temperature within certain boundaries, even when the surrounding temperature is very different.
mechanism_atoms: The hypothalamus acts as the body's thermostat; thermoreceptors in the brain, spinal cord, skin, and internal organs feed temperature information to it.
When core temperature rises above set-point (~37 °C in humans), the hypothalamus triggers sweating and cutaneous vasodilation to increase heat loss.
When core temperature falls, shivering thermogenesis and vasoconstriction conserve or generate heat.
Most body heat is generated in deep organs (liver, brain, heart) and by skeletal muscle contraction.
Fever elevates the thermal set-point via prostaglandin signalling in the hypothalamus, causing heat conservation until the new set-point is reached.

concepts.name: Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS)
concepts.summary_verbatim: The renin–angiotensin system (RAS), or renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS), is a hormone system that regulates blood pressure, fluid and electrolyte balance, and systemic vascular resistance.
mechanism_atoms: Reduced renal blood flow causes juxtaglomerular cells to secrete renin, which cleaves angiotensinogen to angiotensin I.
Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) on vascular endothelial surfaces converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II.
Angiotensin II is a potent vasoconstrictor: it narrows blood vessels, directly raising blood pressure.
Angiotensin II also stimulates the adrenal cortex to secrete aldosterone, which promotes sodium and water reabsorption by renal tubules, increasing blood volume.
Elevated blood pressure and volume feedback to suppress renin secretion, completing the negative-feedback loop.

concepts.name: Baroreceptor reflex (Baroreflex)
concepts.domain: cardiovascular / rapid blood pressure negative feedback
concepts.summary_verbatim: Baroreceptors (or archaically, pressoreceptors) are stretch receptors that sense blood vessel deformation.
mechanism_atoms: Baroreceptors located in the carotid sinus and aortic arch detect vessel wall stretch proportional to blood pressure.
Increased stretch (high BP) sends afferent signals via cranial nerves IX and X to the nucleus tractus solitarius in the brainstem.
The brainstem activates the parasympathetic system (slowing heart rate) and inhibits the sympathetic system (reducing vasomotor tone), rapidly lowering blood pressure.
The reflex operates on a timescale of seconds, providing beat-to-beat blood pressure stabilisation.
Reduced stretch (low BP) has the opposite effect: sympathetic activation increases heart rate and vasoconstriction.

concepts.name: Frank-Starling law of the heart
concepts.summary_verbatim: The Frank–Starling law of the heart (also known as Starling's law and the Frank–Starling mechanism) states that the stroke volume of the heart increases in response to an increase in the volume of blood filling the heart (the end diastolic volume) when all other factors remain the same.
mechanism_atoms: Greater ventricular filling stretches myocytes, increasing the overlap between actin and myosin filaments.
Stretch increases the affinity of troponin C for Ca²⁺ ions, causing more cross-bridges to form and increasing contractile force.
The result is that stroke volume increases proportionally with end-diastolic volume (preload), without requiring neural or hormonal input.
This intrinsic mechanism synchronises left and right ventricular output, preventing pulmonary or systemic congestion.
The mechanism has limits: excessive stretch (volume overload) moves the heart to the descending limb of the Starling curve, reducing contractility.

concepts.name: Action potential
concepts.summary_verbatim: An action potential (also known as a nerve impulse or "spike" when in a neuron) is a series of quick changes in voltage across a cell membrane.
mechanism_atoms: A stimulus depolarises the membrane; if it exceeds the threshold (~−55 mV in neurons), voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open, causing rapid inward Na⁺ current and further depolarisation (all-or-nothing).
The depolarisation phase reaches ~+40 mV; inactivation of Na⁺ channels and opening of voltage-gated K⁺ channels cause repolarisation.
K⁺ efflux drives the membrane transiently below resting potential (hyperpolarisation / refractory period), preventing re-firing too soon.
In myelinated axons, the action potential jumps between Nodes of Ranvier (saltatory conduction), greatly increasing propagation speed.
The signal propagates one-directionally to synaptic boutons where neurotransmitter release transmits the signal to the next cell.

concepts.name: Long-term potentiation (LTP)
concepts.summary_verbatim: In neuroscience, long-term potentiation (LTP) is a persistent strengthening of synapses based on recent patterns of activity.
mechanism_atoms: High-frequency stimulation of a synapse causes sustained depolarisation of the postsynaptic membrane.
Strong depolarisation removes Mg²⁺ ions blocking NMDA receptors, allowing Ca²⁺ influx through NMDA channels.
The rise in postsynaptic Ca²⁺ activates kinases (e.g. CaMKII) that phosphorylate AMPA receptors and recruit additional AMPA receptors to the synapse.
More AMPA receptors at the synapse increase the cell's sensitivity to glutamate, persistently strengthening the synaptic connection.
LTP requires coincident pre- and postsynaptic activity (Hebbian rule), making it a cellular substrate for associative learning and memory.

concepts.name: Gate control theory of pain
concepts.summary_verbatim: The gate control theory of pain asserts that non-painful input closes the nerve "gates" to painful input, which prevents pain sensation from traveling to the central nervous system.
mechanism_atoms: First proposed by Melzack and Wall in 1965, the theory posits a 'gate' mechanism in the spinal cord dorsal horn.
Small-diameter (Aδ and C) fibres carrying nociceptive (pain) signals open the gate; large-diameter (Aβ) fibres carrying touch signals close it.
Stimulation of non-noxious touch fibres (Aβ) activates inhibitory interneurons in the substantia gelatinosa, which suppress pain signal transmission.
The gate can also be closed by descending signals from the brain (e.g. during distraction or opioid analgesia).
Applied clinically: vibration applied during injection, TENS therapy, and acupuncture exploit this mechanism to reduce perceived pain.

concepts.name: Neuromuscular junction
concepts.summary_verbatim: The neuromuscular junction allows the motor neuron to transmit a signal to the muscle fiber, causing muscle contraction.
mechanism_atoms: An action potential reaching the motor nerve terminal triggers voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels to open, causing Ca²⁺ influx.
Ca²⁺ influx drives fusion of acetylcholine (ACh)-containing vesicles with the presynaptic membrane, releasing ACh into the synaptic cleft.
ACh diffuses across the cleft and binds nicotinic ACh receptors (nAChR) on the muscle cell membrane, opening ion channels and generating an end-plate potential.
The end-plate potential triggers a muscle action potential that propagates along the sarcolemma and down T-tubules, releasing Ca²⁺ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and initiating contraction.
Acetylcholinesterase rapidly hydrolyses ACh in the cleft, terminating the signal and allowing the muscle to relax.

concepts.name: Coagulation (clotting cascade)
concepts.summary_verbatim: Coagulation, also known as clotting, is the process by which blood changes from a liquid to a gel, forming a blood clot.
mechanism_atoms: Tissue factor (TF) exposed by vascular injury binds factor VIIa, forming the extrinsic tenase complex that initiates the cascade.
Sequential zymogen-to-protease conversions amplify the signal: small amounts of TF ultimately generate large amounts of thrombin (factor IIa).
Thrombin cleaves soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin strands that cross-link with platelets to form a stable clot.
The cascade has both an extrinsic (tissue factor) and intrinsic (contact activation) pathway; both converge on the common pathway at factor X.
Natural anticoagulants (antithrombin, protein C/S, TFPI) limit clot propagation beyond the injury site.

concepts.name: Hemostasis
concepts.summary_verbatim: Hemostasis or haemostasis is a process to prevent and stop bleeding, meaning to keep blood within a damaged blood vessel.
mechanism_atoms: Primary hemostasis: vascular injury exposes collagen; von Willebrand factor (vWF) bridges collagen and platelet GPIb receptors, causing platelet adhesion.
Platelet activation releases ADP and thromboxane A2, which recruit additional platelets and form a loose platelet plug.
Secondary hemostasis: the coagulation cascade generates fibrin, which cross-links and stabilises the platelet plug.
When endothelium is damaged, endothelial cells stop secreting coagulation inhibitors and instead release vWF and tissue factor, shifting the local balance toward coagulation.
