Fibrinolysis later dissolves the clot via plasmin once tissue repair is complete.

concepts.name: Wound healing
concepts.summary_verbatim: Wound healing refers to a living organism's replacement of destroyed or damaged tissue by newly produced tissue.
mechanism_atoms: Phase 1 – Hemostasis (minutes to hours): platelets aggregate and coagulation forms a fibrin clot to stop bleeding.
Phase 2 – Inflammation (1–3 days): neutrophils and macrophages clear debris; cytokines and growth factors are released to orchestrate repair.
Phase 3 – Proliferation (days to ~1 month): fibroblasts synthesise collagen, keratinocytes migrate to close the wound, and angiogenesis forms new capillaries (granulation tissue).
Phase 4 – Remodelling/maturation (months to >1 year): type III collagen is replaced by stronger type I collagen; unnecessary vessels are removed; scar tissue contracts.
Dysregulation of any phase leads to pathological outcomes: impaired healing (chronic wounds) or excessive fibrosis (hypertrophic scars/keloids).

concepts.name: Angiogenesis
concepts.summary_verbatim: Angiogenesis is the physiological process through which new blood vessels form from pre-existing vessels, formed in the earlier stage of vasculogenesis.
mechanism_atoms: Hypoxic or growing tissue secretes vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and basic fibroblast growth factor (bFGF) to signal need for new blood supply.
VEGF binds receptors on existing endothelial cells, stimulating proliferation and directed migration (sprouting) toward the growth signal.
Tip cells lead sprouts guided by VEGF gradients; stalk cells proliferate to lengthen the new vessel.
Tumours exploit this mechanism: once a tumour exceeds ~1–2 mm³, it secretes angiogenic factors to recruit a blood supply, enabling further growth and metastasis.
Angiogenesis is a fundamental step in the transition of tumours from benign to malignant state, making it a target for anti-cancer therapy (e.g. bevacizumab blocks VEGF).

concepts.name: Metastasis
concepts.summary_verbatim: Metastasis is the spread of a pathogenic agent from an initial or primary site to a different or secondary site within the host's body; the term is typically used when referring to metastasis by a cancerous tumor.
mechanism_atoms: Local invasion: tumour cells degrade extracellular matrix via matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) and invade surrounding stroma.
Intravasation: cancer cells enter blood or lymphatic vessels; survival in circulation requires evasion of immune clearance and anoikis.
Extravasation: circulating tumour cells arrest at distant capillaries, adhere to endothelium, and migrate into the new tissue.
Colonisation: only a small subset of disseminated cells survive and proliferate in the new microenvironment to form macrometastases.
Angiogenesis in the metastatic niche is required for the secondary tumour to grow beyond microscopic size.

concepts.name: Apoptosis
concepts.domain: cell biology / programmed cell death caspase cascade
concepts.summary_verbatim: Apoptosis (from Ancient Greek: ἀπόπτωσις, romanized: apóptōsis, lit. 'falling off') is a form of programmed cell death that occurs in multicellular organisms and in some eukaryotic, single-celled microorganisms such as yeast.
mechanism_atoms: Intrinsic pathway: cellular stress (DNA damage, hypoxia) causes mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilisation (MOMP), releasing cytochrome c, which forms the apoptosome with Apaf-1 and activates caspase-9.
Extrinsic pathway: death ligands (e.g. FasL, TNF) bind death receptors, activating initiator caspases (8, 10) via DISC complex.

Both pathways converge on executioner caspases (3, 6, 7) that cleave cellular proteins, causing the characteristic morphology: cell shrinkage, chromatin condensation, DNA fragmentation, and membrane blebbing.
Apoptotic cells display 'eat-me' signals (phosphatidylserine) on their outer membrane, enabling phagocytic clearance without inducing inflammation.
Bcl-2 family proteins regulate MOMP: pro-apoptotic (Bax, Bak) promote it; anti-apoptotic (Bcl-2, Bcl-xL) inhibit it, setting the threshold for apoptosis.

concepts.name: Inflammation
concepts.domain: innate immunity / vascular and cellular response
concepts.summary_verbatim: Inflammation (from Latin: inflammatio) is part of the biological defence response of body tissues.
mechanism_atoms: Injury or pathogen detection triggers resident immune cells (mast cells, macrophages) to release histamine, prostaglandins, and cytokines.
Vasodilation increases blood flow (causing heat and redness); increased vascular permeability allows plasma proteins and leukocytes to enter tissue (causing swelling).
Chemokines recruit neutrophils (first responders) and monocytes/macrophages to the site to phagocytose pathogens and debris.
The five cardinal signs of acute inflammation are heat (calor), pain (dolor), redness (rubor), swelling (tumor), and loss of function (functio laesa).
Unresolved acute inflammation transitions to chronic inflammation, characterised by macrophage and lymphocyte infiltration and progressive tissue damage.

concepts.name: Gut microbiota
concepts.summary_verbatim: Gut microbiota, gut microbiome, or gut flora are the microorganisms, including bacteria, archaea, fungi, and viruses, that live in the digestive tracts of animals.
mechanism_atoms: The gut microbiota maintains colonisation resistance by competing with pathogens for nutrients and attachment sites and producing antimicrobial metabolites.
Microbial fermentation of dietary fibre produces short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) such as butyrate, which nourish colonocytes and regulate immune signalling.
The microbiota educates and modulates the intestinal immune system, influencing regulatory T-cell development and mucosal IgA production.
Dysbiosis (imbalance of microbial composition) is associated with inflammatory bowel disease, metabolic syndrome, and neurological disorders.
The microbiota metabolises pharmaceutical compounds, altering drug bioavailability and efficacy (microbiome-drug interactions).

concepts.name: Negative feedback (physiological)
concepts.summary_verbatim: Negative feedback (or balancing feedback) occurs when some function of the output of a system, process, or mechanism is fed back in a manner that tends to reduce the fluctuations in the output, whether caused by changes in the input or by other disturbances.
mechanism_atoms: A sensor detects deviation of a physiological variable (e.g. blood pressure, temperature, glucose) from its set-point.
The error signal activates an effector that drives the variable back toward set-point, reducing the error.
Once the variable returns to set-point, the effector stimulus diminishes, preventing overcorrection (self-limiting).
Hormonal negative feedback: a target gland hormone (e.g. cortisol, T3/T4) feeds back to suppress the hypothalamus and pituitary releasing factors that drove its secretion.
Negative feedback enables stable homeostasis; its failure leads to pathological oscillations, runaway states (positive feedback loops), or failure to maintain vital ranges.

concepts.name: Osmosis
concepts.summary_verbatim: Osmosis occurs when two solutions containing different concentrations of solute are separated by a selectively permeable membrane; solvent molecules pass preferentially through the membrane from the low-concentration solution to the solution with higher solute concentration.
mechanism_atoms: Water moves across semipermeable membranes down its own chemical potential gradient (from low solute to high solute side) without requiring energy input.
Osmotic pressure is the hydrostatic pressure required to prevent net water movement; it is proportional to solute concentration (colligative property).
Cells regulate their osmotic environment via ion pumps (Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase) and aquaporin channels that control membrane water permeability.
Renal tubular reabsorption of sodium creates an osmotic gradient that drives water reabsorption, concentrating urine.
Failure of osmotic balance (e.g. hyponatraemia) causes cells to swell and can cause cerebral oedema and other life-threatening effects.

concepts.name: Quorum sensing
concepts.summary_verbatim: In biology, quorum sensing or quorum signaling (QS) is the process of cell-to-cell communication that allows bacteria to detect and respond to cell population density by gene regulation, typically as a means of acclimating to environmental disadvantages.
mechanism_atoms: Bacteria produce and secrete small signaling molecules called autoinducers into the environment.
As bacterial population density increases, autoinducer concentration rises proportionally in the surrounding medium.
When autoinducer concentration crosses a threshold, it binds receptors and triggers coordinated changes in gene expression across the population.
Quorum sensing contains traits of autocrine signaling: a cell produces both the autoinducer molecule and its receptor, creating a self-amplifying loop.
This threshold-triggered gene regulation restricts expression of metabolically costly phenotypes (e.g., biofilm formation, virulence) to high cell densities where they are most beneficial.

concepts.name: Natural selection
concepts.summary_verbatim: Natural selection is the differential survival and reproduction of individuals due to differences in the relative fitness endowed on them by their own particular complement of observable characteristics.
mechanism_atoms: Individuals within a population vary in heritable traits, and some variants confer higher reproductive success (fitness) than others.
Individuals with higher fitness survive and reproduce more, passing advantageous traits to offspring at higher frequency.
Over generations, allele frequencies shift so that beneficial traits become more common in the population — the core evolutionary mechanism.
Darwin identified three linked processes: inheritance (transmission of heritable material), variation (partly from organism's own agency), and struggle for existence.
Natural selection is the key mechanism of evolutionary change, altering the heritable traits characteristic of a population or species over generations.

concepts.name: CRISPR gene editing
concepts.summary_verbatim: CRISPR gene editing is a genetic engineering technique in molecular biology by which the genomes of living organisms may be modified.
mechanism_atoms: Cas9 (CRISPR-associated protein 9) is guided to a specific DNA sequence by an engineered guide RNA (gRNA) that base-pairs with the target.
Cas9 first recognizes a short protospacer-adjacent motif (PAM) on the DNA, then separates the strands upstream and anneals the guide RNA to the complementary target strand.
Cas9 introduces site-specific double-stranded breaks in DNA, which can be repaired by non-homologous end joining (causing insertions/deletions) or homologous recombination (enabling precise edits).
The system derives from a natural bacterial adaptive immune mechanism in which CRISPR loci store fragments of past invader DNA for recognition.
Cas9 acts as a molecular scissors: the RuvC domain cuts the non-template strand and the HNH domain cuts the template strand.

concepts.name: Antibody
concepts.summary_verbatim: An antibody (Ab), also known as an immunoglobulin (Ig), is a large, Y-shaped protein belonging to the immunoglobulin superfamily that is used by the immune system to identify and neutralize antigens such as bacteria and viruses.
mechanism_atoms: Each Y-shaped antibody has two identical antigen-binding sites (paratopes), each of which specifically binds one epitope on an antigen with high complementarity.
Binding involves weak, noncovalent interactions: electrostatic forces, hydrogen bonds, van der Waals forces, and hydrophobic interactions.
Antibodies 'tag' pathogens or infected cells for destruction by phagocytes (opsonization), complement activation, or direct neutralization.
The Fc region of antibodies binds Fc receptors on immune effector cells (NK cells, macrophages) to trigger antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity.
Different immunoglobulin classes (IgG, IgA, IgM, IgE, IgD) perform distinct effector functions determined by their heavy-chain constant regions.

concepts.name: Hox gene (Homeobox)
concepts.summary_verbatim: A homeobox is a DNA sequence, around 180 base pairs long, found within genes that are involved in the regulation of patterns of anatomical development (morphogenesis) in animals, fungi, and plants.
mechanism_atoms: Homeobox genes encode homeodomain proteins — transcription factors with a 60-amino-acid DNA-binding domain — that regulate expression of downstream target genes.
Homeodomain proteins bind specific DNA sequences in promoter regions to activate or repress genes that specify body segment identity during embryonic development.
Hox genes are arranged in genomic clusters and expressed in an anterior-to-posterior spatial pattern (collinearity) corresponding to their chromosomal order.
Homeodomain proteins direct formation of the body axes and body structures; mutations cause homeotic transformations (one body part developing in place of another).
A self-sustaining feedback loop of homeodomain protein expression maintains cell identity and passes it on through cell division.

concepts.name: Nitrogen fixation
concepts.summary_verbatim: Nitrogen fixation is a chemical process by which molecular dinitrogen (N2) in the air is converted into ammonia (NH3) or related nitrogenous compounds, typically in soil or aquatic systems.
mechanism_atoms: Biological nitrogen fixation is catalyzed by nitrogenases — enzyme complexes encoded by nif genes that contain iron, often with a second metal (molybdenum or vanadium).
The conversion of N2 to NH3 occurs at a metal cluster called FeMoco (iron-molybdenum cofactor) via sequential protonation and reduction steps.
The reaction requires a large energy input: 16 ATP and 8 electrons are consumed per molecule of N2 reduced.
Some nitrogen-fixing bacteria (diazotrophs) form symbioses with plants (especially legumes) in root nodules where the plant supplies carbon and the bacterium supplies fixed nitrogen.
Three nitrogenase types exist in bacteria: molybdenum nitrogenase, vanadium nitrogenase, and iron-only nitrogenase, depending on metal availability.

concepts.name: Epigenetics
concepts.summary_verbatim: In biology, epigenetics is the study of heritable phenotype changes that do not involve alterations in the DNA sequence.
mechanism_atoms: DNA methylation adds methyl groups to cytosine residues (especially CpG sites), which attracts proteins that fold chromatin and repress associated genes without altering the DNA sequence.
Histone modification (acetylation, methylation, phosphorylation of histone tails) changes chromatin accessibility, either activating or silencing gene expression.
Epigenetic marks are copied during DNA replication, allowing differentiated cells to stably maintain their gene expression programs through cell division.
Transgenerational epigenetic inheritance enables some epigenetic changes to be transmitted from parent to offspring, influencing evolution without DNA sequence change.
Epigenetic control enables differentiated cells in a multicellular organism to express only the genes necessary for their particular function despite sharing the same DNA.

concepts.name: Genetic drift
concepts.summary_verbatim: Genetic drift, also known as random genetic drift, allelic drift or the Wright effect, is the change in the frequency of an existing gene variant (allele) in a population due to random chance.
mechanism_atoms: Genetic drift results from random sampling of alleles when a finite population reproduces; not all individuals contribute equally to the next generation by chance.
Small populations experience larger per-generation fluctuations in allele frequency than large populations, making drift a stronger force in small populations.
Drift can cause an allele to reach fixation (frequency = 1.0) or be lost entirely from the population, regardless of its fitness effects.
Population bottlenecks (sudden reduction in population size) and founder effects (colonization by a small group) are major scenarios where genetic drift is especially powerful.
Unlike natural selection, genetic drift is random and does not systematically favor beneficial alleles, potentially driving populations away from adaptive optima.

concepts.name: Lotka–Volterra predator–prey equations
concepts.summary_verbatim: The Lotka–Volterra equations, also known as the Lotka–Volterra predator–prey model, are a pair of first-order nonlinear differential equations, frequently used to describe the dynamics of biological systems in which two species interact, one as a predator and the other as prey.
mechanism_atoms: Prey populations grow exponentially in the absence of predators; predator populations decline exponentially in the absence of prey.
Predator–prey encounters reduce the prey population (predation term) and increase the predator population (conversion of prey into predator biomass).
The coupled equations produce neutrally stable limit cycles: prey and predator populations oscillate indefinitely with predator peaks lagging prey peaks.
As prey increase, predators have more food and their numbers grow; as predators increase, prey decline; with fewer prey, predator numbers fall, releasing prey to recover.
The oscillatory dynamics arise from the negative feedback loop between the two populations without any external forcing.

concepts.name: Mycorrhiza
concepts.summary_verbatim: A mycorrhiza (from Ancient Greek: μύκης, romanized: múkēs, lit. 'fungus', and ῥίζα, rhiza, 'root'; pl. mycorrhizae) is a symbiotic association between a fungus and a plant.
mechanism_atoms: Fungal hyphae form a physical interface with plant root cells, dramatically expanding the surface area for nutrient absorption beyond what roots alone can achieve.
The plant provides the fungus up to 30% of the carbon it fixes by photosynthesis; the fungus provides the plant with soil-limiting nutrients, especially phosphorus and nitrogen.
Arbuscular mycorrhizae penetrate root cortex cells and form tree-like arbuscules — the primary sites of bidirectional nutrient exchange.
Ectomycorrhizae form a sheath (mantle) around root tips and a Hartig net between root cortex cells without penetrating the cells themselves.
The mycorrhizal symbiosis is ancient (~400 million years old) and is thought to have been critical for enabling the colonization of land by plants.

concepts.name: Photoperiodism
concepts.summary_verbatim: Photoperiodism is the physiological reaction of organisms to the length of night or a dark period.
mechanism_atoms: Plants measure the length of the uninterrupted dark period (night length), not day length, to determine season — the critical factor for initiating flowering.

Phytochrome photoreceptors exist in two interconvertible forms: Pr (absorbs red light, inactive) and Pfr (absorbs far-red light, active); sunlight drives conversion to Pfr, darkness slowly reverts it to Pr.
Short-day (long-night) plants flower only when continuous darkness exceeds a critical minimum; interrupting the dark period with a brief red light pulse reverts Pfr to Pr and suppresses flowering.
Long-day plants require dark periods shorter than a critical maximum; the ratio of Pfr to Pr at dawn signals whether the night was short enough to trigger flowering.
Circadian rhythms interact with phytochrome signaling to create a time-measuring mechanism by which plants integrate photoperiod information over multiple days.

concepts.name: Swarm behaviour
concepts.summary_verbatim: Swarm behaviour, or swarming, is a collective behaviour exhibited by animals of similar size which aggregate together, perhaps milling about the same spot or perhaps moving en masse or migrating in some direction.
mechanism_atoms: Individual agents follow simple local rules (e.g., alignment, cohesion, separation) with no central control; complex global patterns emerge from these local interactions.
Stigmergy enables indirect coordination: an agent's action modifies the environment (e.g., pheromone trails in ants), which then stimulates subsequent actions by the same or other agents.
Positive feedback amplifies initial choices (e.g., more ants following the shortest trail deposit more pheromone, attracting yet more ants), producing rapid collective decision-making.
Negative feedback (e.g., pheromone evaporation, trail abandonment) prevents the swarm from being locked into suboptimal solutions and allows adaptation.
Examples include ant colony optimization, bee nest-site selection by quorum, bird flocking (starling murmurations), and fish schooling — all without any individual knowing the global pattern.

concepts.name: Gene regulatory network
concepts.summary_verbatim: A gene (or genetic) regulatory network (GRN) is a collection of molecular regulators that interact with each other and with other substances in the cell to govern the gene expression levels of mRNA and proteins which, in turn, determine the function of the cell.
mechanism_atoms: Transcription factors (TFs) bind specific DNA sequences and activate or repress transcription of target genes, including genes encoding other TFs — forming multi-layer regulatory cascades.
Feedback loops (positive or negative) are core network motifs: a 'self-sustaining feedback loop' maintains cell identity and passes it on through cell division.
Network nodes can regulate themselves directly (autoregulation) or indirectly through cyclic chains of dependencies, creating oscillatory or bistable behaviors.
GRNs control development by creating spatial and temporal patterns of gene expression from a single genome through combinatorial transcription factor binding.
Perturbation of key GRN nodes (master regulators) can cause large-scale transcriptional reprogramming and cell fate transitions.

concepts.name: Signal transduction
concepts.summary_verbatim: Signal transduction is the process by which a chemical or physical signal is transmitted through a cell as a series of molecular events, most commonly protein phosphorylation catalyzed by protein kinases, which ultimately results in a cellular response.
mechanism_atoms: A ligand (first messenger) binds a cell-surface or intracellular receptor protein, inducing a conformational change that activates downstream signaling.
Activated receptors trigger a biochemical cascade: sequential activation of adaptor proteins, kinases, and second messengers (e.g., cAMP, Ca2+, IP3) that amplify the signal.
Signal amplification occurs because each activated kinase can phosphorylate many substrate molecules, achieving large cellular responses from few initial receptor binding events.
Signaling cascades ultimately alter transcription, translation, or protein activity — controlling cell growth, proliferation, metabolism, and differentiation.
Signal termination is achieved by phosphatases, GTPase activity (for G-protein-coupled pathways), receptor internalization (endocytosis), or inhibitory feedback molecules.

concepts.name: Competitive exclusion principle
concepts.summary_verbatim: In ecology, the competitive exclusion principle, sometimes referred to as Gause's law, is a proposition that two species which compete for the same limited resource cannot coexist at constant population sizes.
mechanism_atoms: When two species occupy the same niche and compete for identical limiting resources, the species with even a slight competitive advantage will grow at the expense of the other.
The inferior competitor experiences declining population growth (negative growth rate) until local extinction, while the superior competitor reaches its carrying capacity.
Gause demonstrated the principle in laboratory Paramecium experiments: P. aurelia consistently drove P. caudatum to extinction via exploitative resource competition.
Coexistence is possible only if species partition resources (different niches), reducing the overlap in resource use below a critical threshold.
The principle predicts that observed biodiversity requires some degree of niche differentiation among competing species — a foundation of community ecology theory.

concepts.name: Toll-like receptor
concepts.summary_verbatim: Toll-like receptors (TLRs) are a class of proteins that play a key role in the innate immune system as well as the adaptive immune system of vertebrates.
mechanism_atoms: TLRs are pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) that recognize pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) — conserved molecular structures broadly shared by pathogens but absent from host cells.
Ligand binding to TLR triggers receptor dimerization and recruitment of intracellular adaptor proteins (e.g., MyD88, TRIF) to the cytoplasmic TIR domain.
Adaptor proteins activate downstream kinase cascades (IRAK, TRAF6), ultimately activating NF-κB and IRF transcription factors.
NF-κB activation drives expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6, IL-12) and co-stimulatory molecules on antigen-presenting cells.
TLR activation on dendritic cells bridges innate and adaptive immunity by upregulating MHC and co-stimulatory molecules required for T cell activation.

concepts.name: Morphogen gradient
concepts.summary_verbatim: A morphogen is a signaling molecule that acts directly on cells (not through serial induction) to produce specific cellular responses dependent on morphogen concentration.
mechanism_atoms: Morphogens are produced at a localized source and form concentration gradients by diffusing away through surrounding tissue.
Cells interpret their position in a developing field by measuring local morphogen concentration relative to threshold values, activating distinct target gene programs at each concentration range.
Lewis Wolpert's French flag model formalized this: a single morphogen gradient can specify three distinct cell fates by two concentration thresholds dividing the field.
Diffusion, active transport, cytoneme-mediated signaling, extracellular vesicles, and relay signaling all contribute to gradient formation and shaping.
Morphogen gradients provide positional information — a mechanism by which spatial patterns of gene expression are robustly established across embryonic tissue fields.

concepts.name: Symbiogenesis (Endosymbiotic theory)
concepts.summary_verbatim: Symbiogenesis (endosymbiotic theory, or serial endosymbiotic theory) is the leading evolutionary theory of the origin of eukaryotic cells from prokaryotic organisms.
mechanism_atoms: An ancestral host cell engulfed an aerobic bacterium (the proto-mitochondrion) via endocytosis; rather than being digested, it persisted intracellularly and was retained through generations.
A second endosymbiotic event introduced a cyanobacterium into an early eukaryote, which became the chloroplast — providing photosynthetic capability.
As endosymbionts evolved into organelles, most of their genes were transferred to the host nucleus (endosymbiotic gene transfer), reducing the organelle genome.
Both mitochondria and chloroplasts retain their own circular DNA, divide independently of the cell by binary fission, and have bacteria-like 70S ribosomes — evidence for their bacterial ancestry.
The mutualistic exchange — host providing protection and nutrients, endosymbiont providing ATP or fixed carbon — drove the stable evolutionary integration.

concepts.name: RNA interference
concepts.summary_verbatim: RNA interference (RNAi) is a biological process in which RNA molecules are involved in sequence-specific suppression of gene expression by double-stranded RNA, through translational repression or transcript degradation.
mechanism_atoms: Long double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) is cleaved by the enzyme Dicer into short (~21-23 bp) small interfering RNAs (siRNAs).
siRNAs are loaded into the RNA-Induced Silencing Complex (RISC) and unwound; the antisense strand guides RISC to complementary mRNA targets.
The Argonaute (AGO) protein within RISC cleaves the target mRNA at the site of complementary siRNA binding, preventing its translation.
MicroRNAs (miRNAs) operate through a related pathway but often achieve partial complementarity, repressing translation without degrading the mRNA.
RNAi serves as a natural antiviral defense (against dsRNA viruses), transposon silencer, and gene-expression fine-tuner in eukaryotes.

concepts.name: Telomere
concepts.summary_verbatim: A telomere (/ˈtɛləmɪər, ˈtiː-/; from Ancient Greek: τέλος, romanized: télos, lit. 'end' and Ancient Greek: μέρος, romanized: méros, lit. 'part') is a region of repetitive nucleotide sequences associated with specialized proteins at the ends of linear chromosomes.
mechanism_atoms: Telomeres consist of repetitive hexameric sequences (TTAGGG in mammals) that cap chromosome ends, preventing recognition of natural ends as double-strand breaks.
The end-replication problem: DNA polymerase cannot copy the very end of the lagging strand, so each round of replication shortens telomeres by ~25–50 nucleotides.
Progressive telomere shortening acts as a mitotic clock: when telomeres reach a critical minimum length, cells enter replicative senescence or trigger apoptosis.
Telomerase, a reverse transcriptase with an RNA template, elongates telomeres in germ cells, stem cells, and cancer cells — counteracting shortening and enabling unlimited replication.
Shelterin protein complexes bind telomeric DNA and form T-loops that protect chromosome ends from degradation and inappropriate DNA damage signaling.

concepts.name: Chemotaxis
concepts.summary_verbatim: Chemotaxis (from chemo- + Ancient Greek τάξις (taxis) 'arrangement') is the movement of an organism or entity in response to a chemical stimulus.
mechanism_atoms: Bacteria sense chemical gradients temporally: they compare receptor occupancy at consecutive time points while swimming and bias flagellar rotation accordingly.
High attractant concentration (or rising attractant) suppresses tumbling by favoring counterclockwise flagellar rotation; bacteria run straight toward attractants.
High repellent concentration (or falling attractant) increases tumbling frequency via clockwise rotation, causing random reorientation — net movement away from repellents.

Chemoreceptors are methylated in an adaptation mechanism: when attractant is detected, receptor methylation rises over seconds, resetting the baseline and enabling detection of further changes (sensory adaptation).

In eukaryotes (e.g., neutrophils, Dictyostelium), cells detect spatial gradients by comparing receptor occupancy across their cell body and polymerize actin pseudopods toward the high-concentration side.

concepts.name: Insular biogeography (island biogeography)
concepts.summary_verbatim: Insular biogeography or island biogeography is a field within biogeography that examines the factors that affect the species richness and diversification of isolated natural communities.
mechanism_atoms: Species richness on an island is determined by the balance between immigration (colonization from mainland) and local extinction rates.
As more species accumulate on an island, the immigration rate of new species falls (most colonizers are already present) while extinction rate rises (more species competing for limited resources).
An equilibrium species number is reached where immigration rate equals extinction rate; this equilibrium is dynamic, with species turnover continuing.
Larger islands support more species because larger area reduces extinction rates (more habitat, larger populations); islands closer to the mainland have higher immigration rates.
The theory has been extended from oceanic islands to any isolated habitat patches (forest fragments, mountain tops, oases) and underpins conservation biology's analysis of habitat fragmentation.

concepts.name: Neurogenesis
concepts.summary_verbatim: Neurogenesis is the process by which nervous system cells, the neurons, are produced by neural stem cells (NSCs).
mechanism_atoms: Neural stem cells (NSCs) undergo asymmetric division: one daughter cell remains a stem cell (self-renewal) while the other becomes a progenitor committed to differentiating into neurons or glia.
Progenitor cells pass through intermediate neuronal precursor stages before terminal differentiation into postmitotic neurons.
In the adult brain, neurogenesis persists in two main regions: the subgranular zone (SGZ) of the dentate gyrus (hippocampus) and the subventricular zone (SVZ).
Epigenetic modifications (DNA methylation, histone modification) regulate the timing and cell-type outcome of neural stem cell differentiation.
New neurons in the adult hippocampus integrate into existing circuits and are thought to contribute to pattern separation in memory and learning.

concepts.name: Kin selection
concepts.summary_verbatim: Kin selection is the evolutionary strategy that favours the reproductive success of an organism's relatives, even at a cost to the organism's own survival and reproduction.
mechanism_atoms: Hamilton's rule formalizes when altruism is favored: rB > C, where r is the coefficient of relatedness between actor and recipient, B is the fitness benefit to the recipient, and C is the fitness cost to the actor.
Individuals share on average 50% of genes with siblings and offspring (r=0.5); helping relatives propagates copies of the helper's own genes through those relatives (indirect fitness).
Inclusive fitness = direct fitness (own reproduction) + indirect fitness (reproductive success of relatives weighted by r) — the currency that kin selection maximizes.
Altruism therefore evolves when the indirect fitness benefits (rB) exceed direct costs (C), even if the altruist never reproduces itself.
Kin selection explains eusociality in Hymenoptera (worker bees sacrificing personal reproduction to raise siblings) and cooperative breeding in many bird and mammal species.

concepts.name: Allosteric regulation
concepts.summary_verbatim: In biochemistry, allosteric regulation (or allosteric control) is the regulation of an enzyme by binding an effector molecule at a site other than the enzyme's active site.
mechanism_atoms: An effector molecule binds the allosteric (regulatory) site — distinct from the active site — inducing a conformational change in the enzyme that alters its catalytic activity.
Negative allosteric regulation (feedback inhibition): downstream metabolic products bind and inhibit the first committed enzyme in their own biosynthetic pathway, preventing overproduction.

Positive allosteric regulation: an effector binding enhances substrate affinity or catalytic rate, creating feed-forward activation (e.g., ATP activating phosphofructokinase-1 at physiological concentrations).
Cooperative binding: in multimeric enzymes (e.g., hemoglobin), binding of one ligand increases affinity at other subunits (sigmoidal kinetics), enabling threshold-triggered responses.
Allosteric mechanisms allow rapid, reversible fine-tuning of metabolic flux without changing gene expression, maintaining metabolic homeostasis on a timescale of seconds.

concepts.name: Horizontal gene transfer
concepts.summary_verbatim: Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) or lateral gene transfer (LGT) is the movement of genetic material between organisms other than by the ('vertical') transmission of DNA from parent to offspring (reproduction).
mechanism_atoms: Transformation: bacteria take up naked DNA from the environment and integrate it into their genome, especially common in naturally competent species.
Conjugation: a donor cell forms a physical bridge (pilus/type IV secretion system) to a recipient and transfers a plasmid or conjugative transposon via rolling-circle replication.
Transduction: bacteriophages accidentally package host DNA instead of their own genome and inject it into a new host cell during subsequent infection.
HGT is the primary mechanism for the rapid spread of antibiotic resistance genes among bacteria across species barriers.
Over evolutionary time, HGT has contributed entire metabolic pathways between distantly related lineages, blurring the tree-of-life model for prokaryotes.

concepts.name: Stomatal regulation (guard cell mechanism)
concepts.summary_verbatim: Stomata are microscopic pores in the shoot epidermis of plants, each surrounded by a pair of guard cells, which serve as a low-resistance pathway for the diffusional movement of gas and water vapor between a plant and the environment.
mechanism_atoms: Blue light activates a H+-ATPase proton pump on the guard cell plasma membrane, expelling protons and creating an electrochemical gradient.
The electrochemical gradient drives K+ and anions into guard cells through ion channels, raising internal solute concentration.
Increased solute concentration lowers guard cell water potential, causing osmotic water influx, guard cell swelling, and pore opening.
ABA (abscisic acid) — produced under drought stress — triggers guard cell Cl- efflux and K+ efflux, reducing turgor and closing stomata to limit water loss.
The opening/closing cycle balances CO2 uptake for photosynthesis against water loss via transpiration, representing a key physiological feedback control.

concepts.name: Somatic hypermutation
concepts.summary_verbatim: Somatic hypermutation (or SHM) is a cellular mechanism by which the immune system adapts to the new foreign elements that confront it.
mechanism_atoms: After clonal selection, B cells in germinal centers undergo rapid and targeted hypermutation of their immunoglobulin variable region genes at a rate 10^5–10^6 fold above baseline.
The enzyme activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID) deaminates cytosine to uracil specifically in immunoglobulin variable regions, generating the initial mutation.
Error-prone DNA repair pathways (polymerase eta, MSH2/MSH6) extend mutation to surrounding sequence, predominantly at WRCY hotspot motifs in hypervariable (CDR) loops.
B cells with higher-affinity mutant receptors are preferentially selected to survive and proliferate (affinity maturation); low-affinity cells undergo apoptosis.
Iterative cycles of mutation and selection in germinal centers progressively increase antibody affinity for antigen by orders of magnitude over days to weeks.

concepts.name: Circadian clock
concepts.summary_verbatim: A circadian clock, or circadian oscillator, is a biochemical oscillator that cycles with a stable phase and is synchronized with solar time.
mechanism_atoms: The core molecular mechanism is a transcription-translation negative feedback loop: activator proteins (CLOCK/BMAL1 in mammals) drive expression of repressor proteins (PER/CRY).
Accumulating PER and CRY proteins form a complex, enter the nucleus, and inhibit CLOCK/BMAL1 transcriptional activity — suppressing their own production.
As PER/CRY are progressively phosphorylated and degraded (by CK1δ/ε kinases), the repression is released and a new cycle of CLOCK/BMAL1 activation begins (~24 h period).
Light entrains the clock by inducing rapid PER1/2 expression in the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) via photic input from retinal melanopsin-expressing cells.
The ~24 h oscillation persists in constant darkness (free-running), demonstrating it is endogenously generated and not merely a response to external light cycles.

concepts.name: Mitosis
concepts.summary_verbatim: In cell biology, mitosis (/maɪˈtoʊsɪs/) is a part of the cell cycle in which replicated chromosomes are separated into two new nuclei.
mechanism_atoms: During prophase, replicated chromosomes condense and the mitotic spindle (microtubule array nucleated from centrosomes) begins to form.
During prometaphase, the nuclear envelope breaks down and kinetochore microtubules attach to protein complexes (kinetochores) at centromeres of each sister chromatid pair.
During metaphase, chromosomes are aligned at the cell equator (metaphase plate) under tension from kinetochore microtubules pulling toward opposite poles.
The spindle assembly checkpoint prevents anaphase until all kinetochores have achieved correct bipolar attachment, providing error correction for faithful chromosome segregation.
During anaphase, cohesin is cleaved by separase, sister chromatids are pulled to opposite poles by shortening kinetochore microtubules, then cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm.

concepts.name: Classical Mechanics
concepts.summary_verbatim: Classical mechanics is a physical theory describing the motion of objects.
mechanism_atoms: Forces acting on a body change its momentum according to Newton's second law (F = ma), coupling cause and effect deterministically.
The trajectory of any particle is fully determined by its initial position, velocity, and the net force applied to it.
Action-reaction pairs (Newton's third law) ensure momentum is conserved in closed systems.
Energy is partitioned between kinetic and potential forms and is conserved in the absence of dissipative forces.
Lagrangian and Hamiltonian reformulations generalise the framework to constrained systems via generalised coordinates.

concepts.name: Newton's Laws of Motion
concepts.summary_verbatim: Newton's laws of motion are three physical laws that describe the relationship between the motion of an object and the forces acting on it.
mechanism_atoms: First law (inertia): a body remains at rest or in uniform motion unless acted upon by a net external force.
Second law: the net force on a body equals the rate of change of its momentum (F = dp/dt = ma for constant mass).
Third law: for every action force there is an equal and opposite reaction force, conserving total linear momentum.
The laws apply in inertial reference frames; non-inertial frames require pseudo-forces.
Together, the three laws form the closed axiom set underlying all of classical dynamics.

concepts.name: Entropy
concepts.summary_verbatim: Entropy is a scientific concept, as well as a measurable physical property, that is most commonly associated with a state of disorder, randomness, or uncertainty.
mechanism_atoms: Macroscopically, entropy is defined by Clausius as the quotient of reversible heat transfer divided by absolute temperature (dS = δQ_rev / T).
Microscopically (Boltzmann), entropy S = k_B ln Ω where Ω is the number of microstates consistent with the macrostate.
The second law states that in any spontaneous process the total entropy of an isolated system cannot decrease.
Irreversible processes (mixing, heat conduction, friction) permanently increase entropy by spreading energy over more microstates.
Maximum entropy corresponds to thermodynamic equilibrium, where no net macroscopic change occurs.

concepts.name: Second Law of Thermodynamics
concepts.summary_verbatim: The second law of thermodynamics establishes the concept of entropy as a physical property of a thermodynamic system.
mechanism_atoms: It predicts which processes are forbidden even when energy is conserved, selecting the direction of spontaneous change.
In any natural process, the total entropy of the universe (system + surroundings) never decreases.
Heat spontaneously flows from a hotter body to a cooler body, never in reverse without external work.
The Carnot efficiency sets an upper bound on work extracted from any heat engine operating between two temperatures.
Entropy maximization at equilibrium gives rise to the Boltzmann distribution of energy among microstates.

concepts.name: Electromagnetism
concepts.summary_verbatim: In physics, electromagnetism is an interaction that occurs between particles with electric charge via electromagnetic fields.
mechanism_atoms: Electric charges generate electric fields (Coulomb's law); moving charges also generate magnetic fields (Biot–Savart law).
A changing magnetic flux induces an electric field (Faraday's law), and a changing electric field induces a magnetic field (Ampere–Maxwell law).
Maxwell's four equations unify these observations into a self-consistent field theory predicting electromagnetic waves.
Electromagnetic waves propagate at the speed of light c = 1/√(ε₀μ₀), connecting optics to electromagnetism.
The Lorentz force law F = q(E + v × B) describes how fields exert forces on charged particles.

concepts.name: Electromagnetic Induction
concepts.summary_verbatim: Electromagnetic or magnetic induction is the production of an electromotive force (emf) across an electrical conductor in a changing magnetic field.
mechanism_atoms: A time-varying magnetic flux Φ through a conducting loop induces an EMF equal to –dΦ/dt (Faraday's law).
Lenz's law specifies direction: the induced current opposes the change in flux that caused it, embodying energy conservation.
Moving a conductor through a static field separates charges via the Lorentz force, generating a motional EMF.
The magnitude of the induced EMF depends on the rate of flux change, so faster motion or stronger fields produce larger voltages.
This mechanism is the operating principle of generators, transformers, and induction motors.

concepts.name: Coulomb's Law
concepts.summary_verbatim: Coulomb's inverse-square law, or simply Coulomb's law, is an experimental law of physics that calculates the amount of force between two electrically charged particles at rest.
mechanism_atoms: The electrostatic force between two point charges is proportional to the product of their charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.
Like charges repel; unlike charges attract, with the force directed along the line joining the charges.
The constant of proportionality k_e = 1/(4πε₀) depends on the permittivity of the medium.
For continuous charge distributions, the total force is obtained by superposition of individual Coulomb interactions.
Coulomb's law is the electrostatic limit of the full Maxwell equations for charges at rest.

concepts.name: Diffraction
concepts.summary_verbatim: Diffraction is the deviation of waves from straight-line propagation due to an obstacle or through an aperture, without any change in their energy.
mechanism_atoms: Each point on a wavefront acts as a secondary source of spherical wavelets (Huygens–Fresnel principle); these wavelets interfere to produce the diffracted wave.
Constructive interference in certain directions creates bright fringes; destructive interference creates dark fringes.
The angular spread of diffraction is proportional to wavelength and inversely proportional to aperture size (θ ≈ λ/a).
Diffraction gratings exploit periodic arrays of slits so that only specific wavelengths interfere constructively at each angle, separating light into spectra.
In quantum mechanics every particle (electron, neutron) also diffracts according to its de Broglie wavelength.

concepts.name: Doppler Effect
concepts.summary_verbatim: The Doppler effect (also Doppler shift) is the change in the frequency or, equivalently, the period of a wave in relation to an observer who is moving relative to the source of the wave.
mechanism_atoms: When the source approaches the observer, successive wave crests are emitted from progressively shorter distances, compressing the wavelength and raising the observed frequency.
When source and observer recede, wave crests arrive less frequently, stretching the wavelength and lowering the observed frequency.
The fractional frequency shift Δf/f equals v_relative/c for sound (with adjustments for the medium) or v/c for light in the special-relativistic limit.
The relativistic Doppler effect for electromagnetic radiation additionally includes a transverse (time-dilation) component.
Applications include radar speed guns, astronomical redshift measurements, and medical ultrasound imaging.

concepts.name: Resonance
concepts.summary_verbatim: Resonance is a phenomenon that occurs when an object or system is subjected to an external force or vibration whose frequency matches a resonant frequency (or resonance frequency) of the system, defined as a frequency that generates a maximum amplitude response in the system.
mechanism_atoms: When driving frequency equals the system's natural frequency, energy is transferred most efficiently and amplitude grows until limited by damping.
The quality factor Q = f₀/Δf describes the sharpness of the resonance peak; low damping yields high Q and narrow, tall peaks.
In mechanical resonance, inertia and restoring force set the natural frequency (ω₀ = √(k/m)).
In electrical circuits, resonance occurs when inductive and capacitive reactances cancel, maximising current at the resonant frequency.
Feedback-driven resonance can lead to catastrophic structural failure (e.g., Tacoma Narrows Bridge) if the resonance amplitude is not damped.

concepts.name: Quantum Mechanics
concepts.summary_verbatim: Quantum mechanics is the fundamental physical theory that describes the behavior of matter and of light; its unusual characteristics typically occur at and below the scale of atoms.
mechanism_atoms: Physical states are described by wave functions (or state vectors in Hilbert space); the squared modulus gives probability densities for measurement outcomes.
The Schrödinger equation governs how wave functions evolve deterministically in time: iℏ ∂ψ/∂t = Ĥψ.
Measurement collapses the wave function to an eigenstate of the measured observable, introducing irreducible randomness.
The Pauli exclusion principle (for fermions) and Bose–Einstein statistics (for bosons) arise from the symmetry of many-particle wave functions.
Quantisation of energy levels (e.g., atomic orbitals) follows from boundary conditions imposed on solutions to the Schrödinger equation.

concepts.name: Wave Function
concepts.summary_verbatim: In quantum physics, a wave function (or wavefunction) is a mathematical description of the quantum state of an isolated quantum system.
mechanism_atoms: The wave function ψ(x,t) is a complex-valued function; |ψ|² gives the probability density for finding the particle at position x.
It evolves according to the linear Schrödinger equation, so superpositions of solutions are also valid states (principle of superposition).
Boundary and normalisation conditions on ψ quantise allowed energies, generating discrete spectra.
Entanglement arises when the wave function of a multi-particle system cannot be written as a product of single-particle wave functions.
Collapse upon measurement selects one outcome with probability |⟨eigenstate|ψ⟩|², destroying superposition.

concepts.name: Quantum Tunnelling
concepts.summary_verbatim: In physics, quantum tunnelling, barrier penetration, or simply tunnelling is a quantum mechanical phenomenon in which an object such as an electron or atom passes through a potential energy barrier that, according to classical mechanics, should not be passable due to the object not having sufficient energy to pass or surmount the barrier.
mechanism_atoms: The wave function of a quantum particle does not abruptly vanish at a classically forbidden barrier; it decays exponentially through the barrier region.
If the barrier is thin enough, the wave function has non-zero amplitude on the far side, giving a finite transmission probability.
Transmission probability decreases exponentially with barrier width and height above the particle's energy: T ∝ exp(−2κd).
Tunnelling is essential for nuclear fusion in stars (protons tunnel through Coulomb barriers) and for alpha decay of radioactive nuclei.
Scanning tunnelling microscopy exploits the exponential distance-dependence of electron tunnelling current to image surfaces atom by atom.

concepts.name: Uncertainty Principle
concepts.summary_verbatim: The uncertainty principle, also known as Heisenberg's indeterminacy principle, is a fundamental concept in quantum mechanics. It states that there is a limit to the precision with which certain pairs of physical properties, such as position and momentum, can be simultaneously known.
mechanism_atoms: Conjugate observables (position x and momentum p) satisfy σ_x · σ_p ≥ ℏ/2, derived from the non-commutativity of their operators.
A wave packet localised in position space requires a broad spread of wave vectors (momenta), and vice versa — a Fourier transform duality.
Reducing position uncertainty requires high-momentum (short-wavelength) probes that impart a large, unpredictable kick to the particle.
The energy–time uncertainty ΔE · Δt ≥ ℏ/2 governs the lifetime of excited states and the width of spectral lines.
The principle is not an instrumental limitation but an intrinsic property of quantum systems regardless of measurement technology.

concepts.name: Photoelectric Effect
concepts.summary_verbatim: The photoelectric effect is the emission of electrons from a material caused by electromagnetic radiation such as ultraviolet light.
mechanism_atoms: A single photon transfers its entire energy hf to one electron; the electron escapes only if hf exceeds the material's work function φ.
Excess photon energy above the work function becomes the kinetic energy of the emitted electron: KE = hf − φ.
The intensity of light controls the number of emitted electrons (photocurrent), not their kinetic energy.
There is a sharp threshold frequency below which no electrons are emitted regardless of intensity, disproving the classical wave model.
Einstein's 1905 explanation of this threshold provided the first quantitative evidence for the particle (photon) nature of light.

concepts.name: Superconductivity
concepts.summary_verbatim: Superconductivity is a set of physical properties observed in superconductors: materials where electrical resistance vanishes and magnetic fields are expelled from the material.
mechanism_atoms: Below the critical temperature T_c, conduction electrons form Cooper pairs via phonon-mediated attractive interactions (BCS theory).
Cooper pairs are bosons and condense into the same macroscopic quantum ground state described by a single coherent wave function.
The coherent quantum state does not scatter off lattice defects or phonons, so electrical resistance is exactly zero.
The Meissner effect (expulsion of magnetic flux) arises because supercurrents spontaneously form at the surface to cancel any internal magnetic field.
Type II superconductors allow quantised flux vortices to penetrate above the lower critical field H_c1, retaining superconductivity up to H_c2.

concepts.name: Brownian Motion
concepts.summary_verbatim: Brownian motion is the random motion of particles suspended in a medium (a liquid or a gas).
mechanism_atoms: A suspended particle is continuously bombarded from all directions by thermally agitated solvent molecules; the instantaneous force imbalance is never zero.
The net displacement in time t grows as √t (diffusion scaling), with diffusion coefficient D = k_B T / (6πηr) (Einstein–Stokes relation).
Because collisions are uncorrelated, the displacement autocorrelation decays rapidly and the process is Markovian.
At larger scales Brownian motion underlies Fick's laws of diffusion, connecting molecular randomness to macroscopic concentration gradients.
Einstein's 1905 theory of Brownian motion provided experimental proof of atomic/molecular reality via Perrin's measurements of D.

concepts.name: Chemical Bond
concepts.summary_verbatim: A chemical bond is a lasting attraction between atoms or ions that enables the formation of molecules and crystals.
mechanism_atoms: Covalent bonds form when electrons are shared between atoms, lowering total electronic energy by allowing each electron to be attracted to multiple nuclei.
Ionic bonds form by transfer of one or more electrons, creating oppositely charged ions that attract via Coulomb's law.
Bond strength (dissociation energy) and length are determined by the balance between nuclear repulsion and electron-nuclear attraction.
Metallic bonds arise from delocalisation of valence electrons into a 'sea' shared across all metal cations.
Hydrogen bonds and van der Waals interactions are weaker non-covalent forces driven by electrostatic and dispersion interactions between polar or polarisable groups.

concepts.name: Covalent Bond
concepts.summary_verbatim: A covalent bond is a chemical bond that involves the sharing of electrons to form electron pairs between atoms.
mechanism_atoms: Atomic orbitals on adjacent atoms overlap; the constructive overlap of wave functions creates a bonding molecular orbital of lower energy than either atomic orbital.
Two electrons (one from each atom, opposite spin) occupy the bonding orbital, holding the atoms together.
The bond order (single, double, triple) equals the number of shared electron pairs; higher order means shorter, stronger bonds.
Electronegativity difference between bonded atoms determines polarity: large differences give polar covalent bonds, intermediate give ionic character.
Bond angles and molecular geometry emerge from minimisation of electron-pair repulsions (VSEPR) or from the directionality of hybrid orbitals (sp, sp², sp³).

concepts.name: Chemical Kinetics
concepts.summary_verbatim: Chemical kinetics, also known as reaction kinetics, is the branch of physical chemistry that is concerned with understanding the rates of chemical reactions.
mechanism_atoms: Reaction rate depends on the frequency and energy of molecular collisions; only collisions with sufficient energy (≥ activation energy) and correct orientation lead to products.
The rate law (e.g., rate = k[A]^m[B]^n) relates concentration to rate; exponents are determined experimentally, not by stoichiometry alone.
The Arrhenius equation k = A exp(−E_a/RT) shows that rate constants increase exponentially with temperature as more molecules exceed E_a.
Reaction mechanisms consist of elementary steps; the slowest step (rate-determining step) controls the overall rate.
Catalysts provide alternative pathways with lower activation energy, increasing the reaction rate without being consumed.

concepts.name: Arrhenius Equation
concepts.summary_verbatim: In physical chemistry, the Arrhenius equation is a formula for the temperature dependence of reaction rates.
mechanism_atoms: k = A exp(−E_a / RT): the rate constant k increases exponentially as temperature T rises, because a larger fraction of molecules have kinetic energy ≥ E_a.
The pre-exponential factor A encodes collision frequency and steric requirements (fraction of properly oriented collisions).
E_a (activation energy) is the minimum energy barrier between reactants and the transition state.
A plot of ln k vs. 1/T (Arrhenius plot) yields a straight line with slope −E_a/R, allowing graphical determination of activation energy.
The equation underpins the empirical 'rule of thumb' that reaction rates roughly double for every 10 °C temperature increase.

concepts.name: Electrochemistry
concepts.summary_verbatim: Electrochemistry is the branch of physical chemistry concerned with the relationship between electrical potential difference and identifiable chemical change.
mechanism_atoms: Oxidation–reduction reactions involve electron transfer; separating the two half-reactions into anode (oxidation) and cathode (reduction) compartments creates a measurable voltage.
The Nernst equation E = E° − (RT/nF) ln Q relates cell potential to reactant concentrations, showing how potential shifts from standard as equilibrium is approached.
In galvanic cells, spontaneous redox reactions drive current through an external circuit, converting chemical energy to electrical energy.
In electrolytic cells, an external voltage drives non-spontaneous reactions (e.g., electrolysis of water, electroplating).
The Faraday constant (96 485 C mol⁻¹) links the amount of charge passed to the moles of substance deposited or dissolved.

concepts.name: Phase Transition
concepts.summary_verbatim: In chemistry, thermodynamics, and other related fields, a phase transition (or phase change) is the physical process of transition between one state of a medium and another.
mechanism_atoms: First-order transitions (melting, boiling) involve latent heat: the system absorbs or releases energy at constant temperature while the order parameter changes discontinuously.
Second-order (continuous) transitions have no latent heat; the order parameter vanishes continuously and fluctuations diverge at the critical point (critical phenomena).
Symmetry breaking drives the transition: the high-temperature phase has higher symmetry; the low-temperature phase breaks a symmetry (e.g., paramagnetic→ferromagnetic).
Near a critical point, the correlation length ξ diverges and the system is described by universal power laws characterised by critical exponents independent of microscopic details.
Nucleation and growth govern first-order transitions: thermal fluctuations create small nuclei of the new phase that grow if they exceed a critical radius.

concepts.name: Le Chatelier's Principle
concepts.summary_verbatim: In chemistry, Le Chatelier's principle is a principle used to predict the effect of a change in conditions on chemical equilibrium.
mechanism_atoms: When a system at equilibrium is disturbed (by changing concentration, pressure, or temperature), it shifts to partially counteract the disturbance — a negative-feedback mechanism.
Increasing reactant concentration shifts equilibrium toward products; removing products has the same effect, pulling the equilibrium forward.
Increasing pressure (for gaseous systems) shifts equilibrium toward the side with fewer moles of gas, reducing volume to offset the pressure increase.
Raising temperature shifts equilibrium in the endothermic direction, absorbing the added heat; lowering temperature shifts it exothermically.
The equilibrium constant K changes only with temperature; all other disturbances change the reaction quotient Q until Q = K is restored.

concepts.name: Nuclear Fission
concepts.summary_verbatim: Nuclear fission is a reaction in which the nucleus of an atom splits into two or more smaller nuclei.
mechanism_atoms: A heavy nucleus (e.g., U-235) absorbs a slow neutron, becoming an excited compound nucleus (U-236*) that oscillates and deforms.
When the deformation exceeds the nuclear binding force, the nucleus splits into two fission fragments plus 2–3 fast neutrons and gamma rays.
The mass of products is slightly less than the original nucleus + neutron; this mass defect Δm converts to energy via E = Δmc².
Each fission releases ~200 MeV, roughly 50 million times the energy of a typical chemical bond.
If released neutrons cause further fissions, a chain reaction propagates; criticality is reached when on average one neutron from each fission triggers another fission.

concepts.name: Radioactive Decay
concepts.summary_verbatim: Radioactive decay is a stochastic (i.e., random) process at the level of single atoms, in that, according to quantum theory, it is impossible to predict when a given atom will decay.
mechanism_atoms: An unstable nucleus spontaneously transitions to a lower-energy configuration, emitting alpha particles, beta particles, or gamma radiation.
Alpha decay: a heavy nucleus emits a helium-4 nucleus; the daughter nucleus has Z decreased by 2, A by 4.
Beta-minus decay: a neutron converts to a proton, emitting an electron and an electron antineutrino via the weak nuclear force.
Gamma decay: an excited nuclear state releases excess energy as a high-energy photon without changing Z or A.
Each radioactive species has a characteristic half-life t₁/₂ = ln2/λ; the decay constant λ is quantum-mechanically determined by barrier penetration probability.

concepts.name: Fluid Dynamics
concepts.summary_verbatim: In physics, physical chemistry, and engineering, fluid dynamics is a subdiscipline of fluid mechanics that describes the flow of fluids – liquids and gases.
mechanism_atoms: The Navier–Stokes equations describe momentum conservation in a viscous fluid, balancing inertial, pressure, viscous, and body forces.
Continuity (mass conservation) requires that for an incompressible flow the velocity field has zero divergence: ∇·v = 0.
The Reynolds number Re = ρvL/η determines whether flow is laminar (Re ≪ 1) or turbulent (Re ≫ 1); at high Re, inertial forces dominate.
In laminar flow, fluid moves in parallel layers with orderly exchange; in turbulent flow, chaotic eddies of all scales transfer momentum far more effectively.
Bernoulli's principle (energy conservation along a streamline) shows that increased flow speed reduces static pressure.

concepts.name: Bernoulli's Principle
concepts.summary_verbatim: Bernoulli's principle is a key concept in fluid dynamics that relates pressure, speed and height.
mechanism_atoms: For steady, inviscid, incompressible flow along a streamline: P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant (Bernoulli's equation).
Where the flow speeds up (narrowing pipe), kinetic energy increases so pressure must decrease to conserve total mechanical energy.
The relationship is derived from the work-energy theorem applied to a fluid element moving along a streamline.
The principle explains lift on an aerofoil: faster flow over the curved upper surface lowers pressure, creating a net upward force.
Venturi meters exploit the pressure-drop at a constriction to measure volumetric flow rate.

concepts.name: Surface Tension
concepts.summary_verbatim: Surface tension is the tendency of liquid surfaces at rest to shrink into the minimum surface area possible.
mechanism_atoms: Molecules in the bulk liquid are attracted equally in all directions; molecules at the surface have fewer neighbours above, creating a net inward pull.
This inward cohesive force makes the surface behave like a stretched elastic membrane with energy per unit area equal to the surface tension γ.
Capillary rise results from the balance between surface tension pulling the liquid up the wall and gravity pulling it down, with height h = 2γ cos θ / (ρgr).
Young's equation relates the contact angle θ of a droplet on a solid to the relative surface energies of the solid–liquid, solid–vapour, and liquid–vapour interfaces.
Surfactants adsorb at the surface and reduce γ by substituting weaker surfactant–air interactions for stronger water–air interactions.

concepts.name: Hysteresis
concepts.summary_verbatim: Hysteresis is the dependence of the state of a system on its history.
mechanism_atoms: In ferromagnetic materials, magnetic domains align with an applied field; when the field is reversed, domains must overcome pinning energy barriers to flip, so magnetisation lags behind the field.
The B–H (or M–H) hysteresis loop encloses an area equal to the energy dissipated per cycle as heat in the material.
Coercivity (the field required to demagnetise the material) measures how hard it is to switch domain walls across pinning sites.
Hard magnetic materials have wide hysteresis loops (high coercivity), making permanent magnets; soft materials have narrow loops for transformer cores.
Hysteresis also appears in shape-memory alloys, ferroelectrics, and bistable chemical systems, wherever first-order transitions with metastable states occur.

concepts.name: Stefan–Boltzmann Law
concepts.summary_verbatim: The Stefan–Boltzmann law states that the total energy radiated per unit surface area per unit time is directly proportional to the fourth power of the black body's temperature.
mechanism_atoms: j* = σT⁴, where σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴ is the Stefan–Boltzmann constant.
The T⁴ dependence arises from integrating the Planck spectrum over all frequencies; as temperature increases, both peak frequency and peak intensity grow.
For a perfect black body, every photon that strikes the surface is absorbed; emission is isotropic and follows Planck's distribution.
The law explains why hotter objects radiate overwhelmingly more power: doubling T multiplies radiated power by 16.
Real materials emit a fraction ε (emissivity) of the black-body value: j* = εσT⁴; ε depends on surface chemistry and wavelength.

concepts.name: Conservation of Energy
concepts.summary_verbatim: Energy can neither be created nor destroyed; rather, it can only be transformed or transferred from one form to another.
mechanism_atoms: In mechanics, work done on a system equals the change in its kinetic plus potential energy (work-energy theorem).
In thermodynamics, the first law states ΔU = Q − W: the internal energy change equals heat added minus work done by the system.
Noether's theorem shows energy conservation is the consequence of the time-translation symmetry of physical laws.
In relativity, rest mass is a form of energy (E = mc²), so the conserved quantity is the total mass-energy.
In open systems, energy is conserved globally: any apparent loss represents transfer to surroundings (heat, radiation, mechanical work).

concepts.name: Rite of Passage
concepts.summary_verbatim: A rite of passage is a ceremony or ritual of the passage which occurs when an individual leaves one group to enter another.
mechanism_atoms: Van Gennep identified three consecutive structural phases: separation (preliminal), liminality (liminal), and incorporation (postliminal).
In separation, the initiate is symbolically detached or 'cut away' from prior social status through ritual acts.
In the liminal phase, the initiate occupies an ambiguous 'threshold' state: no longer holding the old status but not yet in the new one.
In incorporation, the initiate re-enters society with a new, recognized social role, completing the structural transformation.
The rite functions as a mechanism to ease individuals through status transitions without social disruption.

concepts.name: Liminality
concepts.summary_verbatim: In anthropology, liminality (from Latin limen 'threshold') is the quality of ambiguity or disorientation that occurs in the middle stage of a rite of passage, when participants no longer hold their pre-ritual status but have not yet begun the transition to the status they will hold when the rite is complete.
mechanism_atoms: Coined by Arnold van Gennep (1909) and elaborated by Victor Turner, liminality names the structural middle phase of tripartite rites.
Liminal subjects are symbolically stripped of prior markers: possessions, clothing, name, and rank are removed or equalized.
Turner identified 'communitas' as the egalitarian social bond forming among liminal subjects, temporarily suspending normal social hierarchies.
The liminal state is characterized by symbolic death and rebirth imagery: subjects are considered socially invisible or 'dead' until re-incorporated.
The phase creates a bounded space of potentiality, enabling identity transformation that is structurally impossible in ordinary social life.

concepts.name: Sacrifice
concepts.summary_verbatim: Sacrifice is an act or offering made to a deity.
mechanism_atoms: The sacrificial mechanism typically involves selecting a consecrated victim or object, ritually killing or destroying it, and presenting it to the divine.
Sacrifice operates as a structured exchange: the offerer gives up something of value in expectation of divine favor, atonement, or communion.
Blood sacrifice in many traditions holds that life-force is transferred to the deity through the spilling of blood.
Communal sacrifice involves shared consumption of the victim (as in feast or Eucharist), creating solidarity and marking divine participation.
Substitution logic allows symbolic objects or animals to stand in for the primary sacrificer, maintaining the exchange without literal self-destruction.

concepts.name: Vedic Chant
concepts.summary_verbatim: The oral tradition of the Vedas (Śruti) consists of several pathas, 'recitations' or ways of chanting the Vedic mantras.
mechanism_atoms: Multiple recitation modes (pathas) encode the same text differently: vakya (continuous), pada (word-by-word), krama (successive pairs), and jata (interlocked reversal) among others.
Jata-patha and ghana-patha methods involve reversing and re-combining word sequences, creating multi-directional redundancy that allows error detection.
Pitch accent (svara) is phonemically preserved: high, low, and svarita tones are integral to the text, functioning as an additional error-correction channel.
UNESCO proclaimed this tradition a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity (2008), recognizing it as the oldest unbroken oral tradition in existence.
The system prioritizes phonetic fidelity over semantic interpretation: pronunciation rules (shiksha) are treated as independent of meaning, ensuring preservation independent of understanding.

concepts.name: Method of Loci
concepts.summary_verbatim: The method of loci is a mnemonic technique that uses visual imagination and spatial memory to organize and recall information.
mechanism_atoms: The practitioner selects a well-known physical space (house, route, palace) as a 'memory palace' and mentally maps it into a fixed sequence of distinct locations (loci).
Each piece of information to be remembered is associated with a specific locus via a vivid, often bizarre or exaggerated mental image.
Recall is achieved by mentally retracing the route through the memory palace in sequence, with each locus cuing the associated image and information.
The mechanism exploits the brain's superior spatial and episodic memory systems relative to abstract list recall; neuroimaging confirms recruitment of hippocampal spatial circuits.
Order and directionality are preserved by the fixed spatial sequence, allowing both forward and reverse retrieval of stored items.

concepts.name: Syllogism
concepts.summary_verbatim: A syllogism (Ancient Greek: συλλογισμός, syllogismos, 'conclusion, inference') is a kind of logical argument that applies deductive reasoning to arrive at a conclusion based on two propositions that are asserted or assumed to be true.
mechanism_atoms: The canonical Aristotelian syllogism has three parts: major premise (universal claim), minor premise (particular instantiation), and conclusion (derived necessity).
Validity is determined by the formal relationship between subject, predicate, and middle term—not by the truth of the premises.
The middle term appears in both premises but not in the conclusion; it functions as the inferential bridge between the major and minor terms.
Aristotle categorized syllogisms into four figures based on the placement of the middle term, generating distinct valid and invalid moods.
Syllogistic logic operates as a constraint system: if both premises are true and the form is valid, the conclusion cannot be false.

concepts.name: Dialectic
concepts.summary_verbatim: Dialectic (Ancient Greek: διαλεκτική, romanized: dialektikḗ; German: Dialektik), also known as the dialectical method, refers originally to dialogue between people holding different points of view about a subject but wishing to arrive at the truth through reasoned argument.
mechanism_atoms: The Socratic form proceeds by elenchus: one party proposes a claim, the interlocutor poses counter-questions, and contradictions are surfaced until the claim is refined or abandoned.
Hegel's dialectic formalizes progression as thesis, antithesis, and synthesis: a position generates its negation, and the two are resolved at a higher logical level.
In classical philosophy, dialectic is a form of reasoning based upon dialogue of arguments (theses) and counter-arguments (antitheses), using adversarial structure to converge on truth.
Marxist dialectical materialism applies this triadic structure to historical change: material contradictions in social organization drive transformations of economic systems.
The method functions as a self-correcting reasoning engine: each synthesis becomes a new thesis subject to fresh antithesis, producing iterative refinement.

concepts.name: Falsifiability
concepts.summary_verbatim: Falsifiability, as introduced by philosopher of science Karl Popper, is the capacity for a statement, hypothesis, or theory to be contradicted by evidence.
mechanism_atoms: Popper proposed falsifiability as the demarcation criterion distinguishing scientific from non-scientific claims: a claim is scientific only if it can, in principle, be shown false by observation.
The mechanism is asymmetric: no finite set of confirmatory observations can prove a universal theory true, but a single contradictory observation can falsify it.
Auxiliary hypotheses and the Duhem-Quine problem complicate falsification: when a prediction fails, the fault may lie in auxiliary assumptions rather than the core theory.
Unfalsifiable claims (e.g., 'all events are predetermined') are not thereby shown to be false, only excluded from scientific investigation.
The criterion operationalizes critical rationalism: scientific progress occurs not through verification but through the elimination of false theories.

concepts.name: Occam's Razor
concepts.summary_verbatim: In philosophy, Occam's razor (also spelled Ockham's razor or Ocham's razor; Latin: novacula Occami) is the problem-solving principle that recommends searching for explanations constructed with the smallest possible set of elements.
mechanism_atoms: The principle operates as a constraint on hypothesis generation: when two explanations account for the same evidence equally well, prefer the one with fewer entities or assumptions.
It is not a logical proof but a heuristic: it does not guarantee the simpler hypothesis is correct, only that it should be preferred as a starting point.
In Bayesian terms, simpler hypotheses typically have higher prior probabilities, so Occam's razor can be formalized as a prior probability preference.
The principle has been applied across logic, science, theology, and ethics to eliminate unnecessary postulates (e.g., rejecting supernatural explanations when natural ones suffice).
Named for William of Ockham (14th century), who stated that 'entities should not be multiplied beyond necessity' (non sunt multiplicanda entia sine necessitate).

concepts.name: Consequentialism
concepts.summary_verbatim: In moral philosophy, consequentialism is a class of normative, teleological ethical theories that holds that the consequences of one's conduct are the ultimate basis for judgement about the rightness or wrongness of that conduct.
mechanism_atoms: The evaluation mechanism: an action is right if and only if its actual or expected consequences produce the best overall outcome (e.g., maximized well-being or utility).
Utilitarianism, the most prominent variant, aggregates welfare across all affected parties, treating each person's welfare as equally weighted.
Act consequentialism evaluates each individual action on its consequences; rule consequentialism evaluates rules whose general adoption would produce the best consequences.
The framework requires comparing possible worlds: agents must forecast and compare the outcomes of all available actions, selecting the one with the highest expected value.
Consequentialism can endorse ordinarily prohibited acts (lying, harming one) if their consequences maximize total good, generating the strongest objections to the framework.

concepts.name: Deontological Ethics
concepts.summary_verbatim: In moral philosophy, deontological ethics or deontology (from Ancient Greek δέον (déon) 'duty, obligation' and -λογία (-logía) 'study of') is the normative ethical theory that the morality of an action should be based on whether that action itself is right or wrong under a series of rules and principles, rather than based on the consequences of the action.
mechanism_atoms: Actions are evaluated against moral rules or duties (e.g., 'do not lie', 'keep promises') independently of their outcomes.
Kant's categorical imperative provides the core test: act only according to maxims you could will to be universal laws; treat persons as ends, never merely as means.
The mechanism is rule-governed and consequence-independent: certain acts are intrinsically obligatory or forbidden regardless of outcomes they produce.
Agent-relative constraints are central: an agent may not violate a duty even to prevent a greater number of identical violations by others.
Rights-based variants hold that individuals possess inviolable rights that constrain what others may do to them, generating absolute prohibitions.
