concepts.name: Virtue Ethics
concepts.summary_verbatim: Virtue ethics is a philosophical approach that treats dispositional virtue and character as the primary subjects of ethics.
mechanism_atoms: Rather than evaluating individual acts by rules or consequences, virtue ethics asks what character traits (virtues) a person of excellent moral character would possess and express.
Aristotle's eudaimonia (flourishing) is the telos: virtues are stable dispositions that enable the agent to function excellently and thereby live well.
Virtues are acquired by habituation: one becomes just by repeatedly performing just acts; character is built through practice, not merely through reasoning.
The doctrine of the mean: each virtue is a disposition to feel and act appropriately, occupying a mean between the vices of excess and deficiency (e.g., courage between cowardice and recklessness).
Moral perception (phronesis, practical wisdom) is a meta-virtue: the capacity to discern what virtue requires in particular situations, resisting algorithmic reduction.

concepts.name: Qualia
concepts.summary_verbatim: In philosophy, qualia are individual instances of subjective, conscious experience.
mechanism_atoms: Qualia are defined by their intrinsic, non-relational character: the 'redness of red' or 'painfulness of pain' is a property of experience not reducible to functional role or physical description.
The 'explanatory gap' (Levine) and 'hard problem' (Chalmers) argue that even a complete physical account of brain states leaves unexplained why those states feel like anything at all.

Frank Jackson's 'Mary's Room' thought experiment: a colorblind neuroscientist who knows all physical facts about color perception, upon seeing red for the first time, appears to learn something new—suggesting qualia are not captured by physical description.
Eliminativists (Dennett) deny qualia exist as described, arguing that introspective reports are unreliable and that the concept is incoherent.
The debate turns on whether subjective experience can be fully functionalized: if two systems are functionally identical, must they have the same qualia?

concepts.name: Intentionality
concepts.summary_verbatim: Intentionality is the capacity of mental states to be directed towards (about) or be in relation with something in the external world.
mechanism_atoms: Franz Brentano reintroduced the concept: intentionality ('intentional inexistence') is the mark of the mental—physical phenomena lack it, while all mental acts have it.
An intentional state has a content (what it is about) and an attitude (belief, desire, fear, hope): these two components jointly determine the state's logical role.
Intentional objects need not exist: one can intend toward fictional entities, past events, or impossible states, making intentionality irreducible to physical causation.
Husserl's phenomenological analysis distinguishes noesis (the intentional act) from noema (the intended content or meaning).
The 'intentionality of perception' challenge: whether the aboutness of thoughts is derived from conventions and language use (externalism) or entirely internal to the mind (internalism).

concepts.name: Monomyth (Hero's Journey)
concepts.summary_verbatim: In narratology and comparative mythology, the hero's quest or hero's journey, also known as the monomyth, is the common template of stories that involve a hero who goes on an adventure, is victorious in a decisive crisis, and comes home changed or transformed.
mechanism_atoms: Joseph Campbell identified the pattern across world mythologies in 'The Hero with a Thousand Faces' (1949), proposing a universal 17-stage narrative structure.
The three macro-stages parallel van Gennep's rites of passage: Departure (separation from ordinary world), Initiation (trials in a special world), and Return (re-integration with boon).
The Call to Adventure initiates the hero's departure; Refusal of the Call and Supernatural Aid are standard structural components that build tension before commitment.
Crossing the Threshold marks the boundary between the known world and the unknown; the hero then faces ordeals that test and transform identity.
The pattern functions as a map for psychological individuation (per Jung): external narrative stages correspond to internal processes of growth, confrontation with the shadow, and integration.

concepts.name: Trickster Archetype
concepts.summary_verbatim: In mythology and the study of folklore and religion, a trickster is a character in a story who exhibits a great degree of intellect or secret knowledge and uses it to play tricks or otherwise disobey normal rules and defy conventional behavior.
mechanism_atoms: The trickster occupies liminal structural positions in mythology: existing between human and divine, living and dead, sacred and profane.
Tricksters violate established order through cunning rather than force: deception, shape-shifting, rule-breaking, and improvisation are characteristic tools.
Cross-cultural examples include Loki (Norse), Coyote (Native American), Anansi (West African), Hermes (Greek)—each functions to introduce disorder that paradoxically enables cultural renewal.
Carl Jung treated the trickster as a collective shadow archetype: it embodies the repressed, primitive aspects of the psyche that civilization suppresses.
In structural anthropology (Lévi-Strauss), the trickster mediates binary oppositions (nature/culture, life/death), serving as a logical operator for resolving cultural contradictions.

concepts.name: I Ching
concepts.summary_verbatim: The I Ching, usually translated as Book of Changes or Classic of Changes, is an ancient Chinese divination text that is among the oldest of the Chinese classics.
mechanism_atoms: The system is built on 64 hexagrams, each composed of six stacked lines that are either yang (solid, unbroken) or yin (broken), generating 2^6 = 64 unique figures.
Divination proceeds by manipulating yarrow stalks or coins through a randomizing procedure to determine each of the six lines sequentially, building the hexagram from bottom to top.
Lines are classified as 'old' (changing) or 'young' (stable); changing lines transform into their opposites, generating a second hexagram that indicates future development.
Each hexagram carries associated texts (the gua ci and yao ci) with symbolic interpretations; the diviner matches the question to the hexagram's dynamic situation.
The system encodes a cosmology of continuous change: all 64 hexagrams represent possible states of flux, and the changing-line mechanism models the process of transformation between states.

concepts.name: Augury
concepts.summary_verbatim: Augury was the Roman religious practice of observing the behavior of birds to receive omens.
mechanism_atoms: Augurs were state-appointed specialists who observed specific bird species (eagles, vultures, ravens, chickens) in defined spatial zones to interpret divine will.
The templum was a consecrated observational space oriented by cardinal directions; signs on the left (sinister) or right (dexter) carried opposite valences depending on context.
Chicken augury (auspicium ex tripudiis) observed whether sacred chickens ate eagerly; refusal to eat was a bad omen; the mechanism was thus controlled and repeatable.
Augury functioned as a political-religious gatekeeping system: no major public act (war, election, law) could proceed without favorable auspices from augurs.
The binary outcome structure (favorable/unfavorable) and the fixed interpretive grammar meant augury produced actionable yes/no verdicts on proposed courses of action.

concepts.name: Taboo
concepts.summary_verbatim: A taboo is a social group's ban, prohibition or avoidance of something (usually an utterance or behavior) based on the group's sense that it is excessively repulsive, offensive, sacred or allowed only for certain people.
mechanism_atoms: The concept derives from Polynesian 'tapu' (prohibited, sacred), introduced to English by Captain Cook (1777) after his visit to Tonga.
Taboos operate as boundary-maintenance mechanisms: they demarcate the sacred from the profane, the pure from the polluted, and the permissible from the forbidden.
Violation of taboo is believed to bring automatic supernatural punishment, social ostracism, or ritual pollution—the enforcement mechanism does not require human policing.
Mary Douglas's analysis (Purity and Danger) argues taboos mark categorical anomalies: things that resist classification threaten the conceptual order and are rendered dangerous.
Taboos encode social structure indirectly: food taboos, incest taboos, and speech taboos each reinforce social categories (kinship, purity, rank) without explicit legal sanction.

concepts.name: Ritual Purification
concepts.domain: purity system / restoration of ritual status
concepts.summary_verbatim: Ritual purification is the ritual prescribed by a religion by which a person is considered to be free of uncleanliness.
mechanism_atoms: Purification operates on a pollution/cleanness binary: contact with polluting agents (corpses, blood, forbidden substances) creates ritual impurity that must be actively removed.
The mechanism typically involves physical washing with water (ablution), fire, or other purifying agents, combined with verbal formulae or prayer.
Islamic ritual purity distinguishes wudu (minor purification before prayer) from ghusl (major purification after specific states); the acts are codified sequences with defined ordering.
Jewish tumah and taharah system classifies sources of impurity hierarchically; immersion in a mikveh (ritual bath) is the standard restoration mechanism.
The system encodes a feedback loop: daily activities create pollution, purification restores access to sacred spaces and acts, structuring religious time around cycles of defilement and cleansing.

concepts.name: Meditation
concepts.summary_verbatim: Meditation is a practice in which an individual uses a technique or combination of techniques to train attention and awareness and detach from reflexive, 'discursive thinking', achieving a mentally clear and emotionally calm and stable state, while not judging the meditation process itself.
mechanism_atoms: The core mechanism is iterative attention regulation: the meditator directs attention to a chosen object (breath, mantra, sensation), notices when the mind wanders, and returns attention to the object.
Focused attention (samatha) and open monitoring (vipassana) are the two primary structural modes: the former narrows attention, the latter expands meta-awareness of all arising phenomena.
Repeated practice produces neurological change: research documents increased gray matter density in prefrontal and insular cortices, and reduced amygdala reactivity to stressors.
Mantra-based meditation (Transcendental Meditation, japa) uses repetitive vocalization or subvocalization as an anchor, exploiting the interference properties of verbal working memory.
Contemplative traditions treat meditation as a technology for insight: sustained practice is held to reveal the constructed, impermanent nature of self, reducing attachment and suffering.

concepts.name: Apophatic Theology
concepts.summary_verbatim: Apophatic theology, also known as negative theology and the Via Negativa, is a form of theological thinking and religious practice which attempts to approach God, the Divine, by negation, to speak only in terms of what may not be said about God.
mechanism_atoms: The method proceeds by systematic negation: every positive attribute proposed for God (omniscient, powerful, good) is subsequently denied as inadequate to the divine essence.
Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite formalized the apophatic ladder: one ascends through affirmative theology (cataphatic), then through negation of all affirmations, to reach a silence beyond language.
The mechanism resolves the problem of divine predication: since God is held to transcend all categories, any positive statement necessarily imposes finite categories on the infinite.
The via negativa produces a residual 'knowledge by unknowing': the practitioner is left not with a positive concept of God but with an awareness of the limits of conceptualization itself.

Apophatic reasoning appears across traditions: Jewish Ein Sof, Islamic tanzih (incomparability), Hindu neti neti ('not this, not this'), and Christian mystical theology (Meister Eckhart, Cloud of Unknowing).

concepts.name: Ship of Theseus
concepts.summary_verbatim: The Ship of Theseus, also known as Theseus's Paradox, is a paradox and common thought experiment about whether an object (in the most common stating of the paradox, a ship) is the same object after having all of its original components replaced with others over time.
mechanism_atoms: The paradox exploits two plausible identity criteria that yield contradictory verdicts: continuity of form (the gradually-replaced ship is the same) vs. continuity of matter (the completely-replaced ship is not the same).
Hobbes added a second-ship variant: if the original planks are collected and reassembled, two ships now claim identity with the original—the paradox becomes a conflict between competing claimants.
The puzzle maps onto questions of personal identity: if the cells of a human body are continuously replaced, the criteria for numerical identity across time become unclear.

Endurantism holds that an object is wholly present at each moment and persists through change; perdurantism (four-dimensionalism) holds that objects are extended through time and 'ship at t1' and 'ship at t2' are distinct temporal parts of one four-dimensional entity.
The paradox reveals that ordinary sortal terms ('ship', 'person') are vague with respect to criteria of identity across change, generating genuine ontological underdetermination.

concepts.name: Sorites Paradox
concepts.summary_verbatim: The sorites paradox, sometimes known as the paradox of the heap, is a paradox that results from vague predicates.
mechanism_atoms: The paradox operates via a chain of seemingly valid inductive inferences: if 1,000,000 grains form a heap, and removing one grain from any heap leaves a heap, then 1 grain is a heap—contradiction.
The mechanism exploits tolerance: vague predicates (heap, bald, tall) seem to tolerate small differences, but tolerance plus transitivity yields absurd conclusions.

Proposed resolutions include: epistemicism (there is a sharp boundary, but we cannot know it); supervaluationism (borderline cases are neither true nor false); degree theories (predicates admit of degrees of truth).
The paradox applies to temporal, qualitative, and quantitative domains: 'when does a fetus become a person?', 'when does twilight become night?'—all involve sorites-susceptible predicates.
The paradox reveals a fundamental tension between classical logic's excluded middle and the phenomenological reality of gradual transitions in nature and language.

concepts.name: Theodicy
concepts.summary_verbatim: A theodicy (from Ancient Greek θεός theos, 'god' and δίκη dikē, 'justice'), meaning 'vindication of God', is an argument in the philosophy of religion that attempts to resolve the problem of evil, which arises when all power (omnipotence) and all goodness (omnibenevolence) are attributed to God simultaneously.
mechanism_atoms: The logical problem of evil (Mackie) takes the form of a trilemma: an omnipotent, omniscient, omnibenevolent God and evil cannot logically coexist.

The Free Will Defense (Alvin Plantinga) argues that God could not create free creatures who necessarily choose good: genuine freedom logically permits evil choices, making moral evil compatible with divine goodness.
Soul-making theodicy (Hick) holds that suffering is a necessary condition for the development of virtuous character; a paradise without challenge would prevent moral and spiritual growth.
The Greater Good argument claims that God permits specific evils because they are necessary conditions for goods that outweigh them; critics argue this permits monstrous means for abstract ends.
The distinction between moral evil (caused by free agents) and natural evil (disease, earthquakes) forces theodicists to provide separate accounts for each type.

concepts.name: Cosmogony
concepts.summary_verbatim: Cosmogony is any model concerning the origin of the cosmos or the universe.
mechanism_atoms: Cosmogonies can be classified by generative mechanism: creation ex nihilo (from nothing), emanation (from a primordial substance or being), cosmic egg, division of primal chaos, and combat myths (theomachies).
Creation ex nihilo, prominent in Abrahamic traditions, posits that the creator brought the cosmos into being without pre-existing material, establishing absolute ontological dependence.
Emanationist models (Neoplatonism, some Hindu and Gnostic systems) depict the universe as a hierarchical overflow from a transcendent One or Brahman, with no sharp creator/creation boundary.
Combat cosmogonies (Babylonian Enuma Elish, Norse Ymir myths) derive cosmic order from the violent dismemberment or defeat of a primordial being, whose body becomes the world.
Cosmogonic myths establish temporal and ontological precedence, functioning to legitimate social hierarchies, ritual orders, and cosmological classifications by grounding them in primordial acts.

concepts.name: Magical Thinking
concepts.summary_verbatim: Magical thinking or superstitious thinking is the belief that unrelated events are causally connected despite the absence of any plausible causal link between them, particularly as a result of supernatural effects.
mechanism_atoms: The mechanism involves false causal attribution: co-occurring events are perceived as causally linked due to temporal contiguity or symbolic resemblance, not mechanistic connection.

Frazer's Laws of Sympathetic Magic identify two sub-mechanisms: Homeopathy (like produces like; simulating an event causes it) and Contagion (objects once in contact continue to act on each other at a distance).
Unlike correlation-confusion (which requires statistical co-occurrence), magical thinking can operate with zero statistical relationship between events.
Developmental psychologists (Piaget) documented magical thinking as a normal cognitive stage in children; it persists in adults under uncertainty, stress, or high-stakes decision contexts.
Magical thinking underpins ritual efficacy beliefs: the practitioner believes that performing a ritual correctly causally produces the desired outcome through non-empirical channels.

concepts.name: Catharsis
concepts.summary_verbatim: Catharsis or katharsis is from the Ancient Greek word κάθαρσις, katharsis, meaning 'purification' or 'cleansing', commonly used to refer to the purification and purgation of thoughts and emotions by way of expressing them.
mechanism_atoms: Aristotle's Poetics describes catharsis as the effect of tragedy: witnessing pity and fear in dramatic form produces a discharge (purgation) of those emotions in the audience.
The mechanism is mimetic: the spectator vicariously experiences extreme emotions through fictional representation, achieving emotional release without real-world harm or cost.
Medical analogy: Aristotle drew a parallel to the effect of certain music and physical purgatives on the body—emotional excess is purged, restoring equilibrium.
Breuer and Freud adopted catharsis as a clinical concept: the abreaction of repressed traumatic memories was held to relieve hysterical symptoms by releasing pent-up affect.

The concept bridges religious and aesthetic domains: in Greek religion, cathartic rituals (katharmoi) physically purified individuals of blood-guilt or pollution, establishing a structural homology between dramatic and ritual purification.

concepts.name: Allegory
concepts.summary_verbatim: As a literary device or artistic form, an allegory is a narrative or visual representation in which a character, place, or event can be interpreted to represent a meaning with moral or political significance.
mechanism_atoms: Allegory operates through systematic two-level encoding: every narrative element has a surface (literal) meaning and a parallel deeper (allegorical) meaning, with the two levels running in structural correspondence.

Extended allegory sustains the correspondence across an entire work (e.g., Plato's Allegory of the Cave, Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress), requiring readers to decode each element within the key provided by the frame.

The mechanism enables the communication of dangerous or complex ideas under protective cover: political allegory (Animal Farm) and religious allegory (Dante's Commedia) use fiction as a vehicle for claims that direct statement would expose to censorship or incomprehension.
Allegorical reading (allegoresis) was applied retrospectively to texts not composed as allegory: Stoic philosophers allegorized Homeric myths as encoded cosmological truths.
The success of allegory depends on cultural competence: the reader must share enough context to recognize which elements are vehicles and what their tenors are, making allegory culturally indexed.

concepts.name: Anchoring effect
concepts.summary_verbatim: The anchoring effect is a cognitive bias that describes the common human tendency to rely too heavily on the first piece of information offered (the "anchor") when making decisions.
mechanism_atoms: An initial numerical or qualitative value becomes a reference point that disproportionately constrains subsequent judgements.
Adjustment away from the anchor is typically insufficient, leaving final estimates biased toward the starting value.
The anchor need not be relevant or accurate to exert influence; arbitrary external numbers still shift estimates.
Anchoring operates in negotiations, pricing, sentencing, and medical diagnosis, affecting expert and novice alike.
Awareness of the bias does not reliably neutralise its effect on judgment.

concepts.name: Prospect theory
concepts.summary_verbatim: Prospect theory is a theory of behavioral economics, judgment and decision making that was developed by Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky in 1979.
mechanism_atoms: People evaluate outcomes relative to a reference point (status quo) rather than in terms of final wealth states.
The value function is concave for gains (diminishing sensitivity) and convex for losses, producing risk-aversion for gains and risk-seeking for losses.
Losses loom larger than equivalent gains: the pain of losing $X exceeds the pleasure of gaining $X.
Small probabilities are overweighted and moderate-to-high probabilities are underweighted via a nonlinear probability weighting function.
The theory replaces expected utility with a descriptive model that better matches actual human choices under risk.

concepts.name: Homophily
concepts.summary_verbatim: Homophily is a concept in sociology describing the tendency of individuals to associate and bond with similar others, as in the proverb "birds of a feather flock together".
mechanism_atoms: Individuals preferentially form ties with others who share attributes such as age, ethnicity, education, or political preference.
Network ties that form on similarity are reinforced over time as shared norms and communication reduce friction.
Homophily restricts information flow between groups, creating echo chambers and limiting exposure to diverse perspectives.
In network science, homophily is measured as assortative mixing — the correlation between connected nodes on an attribute.
Over 100 studies have confirmed homophily as a structural feature across social network types.

concepts.name: Diffusion of innovations
concepts.summary_verbatim: Diffusion of innovations is a theory that seeks to explain how, why, and at what rate new ideas and technology spread.
mechanism_atoms: Adopters are classified into five categories — innovators, early adopters, early majority, late majority, laggards — based on timing of adoption.
Adoption follows an S-shaped cumulative curve as each cohort observes earlier adopters and reduces perceived uncertainty.
Key attributes that accelerate diffusion include relative advantage, compatibility, trialability, observability, and low complexity.
Opinion leaders in social networks act as relay points that translate innovation attributes to potential adopters.
The theory was systematised by Everett Rogers in his 1962 book and draws on studies across agriculture, medicine, and technology.

concepts.name: Bystander effect
concepts.summary_verbatim: The bystander effect (also called bystander apathy or the Genovese effect) is a social psychological theory that states that individuals are less likely to offer help to a victim in the presence of other people.
mechanism_atoms: Diffusion of responsibility: each bystander assumes another person will intervene, reducing individual felt obligation.
Pluralistic ignorance: bystanders observe each other's inaction and infer the situation is not an emergency.
The probability of intervention decreases as group size increases, an inverse relationship documented experimentally.
Latane and Darley's 1969 experiments showed bystanders alone responded to emergencies 85% of the time versus 31% in groups of five.
Explicit role assignment or direct eye contact from the victim counteracts the effect by re-focusing individual responsibility.

concepts.name: Operant conditioning
concepts.summary_verbatim: Operant conditioning, also called instrumental conditioning, is a learning process in which voluntary behaviors are modified by association with the addition (or removal) of reward or aversive stimuli.
mechanism_atoms: A behavior followed by a reinforcing stimulus increases in frequency; a behavior followed by a punishing stimulus decreases in frequency.
Positive reinforcement adds a desirable stimulus; negative reinforcement removes an aversive one — both increase target behavior.
Schedules of reinforcement (fixed-ratio, variable-ratio, fixed-interval, variable-interval) produce characteristic patterns of response rates.
Variable-ratio schedules produce the highest and most persistent response rates because reinforcement timing is unpredictable.
B. F. Skinner formalised operant conditioning using the Skinner box, demonstrating control over voluntary behavior through environmental contingencies.

concepts.name: Cognitive dissonance
concepts.summary_verbatim: In psychology, cognitive dissonance is the mental stress or discomfort experienced by an individual who holds two or more contradictory beliefs, ideas, or values at the same time, or is confronted by new information that conflicts with existing beliefs, ideas, or values.
mechanism_atoms: Dissonance is proportional to the importance of the conflicting cognitions and the degree of their incompatibility.
To reduce dissonance, individuals change one belief, add consonant cognitions that outweigh the dissonant ones, or reduce the importance of the conflict.
Post-decision dissonance leads people to revalue chosen options upward and rejected options downward to justify their choice.
Festinger's 1957 theory and the $1/$20 experiment showed that small external justification for counter-attitudinal behavior produces greater attitude change than large justification.
Self-perception and self-affirmation are alternative mechanisms that can bypass or attenuate dissonance reduction.

concepts.name: Stare decisis
concepts.summary_verbatim: Stare decisis is the doctrine that courts will adhere to precedent in making their decisions.
mechanism_atoms: Once a court of competent jurisdiction has ruled on a legal question, that ruling binds lower courts in the same jurisdiction on the same issue.
Vertical stare decisis requires lower courts to follow higher courts; horizontal stare decisis involves courts following their own prior decisions.
Predictability and consistency are the primary rationales: litigants can plan conduct based on settled law.
Courts can distinguish precedents (showing the current case differs on material facts) or overrule them when previous decisions are clearly wrong or outdated.
The doctrine creates a feedback loop where past legal reasoning accumulates, constraining future judicial discretion.

concepts.name: Burden of proof (law)
concepts.summary_verbatim: The burden of proof is the obligation on a party in a dispute to provide sufficient warrant for its position.
mechanism_atoms: The burden of production requires a party to present enough evidence to put a factual issue before the trier of fact.
The burden of persuasion requires convincing the fact-finder to the requisite standard: 'beyond reasonable doubt' in criminal cases, 'balance of probabilities' in civil cases.
Allocation of the burden determines who loses if the evidence is in equipoise at the close of trial.
In criminal law, the presumption of innocence shifts the full persuasion burden to the prosecution.
Some affirmative defenses shift a tactical or persuasion burden to the defendant once raised.

concepts.name: Adverse selection
concepts.summary_verbatim: In economics, insurance, and risk management, adverse selection is a market situation where asymmetric information results in a party taking advantage of undisclosed information to benefit more from a contract or trade.
mechanism_atoms: The better-informed party (seller of risk or quality) can exploit the less-informed party's inability to distinguish types.
Buyers anticipate adverse selection and lower their willingness to pay, driving high-quality sellers out of the market — Akerlof's 'market for lemons' dynamic.
As market quality falls, more high-quality sellers exit, further depressing offered prices in a deteriorating feedback spiral.
Countermeasures include signalling (credible self-disclosure by the informed party) and screening (mechanisms by the uninformed party to elicit private information).
In insurance, adverse selection occurs when the highest-risk individuals disproportionately purchase coverage, raising average costs and premiums.

concepts.name: Signalling (economics)
concepts.summary_verbatim: In contract theory, signalling is the idea that one party (the agent) credibly conveys some information about itself to another party (the principal).
mechanism_atoms: A signal is credible only if it is too costly for low-quality types to mimic, creating a separating equilibrium.
In Spence's education signalling model, education certifies productivity not primarily by imparting skills but by being cheaper for high-ability workers to obtain.
Pooling equilibria occur when both types send the same signal and cannot be distinguished; separating equilibria reveal private information.
Effective signals must satisfy the single-crossing condition: the cost of the signal must differ between types in a way that makes mimicry unprofitable.
Signalling theory applies to warranties, advertising spending, and conspicuous consumption as credibility mechanisms.

concepts.name: Gift economy
concepts.summary_verbatim: A gift economy or gift culture is a system of exchange where valuables are not sold, but rather given without an explicit agreement for immediate or future rewards.
mechanism_atoms: Gifts create social obligations in the recipient, generating diffuse reciprocity that maintains relationships over time rather than clearing debts immediately.
Social norms rather than formal contracts govern giving, embedding exchange in kinship, status, and ritual networks.
Marcel Mauss's 'The Gift' (1925) argued that gifts are never entirely free — they carry obligations to give, receive, and reciprocate.
The Kula ring documented by Malinowski shows gift circulation of shell armbands and necklaces building prestige and alliances across Trobriand Islands.
Failure to give, receive, or reciprocate violates social obligations and can produce loss of status or social exclusion.

concepts.name: Price discovery
concepts.summary_verbatim: In economics and finance, price discovery (also called price discovery mechanism) is the process of determining the price of an asset in the marketplace through the interactions of buyers and sellers.
mechanism_atoms: Buyers and sellers submit bids and offers, and their intersection at a clearing price reveals the market consensus value of an asset.
Futures markets often lead spot markets in price discovery because futures attract informed traders seeking leverage and liquidity.
Continuous double-auction mechanisms aggregate dispersed private information held by many traders into a single publicly observable price.
Order books make the marginal valuations of limit-order traders transparent, improving price accuracy as depth increases.
Price discovery is disrupted by thin markets, circuit breakers, or information asymmetries that prevent orders from reflecting true valuations.

concepts.name: Arbitrage
concepts.summary_verbatim: In economics and finance, arbitrage is the practice of taking advantage of a difference in prices in two or more markets — striking a combination of matching deals to capitalise on the difference, the profit being the difference between the market prices at which the unit is traded.
mechanism_atoms: Arbitrage exploits price discrepancies for identical or equivalent assets across different markets or time frames.
Transactions must occur simultaneously (or near-simultaneously) to eliminate exposure to market risk.
Arbitrageurs' buying in the cheaper market and selling in the dearer market pushes prices toward equality, enforcing the law of one price.
In practice, transaction costs, capital constraints, and execution risk limit the ability to fully exploit mispricings.
Statistical arbitrage extends the concept to portfolios whose prices are historically correlated but temporarily divergent.

concepts.name: Condorcet paradox
concepts.summary_verbatim: In social choice theory, Condorcet's voting paradox is a fundamental discovery by the Marquis de Condorcet that majority rule is inherently self-contradictory.
mechanism_atoms: When voters have transitive individual preferences, collective majority preferences can be intransitive (cyclic): A beats B, B beats C, but C beats A.
The paradox arises because aggregating multiple consistent individual preference orderings does not guarantee a consistent collective ordering.
Cyclic majorities mean no Condorcet winner exists — no option that beats all others head-to-head — making majority rule indeterminate.
Agenda manipulation becomes possible: whoever controls the order of pairwise votes can engineer any preferred outcome.
The paradox motivated Arrow's impossibility theorem, showing the problem is general to all aggregation rules satisfying minimal fairness criteria.

concepts.name: Arrow's impossibility theorem
concepts.summary_verbatim: Arrow's impossibility theorem is a key result in social choice theory, proved by American economist Kenneth Arrow, showing that no procedure for group decision-making under ordinal utilities can satisfy the requirements of rational choice theory.
mechanism_atoms: Arrow specified five minimal conditions: universality, non-dictatorship, Pareto efficiency, independence of irrelevant alternatives, and transitivity of collective ranking.
The theorem proves that no voting rule can simultaneously satisfy all five conditions when there are three or more alternatives.
Independence of irrelevant alternatives (IIA) is the most restrictive condition: adding or removing a losing option must not change the relative ranking of remaining options.
The only aggregation rule satisfying all conditions except non-dictatorship is a dictatorship — one voter's preference determines the social ranking.
The result implies any real-world voting system must sacrifice at least one of Arrow's desiderata, generating persistent fairness trade-offs.

concepts.name: Moral hazard
concepts.summary_verbatim: In economics, a moral hazard is a situation where an economic actor has an incentive to increase its exposure to risk because it will not bear the full costs associated with that risk.
mechanism_atoms: When one party is insured or shielded from consequences, they take more risk than they would if fully exposed to costs.
Post-contractual moral hazard arises after an insurance or employment contract is signed when effort or behavior becomes unobservable.
Hidden action (unobservable effort) by the agent is the classic form; hidden information (private knowledge) is a related but distinct problem.
Deductibles, co-pays, and performance-based compensation are institutional countermeasures that re-expose agents to partial consequences.
In financial markets, 'too big to fail' expectations create systemic moral hazard by implying government bailouts for catastrophic risk-taking.

concepts.name: Principal-agent problem
concepts.summary_verbatim: The principal–agent problem (often abbreviated agency problem) refers to the conflict in interests and priorities that arises when one person or entity (the "agent") takes actions on behalf of another person or entity (the "principal").
mechanism_atoms: Agents possess private information about their actions or type that principals cannot observe without cost.
Divergent incentives arise when agents benefit from effort-minimisation while principals benefit from effort-maximisation.
Contract design attempts to align incentives through performance-linked pay, equity stakes, or output-based bonuses.
Monitoring reduces the information gap but imposes its own costs; residual information asymmetry is rarely eliminated.
Agency costs — comprising monitoring costs, bonding costs, and residual loss — measure the efficiency loss from imperfect incentive alignment.

concepts.name: Loss aversion
concepts.summary_verbatim: In cognitive science and behavioral economics, loss aversion is a cognitive bias in which the same situation is perceived as worse if it is framed as a loss, rather than a gain.
mechanism_atoms: The subjective disutility of losing $X is approximately twice the subjective utility of gaining $X — an asymmetry documented across many studies.
Loss aversion is embedded in prospect theory's S-shaped value function: the slope is steeper below the reference point than above it.
It produces the endowment effect: people demand more to give up an owned object than they would pay to acquire it.
In markets, loss aversion contributes to the equity premium puzzle and disposition effect (holding losing stocks too long, selling winners too soon).
Reference point dependence means loss aversion can be strategically manipulated by framing choices as avoiding losses rather than achieving gains.

concepts.name: Information cascade
concepts.summary_verbatim: An information cascade or informational cascade is a phenomenon described in behavioral economics and network theory in which a number of people make the same decision in a sequential fashion.
mechanism_atoms: Each decision-maker observes the choices of predecessors but not their private information, so early actions carry disproportionate weight.
Once public information (visible actions) outweighs private signals, rational agents ignore their own signal and copy the majority — the cascade begins.
Cascades are fragile: a small shock revealing private information can reverse mass behaviour because the cascade rested on thin informational foundations.
Cascades explain bank runs, fashion trends, technology adoption lock-in, and speculative bubbles as equilibria of rational sequential updating.
The mechanism was formally modelled by Bikhchandani, Hirshleifer, and Welch (1992), showing cascades can persist despite all agents acting rationally.

concepts.name: Adversarial system
concepts.summary_verbatim: The adversarial system is the two-sided structure under which criminal trial courts operate, putting the prosecution against the defense.
mechanism_atoms: Each side — prosecution and defence — presents the strongest possible case for its position before a neutral decision-maker.
The assumption is that truth is most likely to emerge from vigorous partisan competition rather than from neutral inquiry.
A passive judge or jury evaluates competing evidence rather than investigating independently, separating fact-finding from advocacy.
Rules of evidence (hearsay, relevance, privilege) channel what information each side may introduce, balancing fairness against truth-seeking.
The system contrasts with the inquisitorial model where a judge actively investigates and questions witnesses.

concepts.name: Social loafing
concepts.summary_verbatim: In social psychology, social loafing is the phenomenon of a person exerting less effort to achieve a goal when they work in a group than when working alone.
mechanism_atoms: Individual contributions become unidentifiable in a group output, reducing accountability and motivation.
Free-riding on others' efforts is individually rational but collectively suboptimal, reproducing the logic of a public goods dilemma.
The Ringelmann effect showed rope-pulling effort per person declined as group size increased, establishing the empirical baseline.
Loafing is attenuated when individual outputs are identifiable, the task is meaningful, or group cohesion is high.
Sucker effect: if some members believe others are loafing, they reduce effort themselves to avoid being exploited, compounding the problem.

concepts.name: Groupthink
concepts.summary_verbatim: Groupthink is a psychological phenomenon that occurs within a group of people in which the desire for harmony or conformity in the group results in an irrational or dysfunctional decision-making outcome.
mechanism_atoms: High group cohesion suppresses dissent as members self-censor to maintain in-group harmony and avoid social rejection.
Illusion of unanimity develops when silence is interpreted as agreement, masking actual disagreement.
Groups appoint unofficial 'mind guards' who shield the group from contradictory information reaching the consensus.
Symptoms include overconfidence, stereotyping of out-groups, and collective rationalisation of poor decisions already made.
Antidotes include appointing a formal devil's advocate, inviting external critique, and leader impartiality during deliberation.

concepts.name: Social capital
concepts.summary_verbatim: Social capital is a concept used in sociology and economics to define networks of relationships which are productive towards advancing the goals of individuals and groups.
mechanism_atoms: Dense networks with strong ties (bonding social capital) facilitate trust, mutual support, and enforcement of norms within a group.
Bridging social capital — weak ties linking different groups — provides access to novel information and resources unavailable within any single network.
Putnam's research linked civic participation and institutional trust to economic performance and governance quality at regional level.
Social capital can be depleted by opportunism and free-riding; it is sustained by repeated interaction, transparency, and shared norms.
Unlike financial capital, social capital is a relational property — it resides in connections between actors, not within individual actors alone.

concepts.name: Rational ignorance
concepts.summary_verbatim: Rational ignorance is refraining from acquiring knowledge when the supposed cost of educating oneself on an issue exceeds the expected potential benefit that the knowledge would provide.
mechanism_atoms: For any individual voter, the probability of casting the decisive vote is near zero, making the expected return from costly political research negligible.
It is individually rational to remain uninformed about policy even when the collective welfare loss from widespread ignorance is large.
Rational ignorance explains low voter turnout, susceptibility to political advertising, and delegation of opinion formation to trusted proxies.
The theory, developed by Anthony Downs, predicts systematic voter ignorance in large democracies as an equilibrium outcome.
Special-interest groups can exploit rational ignorance by lobbying for concentrated benefits while diffuse costs remain unnoticed by the unaware majority.

concepts.name: Free-rider problem
concepts.summary_verbatim: In economics, the free-rider problem is a type of market failure that occurs when those who benefit from resources, public goods and common pool resources do not pay for them or under-pay.
mechanism_atoms: Public goods are non-excludable and non-rivalrous, so consumption cannot be restricted to paying contributors, eliminating the price signal.
Individually rational actors withhold voluntary contributions expecting others to fund the good, leading to underprovision.
The game-theoretic structure mirrors the prisoner's dilemma: each actor prefers others contribute while they free-ride, but universal free-riding leaves all worse off.
Government taxation and mandatory contribution schemes are the canonical solution because they remove the voluntariness that enables free-riding.
Smaller, more homogeneous groups with repeated interaction and social monitoring can sustain voluntary provision through reputational incentives.

concepts.name: Endowment effect
concepts.summary_verbatim: In psychology and behavioral economics, the endowment effect, also known as divestiture aversion, is the finding that people are more likely to retain an object they own than acquire that same object when they do not own it.
mechanism_atoms: Ownership shifts the reference point so that giving up an item is framed as a loss, which loss aversion makes feel more costly than the equivalent gain from acquisition.
Willingness-to-accept (WTA) prices from owners systematically exceed willingness-to-pay (WTP) prices from non-owners for identical goods.
Thaler's mug experiments demonstrated the effect in controlled settings, with owners requiring roughly twice as much to sell as buyers would pay.
The effect challenges the Coase theorem's assumption that initial allocation is irrelevant to final distribution in the absence of transaction costs.
Mere token ownership or psychological identification with an object is sufficient to trigger the endowment effect, not just monetary investment.

concepts.name: Overton window
concepts.summary_verbatim: The Overton window frames the range of policies that a politician may recommend without appearing too extreme, in order to gain or keep public office given the climate of public opinion at that particular time.
mechanism_atoms: Policy ideas exist on a spectrum from unthinkable to policy, and only ideas within the window are politically viable at any given moment.
The window shifts over time as advocacy, events, or cultural change normalises previously radical positions.
Political actors strategically promote extreme positions to pull the window toward their preferred policy, making previously fringe ideas seem moderate.
Media framing and elite signalling are primary mechanisms for moving the window without changing underlying public opinion through direct persuasion.
Once a policy crosses into the window's range, politicians adopt it opportunistically regardless of their prior stated positions.

concepts.name: Confirmation bias
concepts.summary_verbatim: Confirmation bias is the tendency to search for, interpret, favor, and recall information in a way that confirms or supports one's prior beliefs or values.
mechanism_atoms: Selective exposure: individuals seek out sources and environments likely to confirm existing views while avoiding disconfirming evidence.
Selective interpretation: the same piece of ambiguous evidence is judged as supportive by believers and as counterevidence by disbelievers.
Selective recall: information consistent with prior beliefs is remembered more accurately and vividly than inconsistent information.
Wason's selection task experiments showed that people systematically test hypotheses by seeking confirming rather than falsifying cases.
Confirmation bias strengthens under high emotional investment in a belief, making correction especially difficult in politically charged domains.

concepts.name: Social proof
concepts.summary_verbatim: Social proof (or informational social influence) is a psychological and social phenomenon wherein people copy the actions of others in choosing how to behave in a given situation.
mechanism_atoms: In ambiguous situations, observing others' behavior serves as a heuristic for determining the correct or appropriate action.
The mechanism assumes that the crowd possesses collective knowledge unavailable to the individual observer.
Social proof scales with the number of people acting similarly: larger crowds are treated as stronger evidence of correct behavior.
Cialdini identified social proof as one of six core principles of influence, extensively studied in marketing, charity, and health behavior contexts.
Manufactured social proof (fake reviews, laugh tracks, inflated follower counts) exploits the heuristic to bypass critical evaluation.

concepts.name: Cheese affinage (ripeness judged by touch)
concepts.summary_verbatim: The skilled affineur will need to use their finely-tuned senses (alongside a grading iron) to ascertain the cheese's stage of maturity and make decisions as to whether the cheese is ready for market.
mechanism_atoms: An affineur decides when a wheel of cheese is at peak maturity by pressing it with the fingertips and using accumulated sensory instinct; there is no objective, non-destructive instrument that predicts optimal ripeness per-wheel, so timing-to-market is done by feel.
concepts.open_problem: An affineur decides when a wheel of cheese is at peak maturity by pressing it with the fingertips and using accumulated sensory instinct; there is no objective, non-destructive instrument that predicts optimal ripeness per-wheel, so timing-to-market is done by feel.

concepts.name: Koji (Aspergillus) cultivation timing by smell/feel
concepts.summary_verbatim: Sake craftspeople oversee the process to ensure the mould grows in optimal conditions by adjusting temperature and humidity, and their work determines the quality of the sake.
mechanism_atoms: Koji makers judge when mold growth on rice/beans is finished by looking at the mycelia and smelling/tasting for a fruity-floral note; this finicky tacit skill is passed hand-to-hand and has no reliable in-tray sensor for end-point detection.
concepts.open_problem: Koji makers judge when mold growth on rice/beans is finished by looking at the mycelia and smelling/tasting for a fruity-floral note; this finicky tacit skill is passed hand-to-hand and has no reliable in-tray sensor for end-point detection.

concepts.name: Soy sauce / miso moromi maturity assessment
concepts.summary_verbatim: there is currently a deficiency of an objective, fast, and intuitive evaluation method for maturity.
mechanism_atoms: Maturity of the moromi (fermenting mash) over 6-18+ months is still gauged by an experienced brewer's nose and eye; the literature itself notes the lack of any objective, fast, intuitive maturity metric.
concepts.open_problem: Maturity of the moromi (fermenting mash) over 6-18+ months is still gauged by an experienced brewer's nose and eye; the literature itself notes the lack of any objective, fast, intuitive maturity metric.

concepts.name: Dry-cured ham testing by the 'cala' (bone-needle smell test)
concepts.summary_verbatim: The 'cala' is a very complex process and it is necessary to have an excellent and highly developed sense of smell developed through experience.
mechanism_atoms: Whether a 24-36 month jamon is correctly cured is verified by a 'calador' who pierces the ham at four points with a bone spike and judges the released aroma; the entire quality gate depends on one expert's trained sense of smell with no instrument substitute.
concepts.open_problem: Whether a 24-36 month jamon is correctly cured is verified by a 'calador' who pierces the ham at four points with a bone spike and judges the released aroma; the entire quality gate depends on one expert's trained sense of smell with no instrument substitute.

concepts.name: Sourdough bulk-fermentation / proof end-point ('poke test')
concepts.summary_verbatim: Use time as a guideline, but let the dough tell you when it's ready.
mechanism_atoms: Bakers ignore the clock and decide dough is proofed by how it looks and springs back to a finger poke; end-point depends on temperature and starter vigor and is learned by watching the dough, with no consumer-accessible objective readiness signal.
concepts.open_problem: Bakers ignore the clock and decide dough is proofed by how it looks and springs back to a finger poke; end-point depends on temperature and starter vigor and is learned by watching the dough, with no consumer-accessible objective readiness signal.

concepts.name: Wine harvest timing (post-veraison ripeness call)
concepts.summary_verbatim: harvest typically follows 30 to 70 days after véraison, depending on variety, climate, and the winemaker's stylistic goals.
mechanism_atoms: The pick date 30-70 days after veraison is a judgment blending lab Brix/pH with tasting seeds and skins; picking a day early or late shifts the wine, and the final call remains a stylistic sensory decision.
concepts.open_problem: The pick date 30-70 days after veraison is a judgment blending lab Brix/pH with tasting seeds and skins; picking a day early or late shifts the wine, and the final call remains a stylistic sensory decision.

concepts.name: Traditional balsamic vinegar barrel maturation
concepts.summary_verbatim: As master tasters know well, each balsamic vinegar is unique and releases an inimitable range of flavours and aromatic notes.
mechanism_atoms: Over 12-25 years of annual barrel transfers in an acetaia, the maestro decides which barrel/vintage is ready purely by tasting; each acetaia's progression is idiosyncratic and assessment is by master palate, not measurement.
concepts.open_problem: Over 12-25 years of annual barrel transfers in an acetaia, the maestro decides which barrel/vintage is ready purely by tasting; each acetaia's progression is idiosyncratic and assessment is by master palate, not measurement.

concepts.name: Blacksmithing / forge welding heat judged by color
concepts.summary_verbatim: The exact temperature is almost always judged by eye and learned by experience on your set of equipment.
mechanism_atoms: Smiths bring steel to forge-welding heat by reading the incandescent color of the metal by eye; the exact temperature is judged visually and learned per-forge, complicated by ambient light, with no affordable real-time guidance.
concepts.open_problem: Smiths bring steel to forge-welding heat by reading the incandescent color of the metal by eye; the exact temperature is judged visually and learned per-forge, complicated by ambient light, with no affordable real-time guidance.

concepts.name: Pottery kiln firing without instruments
concepts.summary_verbatim: Without pyrometers or electric kilns, traditional potters relied on the color of the flames, the glowing embers, and the appearance of the pots themselves to gauge temperature, duration, and atmosphere parameters.
mechanism_atoms: Traditional potters control temperature, soak time and oxidation/reduction atmosphere by reading flame color, ember glow and the look of the pots; this is instinctive expert knowledge with no low-cost sensing of in-kiln atmosphere/temperature for the artisan.
concepts.open_problem: Traditional potters control temperature, soak time and oxidation/reduction atmosphere by reading flame color, ember glow and the look of the pots; this is instinctive expert knowledge with no low-cost sensing of in-kiln atmosphere/temperature for the artisan.

concepts.name: Glassblowing (working glass at the right viscosity by eye)
concepts.summary_verbatim: The working temperature is reduced in the furnace to around 1,090 °C (2,000 °F), at which stage the glass appears to be a bright orange color.
mechanism_atoms: A gaffer keeps molten glass in the narrow workable viscosity band by reading its color (e.g. bright orange near 1090 C) and feel, knowing when to reheat; it is kinesthetic memory built over years with no instrument feeding the working state in real time.
concepts.open_problem: A gaffer keeps molten glass in the narrow workable viscosity band by reading its color (e.g. bright orange near 1090 C) and feel, knowing when to reheat; it is kinesthetic memory built over years with no instrument feeding the working state in real time.

concepts.name: Handloom weaving warp-tension management by feel
concepts.summary_verbatim: Traditional shuttle looms depend entirely on human judgment, and they require a weaver who can feel the tension, read the cloth, and respond to the material as it behaves under their hands.
mechanism_atoms: On traditional shuttle looms the weaver continuously feels warp tension, reads the cloth and adjusts by hand for hours; even tension across hundreds of threads is maintained purely by tactile judgment with no assistive feedback.
concepts.open_problem: On traditional shuttle looms the weaver continuously feels warp tension, reads the cloth and adjusts by hand for hours; even tension across hundreds of threads is maintained purely by tactile judgment with no assistive feedback.

concepts.name: Dry stone walling (stone selection and fit by eye)
concepts.summary_verbatim: Dry stone walling is so durable because it contains no mortar to crack and fail, but is held together merely by the weight of stone, and by the skill of the builder who selected and fitted the stones together.
mechanism_atoms: A mortarless wall stands only by gravity, friction and the waller's eye for which irregular stone to place where; certification is a timed hands-on rebuild, and stone selection/placement is an un-tooled spatial-reasoning skill judged by experts.
concepts.open_problem: A mortarless wall stands only by gravity, friction and the waller's eye for which irregular stone to place where; certification is a timed hands-on rebuild, and stone selection/placement is an un-tooled spatial-reasoning skill judged by experts.

concepts.name: Japanese kumiko / nail-free joinery fitting
concepts.summary_verbatim: Thinly-slit wooden pieces are grooved, punched, and mortised, and then fitted individually using a plane, saw, chisel, and other tools to make fine-adjustments.
mechanism_atoms: Kumiko pieces hold together by pressure alone, requiring each thin slat to be planed, sawn and chiseled to a hand-fitted tolerance; achieving the exact interference fit is a by-hand fine-adjustment skill with no digital aid for the artisan.
concepts.open_problem: Kumiko pieces hold together by pressure alone, requiring each thin slat to be planed, sawn and chiseled to a hand-fitted tolerance; achieving the exact interference fit is a by-hand fine-adjustment skill with no digital aid for the artisan.

concepts.name: Vegetable tanning of leather (recipe and feel by master tanner)
concepts.summary_verbatim: The master tanner creates the ideal blend keeping in mind the result he wants to achieve in terms of softness, strength, colour and touch feeling.
mechanism_atoms: A master tanner sets tannin sources, concentrations, temperatures and weeks-to-months timings by judgment to hit a target softness/strength/touch; recipes are secret, hide-by-hide, and tuned by feel rather than by a predictive model.
concepts.open_problem: A master tanner sets tannin sources, concentrations, temperatures and weeks-to-months timings by judgment to hit a target softness/strength/touch; recipes are secret, hide-by-hide, and tuned by feel rather than by a predictive model.

concepts.name: Apiculture queen detection / hive inspection
concepts.summary_verbatim: Manual inspections are laborious and disruptive, motivating the need for automated, non-invasive detection methods.
mechanism_atoms: Beekeepers must manually open hives and inspect frames to confirm the queen is present and laying; her loss can collapse a colony, but inspection is intrusive, time-consuming, weather-limited, and depends on the beekeeper's eye for spotting a single bee or fresh eggs among thousands.
concepts.open_problem: Beekeepers must manually open hives and inspect frames to confirm the queen is present and laying; her loss can collapse a colony, but inspection is intrusive, time-consuming, weather-limited, and depends on the beekeeper's eye for spotting a single bee or fresh eggs among thousands.

concepts.name: Varroa mite monitoring (alcohol wash / sugar roll)
concepts.summary_verbatim: The powdered sugar roll is currently the most common and quickest tool to monitor mites.
mechanism_atoms: To decide whether to treat for varroa, beekeepers take a ~300-bee sample, dislodge mites with alcohol or powdered sugar, and count mites by hand against seasonal thresholds; counting is tedious, error-prone, kills the sample (alcohol), and is done by feel/eye rather than any automated sensor.
concepts.open_problem: To decide whether to treat for varroa, beekeepers take a ~300-bee sample, dislodge mites with alcohol or powdered sugar, and count mites by hand against seasonal thresholds; counting is tedious, error-prone, kills the sample (alcohol), and is done by feel/eye rather than any automated sensor.

concepts.name: Sericulture cocoon grading and silk reeling
concepts.summary_verbatim: Because an emerging moth would break the cocoon filament, the larva is killed in the cocoon by steam or hot air at the chrysalis stage.
mechanism_atoms: Silk quality depends on grading cocoons and reeling filament from them, traditionally judged by experienced workers by eye/feel (shell ratio, defects, seasonal quality); the larva must be killed at the chrysalis stage before the moth breaks the filament, and grading remains a hands-on craft.
concepts.open_problem: Silk quality depends on grading cocoons and reeling filament from them, traditionally judged by experienced workers by eye/feel (shell ratio, defects, seasonal quality); the larva must be killed at the chrysalis stage before the moth breaks the filament, and grading remains a hands-on craft.

concepts.name: Orphan / underutilized crop breeding
concepts.summary_verbatim: Orphan crops are also known as underutilized crops, neglected crops or crops for the future, named for the lack of genetic improvement, not for lack of use or incorporation into cultural diets.
mechanism_atoms: Neglected crops vital to smallholders (e.g. fonio, bambara groundnut, teff) have almost no genomic or breeding resources and little institutional data; improvement is done with minimal investment and lost institutional memory, far behind wheat/rice/maize.
concepts.open_problem: Neglected crops vital to smallholders (e.g. fonio, bambara groundnut, teff) have almost no genomic or breeding resources and little institutional data; improvement is done with minimal investment and lost institutional memory, far behind wheat/rice/maize.

concepts.name: Agroforestry / alley cropping design
concepts.summary_verbatim: As trees and shrubs grow, they influence light, water and nutrient regimes in the field, and these interactions are what sets alley cropping apart from more common monocropping systems.
mechanism_atoms: Designing tree-crop alley systems requires predicting decades of light/water/nutrient competition between rows of trees and alley crops, but interactions are poorly characterized and the long time horizon means design is largely by rule-of-thumb and farmer judgment.
concepts.open_problem: Designing tree-crop alley systems requires predicting decades of light/water/nutrient competition between rows of trees and alley crops, but interactions are poorly characterized and the long time horizon means design is largely by rule-of-thumb and farmer judgment.

concepts.name: Seed saving: roguing and isolation
concepts.summary_verbatim: Roguing is the process of removing weak or "off-type" plants before they spread their pollen.
mechanism_atoms: Keeping a landrace/heirloom variety true-to-type requires the saver to recognize and remove off-type plants (roguing) before pollination and to maintain isolation distances; this is judgment-by-eye over whole populations with essentially no decision-support tooling.
concepts.open_problem: Keeping a landrace/heirloom variety true-to-type requires the saver to recognize and remove off-type plants (roguing) before pollination and to maintain isolation distances; this is judgment-by-eye over whole populations with essentially no decision-support tooling.

concepts.name: Soil judging / field texture-by-feel
concepts.summary_verbatim: In the field, it is necessary to estimate the soil texture by feeling it with the fingers, a skill that can be developed with practice and will be used in contests.
mechanism_atoms: Classifying a soil in the field (texture, clay/sand percentage, horizons) is done by hand-feel ribboning and color books in a pit, a tacit skill built by practice; there is no portable instrument that replaces the trained fingers used in soil/land judging.
concepts.open_problem: Classifying a soil in the field (texture, clay/sand percentage, horizons) is done by hand-feel ribboning and color books in a pit, a tacit skill built by practice; there is no portable instrument that replaces the trained fingers used in soil/land judging.

concepts.name: Polynesian wayfinding (star compass & wave piloting)
concepts.summary_verbatim: The star compass is a mental construct and not physical like a western compass.
mechanism_atoms: Traditional navigators cross open Pacific ocean with no instruments, holding course by a memorized 32-house star compass and reading swell patterns/refraction off islands entirely in the head; the knowledge is oral, hard to teach, and has no computational model.
concepts.open_problem: Traditional navigators cross open Pacific ocean with no instruments, holding course by a memorized 32-house star compass and reading swell patterns/refraction off islands entirely in the head; the knowledge is oral, hard to teach, and has no computational model.

concepts.name: Inuit snow/wind (sastrugi) wayfinding
concepts.summary_verbatim: The snowdrifts left by prevailing winds are the most reliable source of spatial orientation, and only the drifts left by prevailing winds can last throughout the winter.
mechanism_atoms: Arctic travelers orient in whiteouts and on featureless sea ice by reading wind-carved snow ridges (sastrugi), named prevailing winds, ice sounds, and animal cues; this is a multi-sensory tacit skill with no GPS-independent tooling that captures it.
concepts.open_problem: Arctic travelers orient in whiteouts and on featureless sea ice by reading wind-carved snow ridges (sastrugi), named prevailing winds, ice sounds, and animal cues; this is a multi-sensory tacit skill with no GPS-independent tooling that captures it.

concepts.name: Maritime pilotage (local-knowledge ship handling)
concepts.summary_verbatim: A maritime pilot is a mariner who has specific knowledge of an often dangerous or congested waterway, such as harbors or river mouths.
mechanism_atoms: Harbour/river pilots con large ships through dangerous waterways using visual references and intimate local knowledge of tides, currents, silting and shoals not shown on charts; this expertise is tacit, firsthand, and resists codification.
concepts.open_problem: Harbour/river pilots con large ships through dangerous waterways using visual references and intimate local knowledge of tides, currents, silting and shoals not shown on charts; this expertise is tacit, firsthand, and resists codification.

concepts.name: Orienteering route choice / map-terrain matching
concepts.summary_verbatim: A handrail is defined as a linear feature on a map that parallels your route and can be used as a quick aid to navigating yourself to the next control.
mechanism_atoms: Orienteers must continuously match a topographic map to terrain while moving at speed and choose among routes weighing distance, climb, vegetation and footing; route choice and proactive map-reading are cognitive skills with little algorithmic support for the runner.
concepts.open_problem: Orienteers must continuously match a topographic map to terrain while moving at speed and choose among routes weighing distance, climb, vegetation and footing; route choice and proactive map-reading are cognitive skills with little algorithmic support for the runner.

concepts.name: Cave navigation & survey (compass/clinometer/tape)
concepts.summary_verbatim: The DistoX2 unit is a beefed-up laser rangefinder used to measure the distance and direction between survey stations underground.
mechanism_atoms: Underground there is no GPS and no map until someone makes one; cavers find their way and build surveys leg-by-leg with magnetic compass, clinometer and tape, fighting magnetic interference, reading error and slowness, often relying on a guideline to find the way out.
concepts.open_problem: Underground there is no GPS and no map until someone makes one; cavers find their way and build surveys leg-by-leg with magnetic compass, clinometer and tape, fighting magnetic interference, reading error and slowness, often relying on a guideline to find the way out.

concepts.name: Desert wayfinding (Tuareg/Bedouin dune navigation)
concepts.summary_verbatim: While the wind in the desert is constantly changing the landscape, the big dune systems are moving very slowly, so they are more recognizable and can be used as landmarks.
mechanism_atoms: Desert nomads cross shifting sand seas by recognizing slow-moving dune systems, named dunes, rock formations, sun and stars, with routes and dune names taught orally; the landscape changes with wind and the skill lives only in inherited memory.
concepts.open_problem: Desert nomads cross shifting sand seas by recognizing slow-moving dune systems, named dunes, rock formations, sun and stars, with routes and dune names taught orally; the landscape changes with wind and the skill lives only in inherited memory.

concepts.name: Whistled language interpretation (Silbo Gomero)
concepts.summary_verbatim: Silbo replaces each vowel or consonant with a whistling sound.
mechanism_atoms: Whistled registers like Silbo Gomero compress a full spoken language into a tiny set of pitch/continuity contrasts (only ~2-4 whistled vowels and 4-10 consonants), and decoding them back into speech is done entirely by trained human ears in real time; there is no robust tool to transcribe or translate whistled speech, and the practice survives in only a handful of communities worldwide.
concepts.open_problem: Whistled registers like Silbo Gomero compress a full spoken language into a tiny set of pitch/continuity contrasts (only ~2-4 whistled vowels and 4-10 consonants), and decoding them back into speech is done entirely by trained human ears in real time; there is no robust tool to transcribe or translate whistled speech, and the practice survives in only a handful of communities worldwide.

concepts.name: Sign language transcription and glossing (no standard notation)
concepts.summary_verbatim: There is no commonly accepted transcription system for describing the form of signs.
mechanism_atoms: Signed languages have no commonly accepted written or transcription system, so linguists hand-gloss video utterance-by-utterance using ad hoc systems (Stokoe, HamNoSys, glosses); annotation is slow, inconsistent across labs, and there is no widely usable automatic notation/transcription pipeline for the spatial-simultaneous structure of signs.
concepts.open_problem: Signed languages have no commonly accepted written or transcription system, so linguists hand-gloss video utterance-by-utterance using ad hoc systems (Stokoe, HamNoSys, glosses); annotation is slow, inconsistent across labs, and there is no widely usable automatic notation/transcription pipeline for the spatial-simultaneous structure of signs.

concepts.name: Prosody and intonation labeling (ToBI)
concepts.summary_verbatim: A ToBI prosodic labeling of speech typically takes even experienced labelers from 100 to 200 times real time.
mechanism_atoms: Labeling the intonation/prosody of speech with the standard ToBI system is extraordinarily slow expert manual work (roughly 100-200x real time per minute of audio) and even trained labelers achieve only moderate inter-transcriber agreement, leaving most speech corpora unannotated for prosody.
concepts.open_problem: Labeling the intonation/prosody of speech with the standard ToBI system is extraordinarily slow expert manual work (roughly 100-200x real time per minute of audio) and even trained labelers achieve only moderate inter-transcriber agreement, leaving most speech corpora unannotated for prosody.

concepts.name: Tone-language transcription in phonetic fieldwork
concepts.summary_verbatim: Current phonetic fieldwork relies on manual effort, resulting in substantial time and financial costs, especially challenging for endangered languages that are rapidly disappearing with limited funding.
mechanism_atoms: Documenting the tone systems of under-described African and Asian languages relies on manually marking pitch height and contour (e.g. numeric 1-5 notation) by ear; transcribers need months of specialised training, the work is slow and costly, and it is racing against the rapid disappearance of endangered tone languages.
concepts.open_problem: Documenting the tone systems of under-described African and Asian languages relies on manually marking pitch height and contour (e.g. numeric 1-5 notation) by ear; transcribers need months of specialised training, the work is slow and costly, and it is racing against the rapid disappearance of endangered tone languages.

concepts.name: Dialectology fieldwork and linguistic-atlas compilation
concepts.summary_verbatim: The preparation and compilation of linguistic atlases is a difficult, costly, voluminous, and time-consuming job.
mechanism_atoms: Traditional dialect mapping still depends on painstaking in-person fieldwork (questionnaires, hand phonetic transcription, isogloss drawing) targeting specific NORM speakers; compiling a linguistic atlas is slow, expensive and labour-intensive, so most regions and dialect continua remain only partially surveyed.
concepts.open_problem: Traditional dialect mapping still depends on painstaking in-person fieldwork (questionnaires, hand phonetic transcription, isogloss drawing) targeting specific NORM speakers; compiling a linguistic atlas is slow, expensive and labour-intensive, so most regions and dialect continua remain only partially surveyed.

concepts.name: Cuneiform tablet reading backlog (Assyriology)
concepts.summary_verbatim: An estimated half a million tablets are held in museums across the world, but comparatively few of these are published.
mechanism_atoms: Of the hundreds of thousands of excavated cuneiform tablets, the large majority have never been read or published because transliteration requires years of training and only a few hundred qualified experts exist worldwide; the script has no word spacing and signs are polyvalent, making automated reading still nascent and unreliable.
concepts.open_problem: Of the hundreds of thousands of excavated cuneiform tablets, the large majority have never been read or published because transliteration requires years of training and only a few hundred qualified experts exist worldwide; the script has no word spacing and signs are polyvalent, making automated reading still nascent and unreliable.

concepts.name: Historical linguistic reconstruction via the comparative method
concepts.summary_verbatim: Reconstruction becomes unreliable beyond roughly 8,000 to 10,000 years, as sound changes accumulate to the point where cognates are no longer recognizable.
mechanism_atoms: Reconstructing proto-languages is done by hand: linguists identify cognate sets, line up sound correspondences, and propose proto-forms following phonetic rules; this is slow expert judgement work with little tooling, and it breaks down beyond ~8,000-10,000 years as cognates become unrecognisable.
concepts.open_problem: Reconstructing proto-languages is done by hand: linguists identify cognate sets, line up sound correspondences, and propose proto-forms following phonetic rules; this is slow expert judgement work with little tooling, and it breaks down beyond ~8,000-10,000 years as cognates become unrecognisable.

concepts.name: Snakebite responsible-species identification
concepts.summary_verbatim: In many cases of envenoming following snake bite, the snake responsible for the accident remains unidentified; this frequently results in difficulty deciding which antivenom to administer to the systemically-envenomed victim, especially when only monospecific antivenoms are available.
mechanism_atoms: Choosing the right antivenom depends on knowing which snake bit the patient, but the snake is rarely seen, victim descriptions are misleading, and frontline rural hospital staff are usually not trained to identify the biting species even when it is brought in dead - so antivenom choice is often guesswork in exactly the low-resource settings where snakebite kills most.
concepts.open_problem: Choosing the right antivenom depends on knowing which snake bit the patient, but the snake is rarely seen, victim descriptions are misleading, and frontline rural hospital staff are usually not trained to identify the biting species even when it is brought in dead - so antivenom choice is often guesswork in exactly the low-resource settings where snakebite kills most.

concepts.name: Chronic wound assessment (visual and manual measurement)
concepts.summary_verbatim: Wound assessment and measurement depend on visual examination, which can be highly subjective and dependent on the clinician's experience.
mechanism_atoms: Tracking whether a chronic wound is healing relies on a clinician's naked-eye judgement of size and tissue type plus manual ruler measurement; this is highly subjective, varies with the clinician's experience, and manual area estimates can deviate enormously (up to 40-75%) from true wound size, with poor inter-rater reliability.
concepts.open_problem: Tracking whether a chronic wound is healing relies on a clinician's naked-eye judgement of size and tissue type plus manual ruler measurement; this is highly subjective, varies with the clinician's experience, and manual area estimates can deviate enormously (up to 40-75%) from true wound size, with poor inter-rater reliability.

concepts.name: Ethnobotanical / traditional herbal medicine knowledge documentation
concepts.summary_verbatim: Most cultures possess a huge store of undocumented traditional knowledge of applying herbal remedies in the treatment of diseases.
mechanism_atoms: Vast bodies of traditional herbal-remedy knowledge held by healers are undocumented and passed only by word of mouth; with the spread of modern medicine this knowledge is being eroded and lost generation by generation, and capturing it depends on slow manual ethnobotanical surveys.
concepts.open_problem: Vast bodies of traditional herbal-remedy knowledge held by healers are undocumented and passed only by word of mouth; with the spread of modern medicine this knowledge is being eroded and lost generation by generation, and capturing it depends on slow manual ethnobotanical surveys.

concepts.name: Ethnoveterinary medicine documentation and dosing
concepts.summary_verbatim: Some farmers have failed to use ethnoveterinary medicine due to poor knowledge of application rates (dosage), inadequate diagnosis, lack of documentation and side effects of the concoctions.
